Question 1 · 10 marks

Q1. What are the articulating structures in the musculoskeletal system? Explain in detail about them.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit 1 — Basic Concepts of Musculoskeletal System (skeletal, articular, neuro-muscular systems)

★ Memory hook — Joint classification anchor: what tissue unites the bones? Fibrous (suture, syndesmosis) — cartilaginous (synchondrosis = hyaline, symphysis = disc) — synovial (cavity + cartilage + capsule). The intervertebral disc is a symphysis.

1Introduction

The musculoskeletal system is composed of articulations formed between bones, stabilised by connective tissue elements, and moved by the neuro-muscular unit. An articulation (joint) is defined as the site where two or more bones meet, whether movement occurs between them or not. Four families of structures participate in a joint: bone, cartilage, the fibrous capsule–ligament complex, and the muscular–tendinous unit, all supervised by the nervous system.

2Physiology

The adult skeleton has 206 bones, divided into the axial skeleton (80) and appendicular skeleton (126). Structurally: long, short, flat, irregular and sesamoid bones. A long bone bears an epiphysis covered by hyaline articular cartilage at each end, a metaphysis, and a diaphysis built of dense cortical bone enclosing medullary cavity.

  • Functions: protection, mineral (Ca²⁺, PO₄³⁻) reservoir, haemopoiesis, muscle attachment, and transmission of compressive forces — Wolff's law: bone remodels along lines of mechanical stress.
  • Composition: ~35% organic matrix (mainly type I collagen, osteoid) giving tensile strength, ~65% inorganic hydroxyapatite giving compressive rigidity.
  • Bone is vascular and innervated by periosteal nerves, so fracture pain is sharp and localised — unlike cartilage, which is aneural and avascular.
  • Hyaline (articular) cartilage — covers the weight-bearing ends of bones in synovial joints; type II collagen; avascular, aneural, alymphatic; nourished by synovial fluid diffusion and cyclic loading ("use it or lose it" of chondrocytes). Low friction (~0.01 coefficient) and load distribution.
  • Fibrocartilage — dense type I collagen; forms labra (glenoid, acetabular), menisci of the knee, intervertebral discs and articular discs (TMJ); resists compression and shear.
  • Elastic cartilage — with elastin; ear, epiglottis (relevant to general articulating structure knowledge).

3Pathophysiology

When these articulating structures fail, the same design features that make joints efficient also explain their vulnerability. Articular (hyaline) cartilage is avascular and aneural, so it cannot mount an inflammatory repair response and heals poorly — the basis of degenerative change in osteoarthritis. Bone, by contrast, is vascular and innervated, so fracture produces sharp, localised pain. Loss of the fibrous capsule–ligament complex (as in a ligament sprain) removes the mechanoreceptor-based reflex joint stabilisation and predisposes to instability and further wear. Fibrocartilaginous structures such as the menisci and the intervertebral disc (symphyses) are load-bearing and, once torn, alter joint mechanics and load sharing. This structure–function link is why physiotherapy targets the whole articulating unit — muscle control, joint mobility and load — rather than cartilage alone.

4Answer

1. Fibrous joints — bones united by fibrous tissue, minimal movement: sutures of the skull (synarthrosis), syndesmosis (inferior tibiofibular joint, interosseous membranes), and gomphosis (tooth in socket).

2. Cartilaginous joints — united by cartilage: synchondrosis (epiphyseal/growth plate, first costochondral — temporary, hyaline) and symphysis (pubic symphysis, intervertebral disc — permanent, fibrocartilage, slight movement).

3. Synovial (diarthrodial) joints — freely movable, the most important group clinically. By shape and axes:

TypeExampleAxes
Plane (gliding)Acromioclavicular, intercarpalNon-axial
HingeElbow (ulnohumeral), ankle, IP jointsUniaxial
PivotAtlanto-axial, superior radio-ulnarUniaxial (rotation)
Condyloid (ellipsoid)MCP, wristBiaxial
SaddleFirst CMC (thumb), sternoclavicularBiaxial
Ball-and-socketShoulder (glenohumeral), hipMultiaxial

  • Articular (hyaline) cartilage — 2–4 mm thick bearing surface.
  • Joint capsule — outer fibrous capsule (dense irregular CT) + inner synovial membrane which secretes synovial fluid (~1–3 mL in a knee), a dialysate of plasma plus hyaluronic acid; lubricates (boundary lubrication) and nourishes cartilage.
  • Ligaments — intrinsic thickenings of the capsule (e.g. glenohumeral ligaments) and extrinsic check-reins (e.g. coracohumeral); mainly type I collagen, mostly mechanoreceptors at insertions — the basis of reflex joint stabilisation.
  • Accessory structures — intra-articular fibrocartilaginous discs/menisci, labra that deepen sockets, bursae, and fat pads (Hoffa's) filling dead space.
Fig 1.1 — Typical synovial joint (sketch for your answer script). Draw this one; it earns the diagram credit.
Marks are lost when students write "206 bones and types of joints" as one blob. Keep the classification pyramid visible: fibrous → cartilaginous → synovial, then the six synovial subtypes WITH examples. Saying "hip is a hinge joint" in the table is an instant credibility loss — ball-and-socket.

5Recent advances

  • Bricca et al. (2019) — Systematic review of randomised trials in the British Journal of Sports Medicine showing that knee joint-loading exercise is not harmful to articular cartilage in people at risk of, or with, knee osteoarthritis, supporting therapeutic exercise as a joint-safe way to keep synovial joints healthy.
  • Tsokanos et al. (2021) — Systematic review of randomised trials showing that manual therapy (joint mobilisation and manipulation) produces short-term pain relief and improved knee range of motion and function in knee osteoarthritis, supporting hands-on mobilisation of the synovial joint.
  • Nigam et al. (2021) — Randomised trial showing that mobilisation with movement produces long-term (up to 6 months) improvement in pain and functional status in knee osteoarthritis, evidence that specific accessory joint mobilisation benefits the osteoarthritic joint.
  • Runge et al. (2022) — Systematic review with meta-analysis in the Journal of Orthopaedic and Sports Physical Therapy showing that adding manual therapy to exercise therapy improves pain and function in people with knee or hip osteoarthritis more than exercise alone.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT-MSK 2020 Ordinance & Syllabus, Paper II, Unit 1 (a–d) — Basic Concepts of Musculoskeletal System.
  2. Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins — chapters on the musculoskeletal system and joint biomechanics.
  3. Levangie PK, Norkin CC. Joint Structure and Function: A Comprehensive Analysis. F.A. Davis — chapter on joint structure and classification.
  4. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques. F.A. Davis — connective tissue and joint architecture sections.
  5. Lin W, Klein J. Recent progress in cartilage lubrication. Adv Mater / arXiv 2023 — hydration lubrication and boundary lubrication of articular cartilage.
  6. Rong M, et al. Research progress of cartilage lubrication and biomimetic cartilage lubrication materials. Front Bioeng Biotechnol. 2022;10:1012653.
Question 2 · 10 marks

Q2. How do you calculate BMI? Mention its application in degenerative conditions.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit 2 — Basic Concepts of Anthropometry (body size, body composition, human variation)

★ Memory hook — Asian-Indian cut-offs: BMI 23 overweight, 25 obese; waist ≥90 cm (men) / ≥80 cm (women) = abdominal obesity.

1Introduction

BMI (Body Mass Index, formerly Quetelet's index) is an anthropometric index of weight-for-height used to classify individuals into body-size categories. It is the ratio of body mass to the square of height:

BMI = weight (kg) / height² (m²)

Worked example (an Indian clinic patient): a 58-year-old woman weighing 68 kg with height 1.55 m → BMI = 68 / (1.55 × 1.55) = 68 / 2.40 = 28.3 kg/m² → Class I obesity by Indian criteria. Measurement technique: wall-mounted stadiometer, shoes off, weight on a calibrated balance in minimal clothing.

2Physiology

BMI rests on anthropometry — the measurement of body size, proportions and composition. Body weight is the sum of fat mass and lean (fat-free) mass; BMI uses weight-for-height as a practical surrogate for adiposity because, across a population, weight rises roughly with the square of height. Adipose tissue is not inert storage: it is metabolically active endocrine tissue, secreting adipokines (leptin, adiponectin) and pro-inflammatory cytokines. Energy balance — the relation between intake and expenditure, dosed in METs — determines whether weight is gained or lost and is the physiological lever behind every BMI-based intervention. Because BMI cannot separate fat from lean mass, it estimates rather than measures adiposity.

3Pathophysiology

  • Load on weight-bearing joints: each step transmits about 3–4 times body weight through the knee; every extra kilogram of fat multiplies tibiofemoral and patellofemoral load over thousands of steps per day → accelerated cartilage wear in knee osteoarthritis. Obesity is one of the strongest modifiable risk factors for knee OA, particularly in women.
  • Obesity–inflammation link: adipose tissue is metabolically active — adipokines (leptin, adiponectin imbalance) act as a systemic inflammatory drive that worsens synovitis and pain in OA and chronic low-back degeneration.
  • Prognosis and management triage: BMI decides whether arthroplasty risk counselling (wound healing, infection, anaesthetic risk) is needed, and gates conservative versus surgical planning.
  • Physiotherapy prescription: high BMI modifies exercise selection — non/low-weight-bearing aerobic work (cycling, aqua therapy) early, treadmill jogging later; it also re-baselines the MET targets for endurance dosing.
  • Outcome prediction: weight reduction of ~10% with exercise gives clinically meaningful functional improvement and pain relief in overweight/obese knee-OA patients (IDEA trial evidence classically quoted in Indian theses on tibiofemoral OA).
  • Low BMI in the elderly: flags sarcopenia and fall/fracture risk, poor bone stock (osteoporosis screening) and poor postural endurance — degeneration is not only an overweight story.

4Answer

BMI (kg/m²)WHO categoryAsian-Indian consensus*
< 18.5Underweight< 18.0 underweight
18.5–24.9Normal18.0–22.9 normal
25–29.9Overweight23–24.9 overweight
30–34.9Obese class I≥ 25 obese
35–39.9Obese class II—
≥ 40Obese class III—

*Indians develop metabolic risk at lower BMI ("thin-fat Indian phenotype"); Indian consensus thresholds are stricter than WHO global cutoffs.

Fig 2.1 — The formula, boxed the way I sketch it in correction margin notes. The cm-vs-m slip is the commonest arithmetic error I see.

BMI cannot distinguish fat mass from lean mass (a stocky athlete is "obese" by BMI), says nothing about fat distribution (waist circumference / waist-hip ratio should be added for metabolic risk), and is unreliable in pregnancy, oedema and amputees. Used together with waist circumference and body-composition methods, it remains the fastest screening anthropometric tool in an Indian outpatient department.

Always write the Indian cutoffs — RGUHS evaluators love the Asian-Indian consensus values (23/25) alongside WHO's 25/30. And do the arithmetic: I award the "worked example" mark only when a real patient's numbers appear.

5Recent advances

  • Messier et al. (2013) — IDEA randomised trial showing that combined diet plus exercise is the most effective weight-loss strategy for knee OA and that exercise is essential to preserve lean body mass and avoid sarcopenia.
  • Panunzi et al. (2021) — Network meta-analysis quantifying the dose-response: every 1% of body weight lost improves WOMAC pain, function and stiffness by about 2%, and roughly 25% weight loss is needed for a 50% reduction in pain.
  • Bannuru et al. (2019) — OARSI guidelines making arthritis education, structured land-based exercise and dietary weight management the core treatments, and stressing maintenance of lost weight rather than loss alone.
  • Messier et al. (2022) — WE-CAN randomised trial showing that a community diet-and-exercise programme lowered body weight by about 8% and produced a small but statistically significant reduction in knee pain in overweight adults with knee OA.
  • Messier et al. (2021) — START randomised trial finding that high-intensity strength training did not reduce knee pain or knee joint compressive forces more than low-intensity training, informing safe exercise dosing in obese knee OA.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT-MSK 2020 Ordinance & Syllabus, Paper II, Unit 2 — Basic Concepts of Anthropometry.
  2. American College of Sports Medicine. ACSM's Resource Manual for Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins — body composition and health status sections (syllabus reference 12).
  3. Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology. Elsevier — obesity, energy balance and metabolic chapters.
  4. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. F.A. Davis — assessment chapters (anthropometry in examination).
  5. Consensus Statement for Diagnosis of Obesity, Abdominal Obesity and the Metabolic Syndrome for Asian Indians and Recommendations for Physical Activity, Medical and Surgical Management (Misra A. et al., JAPI 2009) — Indian cutoffs.
  6. Panunzi S, et al. Comparative efficacy of different weight-loss treatments on knee osteoarthritis: a network meta-analysis. Obes Rev. 2021;22(8):e13230.
  7. Messier SP, et al. Intentional weight loss in overweight and obese patients with knee osteoarthritis: is more better? Arthritis Care Res. 2018;70(11):1569–1575.
Question 3 · 10 marks

Q3. Role of power and endurance in training.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit 5 — Physiological Basis of Human Movement (exercise metabolism, exercise capacity); Paper IV Unit 1 — impaired muscle performance

★ Memory hook — Power = strength × speed (force × velocity, in watts); endurance = strength sustained. Type I = endurance, IIx = power, IIa = the hybrid in between.

1Introduction

  • Strength — the ability of a muscle or muscle group to generate force against a resistance.
  • Power — the rate of doing work: Power = Work / Time = Force × Velocity (measured in watts). It has a force component AND a speed component — that is the whole secret of power training.
  • Endurance — the ability to sustain a physical activity (whole-body) or to perform repeated muscle contractions (muscle endurance) against a submaximal resistance for an extended time.
Fig 3.1 — Hill's force–velocity curve (blue) with the power curve (orange). Power peaks at roughly one-third of maximum shortening velocity — the reason a very heavy, very slow lift is NOT powerful.

2Physiology

Muscle fibres: type I (slow oxidative — fatigue-resistant, mitochondria-rich → endurance machinery), type IIa (fast oxidative-glycolytic — the hybrid, both force and endurance), type IIx (fast glycolytic — force and power, fatigable). Energy supply follows the task: ATP-PC (phosphagen) for seconds of explosive power, anaerobic glycolysis for ~2 minutes of high effort, and the oxidative (aerobic) system — the only sustainable one — for endurance. Motor-unit recruitment follows the size principle: small units first, large high-force units only when demand is high.

3Pathophysiology

When muscle performance fails, the same power–endurance continuum is lost in disease. Sarcopenia preferentially atrophies fast (type II) fibres and reduces power faster than maximal strength — a key reason older adults fall during rapid balance corrections rather than during slow effort. Disuse and immobilisation shrink the oxidative machinery (reduced mitochondria, capillaries and type I fibres), so endurance falls early and fatigue-related compensations appear (e.g., the knee-OA patient who vaults after 200 m, or the scapular stabilisers that fatigue and allow late rotator-cuff overload). Pain and effusion cause arthrogenous inhibition of large motor units, so the patient fatigues before the target repetition range. Rehabilitation must therefore rebuild both ends of the continuum — power for function, endurance to resist fatigue-driven decompensation.

4Answer

  • Functional demand is a power demand in real life — rising from a chair, stair ascent, a cricketer's bowling action, a sprinter's push-off. Loss of power (sarcopenia hits fast fibres hardest) explains why elderly patients fall during quick corrections of balance.
  • Training method: moderate loads moved as fast as possible (30–60% 1RM for upper body and 30–60% for lower-body ballistic work (ACSM)), plyometrics — stretch-shortening cycle drills (box jumps, medicine-ball throws).
  • Adaptations: improved rate of force development, motor-unit firing frequency and synchronisation, elastic-tendon stiffness, and inter-muscular coordination — largely neural.
  • Clinical application in MSK rehab: late-stage ACL/arthroplasty return-to-sport criteria include hop tests — pure strength clearance is not enough; power plus landing mechanics decide safe return.
  • Endurance is the platform for recovery and repeated function — the postural muscles (trunk stabilisers, soleus) are endurance organs by design.
  • Training method: low load, high repetitions (muscle endurance: > 12–15 reps at < 60% 1RM) and continuous aerobic exercise (whole-body endurance: walking/cycling ≥ 20–30 min, target ~60–80% HR reserve for 150 min/week, ACSM).
  • Adaptations: increased mitochondrial density, capillary density, myoglobin, oxidative enzyme activity, improved lactate clearance; central adaptations — increased stroke volume and VO₂max, decreased resting HR, better autonomic balance.
  • Clinical application: endurance work counters fatigue-related compensations — e.g., the tired knee-OA patient who develops a vaulting gait at 200 m; endurance of the scapular stabilisers prevents late rotator-cuff overload.

Strength, power and endurance lie on one continuum of muscle performance, and both derive from a strength base: power = strength expressed fast, endurance = strength sustained. Prescription follows the SAID principle (Specific Adaptation to Imposed Demand) and overload; sequencing is strength → power → endurance integration within a periodised plan.

Two things separate a 6/10 from a 9/10 here: (1) writing the power formula with BOTH force and velocity — "power = strength × speed" in one line; (2) giving at least one Indian-context clinical example (chair-rise in the elderly, return-to-field after ACL reconstruction). Fibre types must be mentioned by name.

5Recent advances

  • Reid and Fielding (2012) — Review showing that muscle power declines earlier and faster with age than maximal strength and, more than strength alone, predicts functional capacity such as chair-rise and stair climbing.
  • de Vos et al. (2005) — Explosive resistance-training trial in older adults finding similar peak-power gains at 20%, 50% and 80% of 1RM, so power can be trained safely with lighter loads moved fast.
  • Fragala et al. (2019) — NSCA position statement recommending moderate-to-high intensity (about 70-85% 1RM) resistance training 2-3 days per week, 2-3 sets of 8-12 repetitions, to counter sarcopenia.
  • Tschopp et al. (2011) — Meta-analysis of 11 trials in older adults showing that power training with high movement velocity has a small but significant advantage over conventional strength training for functional outcomes such as gait and balance.
  • Cadore et al. (2014) — Randomised trial in frail nonagenarians showing that a multicomponent programme including muscle power training enhanced muscle mass, power output and functional outcomes, supporting power training even in the very old.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT-MSK 2020 Ordinance & Syllabus, Paper II Unit 5 (Physiological Basis of Human Movement) and Paper IV Unit 1 (Impaired Muscle Performance / Impaired Endurance).
  2. American College of Sports Medicine. ACSM's Resource Manual for Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins — muscular strength/power/endurance prescription chapters (syllabus reference 12).
  3. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques. F.A. Davis — resistance exercise chapter: strength vs power vs endurance training parameters.
  4. Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology. Elsevier — sports physiology and motor unit recruitment sections.
  5. Hislop H, Avers D, Brown M. Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing. Elsevier — muscle performance definitions (syllabus reference 7).
  6. Byrne C, et al. Effectiveness of power training compared to strength training in older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Eur Rev Aging Phys Act. 2022;19:23.
  7. Hurst C, et al. Resistance exercise as a treatment for sarcopenia: prescription and delivery. Age Ageing. 2022;51(2):afac003.
Question 4 · 10 marks

Q4. Describe about the oxygen supply during training in post-traumatic knee stiffness.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit 5 — Physiological Basis of Human Movement (oxygen supply during exercise; physiology of movement in MSK injury and dysfunction)

★ Memory hook — Write Fick and annotate: VO₂ = (HR × SV) × (a−v)O₂ — each term is one adaptation site of aerobic training.

1Introduction

Every sustained muscular effort depends on a continuous supply of oxygen from the atmosphere to the working muscle's mitochondria. This question asks how that supply is organised during training and what happens to it in post-traumatic knee stiffness — the loss of knee range of motion and quadriceps function that follows intra-articular or peri-articular injury and prolonged immobilisation. The answer runs from the whole-body oxygen transport chain, through muscle-level delivery, to the specific impairments of the stiff, post-traumatic knee, and finally to the training implications for the physiotherapist.

2Physiology

Oxygen travels from atmosphere to mitochondrion through four linked steps:

  1. Pulmonary ventilation — alveolar ventilation rises from ~6 L/min at rest to ~100+ L/min in maximal exercise (respiratory rate and tidal volume both climb).
  2. Diffusion across the alveolo-capillary membrane (driven by a PO₂ gradient of about 60 mmHg — alveolar PO₂ ~104 mmHg versus venous PO₂ ~40 mmHg at rest, widening during exercise as venous PO₂ falls).
  3. Circulatory transport — cardiac output rises from ~5 L/min to ~20–25 L/min in young adults; the Frank–Starling mechanism (increased venous return stretches the ventricle) plus sympathetic drive raise both stroke volume and heart rate.
  4. Peripheral extraction — the arterio-venous O₂ difference widens (from ~4–5 to ~15+ mL O₂/dL) as working muscle pulls oxygen out of blood.

Summed in the Fick equation: VO₂ = Cardiac Output × a-vO₂ difference — every training adaptation fits into one of its two terms.

Fig 4.1 — The oxygen transport chain with the Fick equation underneath. In viva, draw the four boxes and this equation first.
  • Arteriolar dilatation — local metabolites (CO₂, H⁺/lactate, adenosine, K⁺) relax arteriolar smooth muscle; muscle blood flow rises up to 15–20-fold, far beyond the ~4–5-fold rise in cardiac output, because flow is also redistributed from splanchnic and non-working beds.
  • Capillary recruitment and better perfusion — at rest some capillaries are closed; exercise opens the reserve, shortening diffusion distance.
  • The muscle pump — rhythmic contraction milks venous blood proximally, and the venous valves keep it one-way; this is why pain-free, active cyclical exercise beats passive work for stiff knees.
  • Oxygen extraction — myoglobin releases O₂ as PO₂ falls; the Bohr effect (acidosis shifts the Hb-dissociation curve right) unloads more O₂ exactly where it is needed.

3Pathophysiology

Post-traumatic knee stiffness (after intra-/peri-articular fracture, multi-ligament injury, prolonged immobilisation) is associated with:

  • Disuse atrophy of quadriceps, preferentially type I (slow oxidative) fibres of vastus medialis obliquus and the anti-gravity extensors; decreased mitochondrial density and oxidative enzyme activity → early fatigability.
  • Reduced capillarisation and prolonged re-perfusion after ischaemic effort; intra-compartmental pressure from effusion and capsular tightening can further impede perfusion at low angles of knee flexion.
  • Pain inhibition (arthrogenous muscle inhibition) delays activation — recruitment of large motor units suffers, and the patient fatigues long before the target repetition range.

4Answer

  • Start early with pain-free cyclical, rhythmic activity (stationary cycling with seat raised, foot pumps, heel slides) to use the muscle pump without provoking reactive synovitis.
  • Isometrics in a pain-free arc sustain trophic tone — but sustained maximal isometrics occlude local blood flow; use rhythmic/brief-hold isometrics ("hold 6 s, breathe, repeat ×10) so oxygen delivery continues between holds.
  • Avoid the Valsalva manoeuvre — breath-holding against a closed glottis spikes blood pressure and reduces venous return; teach exhale-on-effort.
  • Progress toward aerobic conditioning (walk/cycle programmes at ~60% HR reserve) to rebuild the central oxygen-transport capacity that bed rest deconditioning erodes; add interval work only after reactive inflammation settles.
  • Warm-up literally raises tissue temperature and shifts the Hb curve rightward — a physiologic justification every answer should include.
This question is where pure physiology answers die: if you never write the words "post-traumatic knee stiffness" after page one, you lose the 4 application marks. Chain the physiology to the pathology in every paragraph. Fick equation = guaranteed half-mark.

5Recent advances

  • Lixandrão et al. (2018) — Meta-analysis showing that low-load blood-flow-restriction training builds muscle mass comparable to high-load training and strength close to it, with far less mechanical joint stress, making it valuable after knee trauma or surgery.
  • Ozaki et al. (2011) — Walk training with leg blood-flow restriction in older adults increased aerobic capacity and thigh muscle volume, with related work showing upregulation of angiogenic factors (VEGF, HIF-1alpha) in working muscle.
  • Hughes et al. (2017) — Systematic review and meta-analysis in the British Journal of Sports Medicine showing that low-load blood-flow-restriction training is more effective than low-load training alone and is a tolerable clinical tool when heavy joint loading is not yet possible.
  • Olivier et al. (2010) — Randomised study showing that one-leg aerobic cycling with the uninjured limb after knee surgery prevented the fall in peak oxygen uptake and power that occurred with conventional rehabilitation alone, preserving oxygen supply and aerobic fitness during knee immobilisation.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT-MSK 2020 Ordinance & Syllabus, Paper II Unit 5 — Physiological Basis of Human Movement: (c) oxygen supply during exercise, (f) physiology of movement in musculoskeletal disease, injury and dysfunction.
  2. Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology. Elsevier — cardiac output and venous return during exercise; sports physiology; oxygen transport chapters.
  3. American College of Sports Medicine. ACSM's Resource Manual for Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins (syllabus reference 12).
  4. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. F.A. Davis — aerobic endurance and isometric exercise sections.
  5. Dose-response relationship of blood-flow-restriction training on isometric muscle strength, maximum strength and lower-limb extensor strength: a meta-analysis. Front Physiol. 2022;13:1046625.
  6. Smith NDW, Scott BR, Girard O, Peiffer JJ. Aerobic training with blood flow restriction for endurance athletes. J Strength Cond Res. 2022;36(12):3541–3550.
Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. Applied mechanics and pathomechanics following rotator cuff injury.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit 6 — Mechanics and Pathomechanics of Joints (upper extremity joints, soft tissues)

★ Memory hook — SITS = Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, Teres minor, Subscapularis. The cuff is the deltoid’s brake — depressor force couple keeping the head centred in the glenoid.

1Introduction

The glenohumeral (GH) joint sacrifices bony congruence for range of motion: the large humeral head sits on a small, shallow glenoid cavity (only about a third of the head is in contact at any position) deepened a little by the glenoid labrum. Static restraints (capsule, glenohumeral ligaments) are lax by design, so dynamic stability depends on the rotator cuff — supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis (SITS).

2Physiology

  • Concavity compression: supraspinatus, and the cuff as a whole, compresses the humeral head into the concave glenoid — the primary mechanism keeping the head centred through mid-range, where ligaments are slack.
  • Transverse (force) couple: during abduction, the line of deltoid pull passes above the centre of the head and would translate the head upward; the inferiorly-directed pull of subscapularis (anterior) and infraspinatus + teres minor (posterior) depresses and centres the head. Cuff–deltoid balance converts deltoid's shear into pure rotation.
  • Scapulohumeral rhythm: ~2:1 ratio — for 180° of elevation, ~120° occurs at GH and ~60° at scapulothoracic (upward rotation by trapezius/serratus anterior), keeping the glenoid track facing the moving head and preserving the subacromial space.
  • Supraspinatus also contributes an initial abduction torque and, with the others, provides proprioceptive guarding — the reflex stiffening of the joint under load.
Fig 5.1 — The force couple in health and after a cuff tear. This two-panel sketch is exactly what a 10/10 script draws in the margin.

3Pathophysiology

  • Loss of concavity compression & depressor action → superior translation of the humeral head during elevation — the deltoid now pulls the head upward unopposed against the coraco-acromial arch.
  • Secondary subacromial impingement — the head, greater tuberosity and bursal tissue crowd the subacromial space, already narrowed in abduction–external rotation positions; repetitive micro-trauma → bursitis, tendinopathy, partial- then full-thickness tear (a self-perpetuating cycle).
  • Scapulohumeral rhythm breakdown — pain inhibits serratus anterior/lower trapezius, producing scapular dyskinesis (excessive scapular elevation, reduced upward rotation, dysrhythmia); the glenoid no longer follows the head, so GH elevation reduces and scapular substitution (shoulder shrug) appears.
  • Strength and function: painful arc and weak abduction/external rotation; night pain lying on the side is classical. In massive chronic tears the head may erode the acromion — cuff-tear arthropathy.
  • Glenohumeral arthrokinematics change: the normal spin of the head is replaced by an abnormal roll-and-slide, further jamming the head under the arch.

4Answer

Put applied mechanics and pathomechanics side by side — the contrast is exactly what the question asks for:

FeatureNormal applied mechanicsPathomechanics after cuff injury
Humeral-head centringConcavity compression by supraspinatus and the cuff keeps the head in the glenoidLoss of compression → superior migration of the head
Coronal force coupleDeltoid's upward pull balanced by subscapularis (front) and infraspinatus/teres minor (back)Deltoid unopposed → head rides up under the acromion
Scapulohumeral rhythm2:1 glenohumeral:scapulothoracic; serratus anterior and trapezius rotate the scapula upScapular dyskinesis, reduced upward rotation, shrug substitution
Subacromial spacePreserved — the cuff tendon clears the arch in elevationNarrowed → secondary impingement, bursitis, tear progression
ArthrokinematicsNormal spin and roll-and-slide of the head on the glenoidAbnormal roll-and-slide jams the head under the arch

Clinical reasoning — the self-perpetuating cycle. Cuff failure removes the head's depressor, so the head migrates superiorly, the subacromial space narrows, and repetitive micro-trauma produces bursitis and tendinopathy that weaken the cuff further. Pain then inhibits serratus anterior and lower trapezius, so the scapula no longer tracks the moving head — a vicious cycle of impingement → tear → weakness → more impingement.

Applied to assessment and treatment. Clinically the patient shows a painful arc (roughly 60–120°), weak abduction and external rotation, night pain lying on the affected side, and in a chronic massive tear a cuff-tear arthropathy. Rehabilitation is therefore ordered to reverse the mechanics, not merely to relieve pain: (i) restore scapular control and upward rotation first (serratus anterior, lower trapezius), because the glenoid must follow the head; (ii) re-establish the cuff–deltoid force couple with progressive cuff loading (external rotation, subscapularis) so the head is depressed and centred again; (iii) only then progress to overhead power and sport-specific loading. In Indian practice — overhead lifting, load-carrying and floor work are daily — restoring the couple matters for function as much as for pain.

Conclusion. Rotator cuff injury converts a finely balanced force couple into an unopposed deltoid pull: the joint loses its brake, the head drifts up, and impingement–tear–weakness feeds itself. Physiotherapy restores scapular rhythm first and the cuff–deltoid couple second — precisely the mechanics we are trying to rebuild.

5Recent advances

  • Berthold et al. (2021) — Dynamic shoulder-simulator study confirming that irreparable, retracted posterosuperior cuff tears increase glenohumeral superior translation and subacromial contact pressure, whereas small non-retracted tears are compensated by the intact cuff.
  • Kibler et al. (2013) — Scapular Summit consensus statement recognising scapular dyskinesis as both a cause and a consequence of cuff pathology that worsens clinical outcomes and range of motion.
  • Kolk et al. (2016) — Three-dimensional kinematic study showing scapular motion normalises toward the asymptomatic side after cuff repair, with time to normalisation varying from about 5 months to 2 years.
  • Kukkonen et al. (2014) — Randomised trial in patients over 55 showing that physiotherapy alone gave one-year outcomes equal to acromioplasty or cuff repair for non-traumatic supraspinatus tears, and was the most cost-effective option.
  • Littlewood et al. (2015) — Systematic review of exercise prescription for rotator cuff tendinopathy showing that including resistance, using three sets and higher repetitions, and allowing home-based programmes are the key ingredients of effective rehabilitation.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT-MSK 2020 Ordinance & Syllabus, Paper II Unit 6 — Mechanics and Pathomechanics of Joints: (a) upper extremity joints, (f) soft tissues.
  2. Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins — biomechanics of the shoulder.
  3. Levangie PK, Norkin CC. Joint Structure and Function. F.A. Davis — the shoulder complex chapter.
  4. Donatelli RA, Wooden MJ. Orthopaedic Physical Therapy. Elsevier — shoulder dysfunction and rotator cuff chapters (syllabus reference 5).
  5. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. F.A. Davis — shoulder impingement/instability chapters.
  6. Berthold DP, et al. Biomechanical consequences of isolated, massive and irreparable posterosuperior rotator cuff tears on the glenohumeral joint. Obere Extremität. 2021;16:120–129.

Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. Define Posture. Explain the methods to control posture following IVDP.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit 7 — Posture (normal/abnormal posture, control of posture, postural deformities); Paper IV Unit 3 — postural stability and core stability

★ Memory hook — Posture control pair: TrA = corset, multifidus = segmental strings; feed-forward fires BEFORE the limb moves — delayed after LBP.

1Introduction

Posture is the relative alignment of body segments to one another and to gravity at any given moment — classically, "the position from which movement begins and ends." Ideal upright posture places the plumb line through the ear, shoulder, hip, knee and lateral malleolus, with the cervical and lumbar lordoses balanced by the thoracic and sacral kyphoses.

2Physiology

  • Sensory input: visual (eyes), vestibular (otoliths for static, semi-circular canals for dynamic), and somatosensory/proprioceptive input from joints, muscles and skin — the dominant input in healthy adults.
  • Central integration: spinal reflex arcs (stretch reflex for tone), brainstem (vestibulo- and rectospinal tracts), cerebellum (timing/smoothing), and cortical representation for anticipatory and voluntary corrections.
  • Motor output: tonic postural muscles and phasic mobilisers, plus anticipatory feed-forward postural adjustments — e.g., transversus abdominis fires before limb movement — and reactive strategies: ankle, hip and stepping strategies.

3Pathophysiology

In intervertebral disc prolapse, a posterior/postero-lateral prolapse (the common direction) is aggravated by flexion + loading, which raises intradiscal pressure and pushes nuclear material backward toward the posterior annulus and nerve root — the basis of a peripheralising pain pattern. Patients adopt a shift/list, lose the lumbar lordosis and inhibit their deep stabilisers (transversus abdominis, multifidus) reflexively through pain. The goal of postural control is therefore to maintain the neutral spine — the position of least disc stress — and to abolish peripheralisation (McKenzie's centralisation principle).

4Answer

  1. Education and conscious correction: teaching neutral spine in sitting, standing and lifting; avoiding prolonged flexion, and combining flexion with rotation (the classic provocative couple) — use of a lumbar roll/cushion for chair sitting, knees and hips at 90°, feet supported; sitting-reclined alternative in the acute phase because a reclined posture lowers the load on the disc: Nachemson's classic intradiscal-pressure studies showed sitting slumped loads the L3–4 disc more than standing.
  2. Positioning and bed rest discipline: short-term rest in the most reducing posture (commonly prone extension or side-lying with pillow between knees); log-rolling technique to get in and out of bed; avoid early-morning unsupported sitting (disc is hydrated and turgid after overnight water imbition).
  3. Core stabilisation programme: re-training transversus abdominis drawing-in, multifidus activation, diaphragmatic breathing and pelvic floor co-activation — progressing from isolated activation to integrated functional positions (Hook-lying → quadruped → standing).
  4. Direction-specific exercise (McKenzie method): prone/supported extension to centralise symptoms when the derangement responds to extension; the sagittal-plane rule — movements that centralise pain are prescribed, those that peripheralise are avoided.
  5. Proprioceptive/balance retraining: wobble-board and unstable-surface work to restore somatosensory postural reflexes once pain settles.
  6. Ergonomics and ADL modification: workstation redesign, hip-hinge lifting with load close to body, micro-breaks every 30–40 min, and avoidance of prolonged postures of flexion.
  7. External support: a temporary lumbosacral corset as a proprioceptive reminder — never a substitute for the muscle corset.
  8. General conditioning: weight reduction, walking programme and thoracic mobility work to distribute stress across the whole spine.
Fig 6.1 — Neutral spine with the four balanced curves vs the flexed IVDP spine with posterior bulge and root irritation.
Two marking magnets: Nachemson's intradiscal pressure data (slumped sitting > upright sitting > standing) and centralisation vs peripheralisation. Also, "IVDP" must be expanded — "intervertebral disc prolapse" written once in full. Centralisation is McKenzie's single most examinable concept in this paper.

5Recent advances

  • Pourahmadi et al. (2022) — Meta-analysis of 16 trials (861 patients) finding that motor-control training improves pain and function in symptomatic lumbar disc herniation, though the certainty of evidence is low.
  • El Melhat et al. (2024) — Narrative review grading moderate (Level B) evidence for patient education/self-management, the McKenzie method, mobilisation/manipulation, exercise therapy, neural mobilisation and epidural injection in lumbar disc herniation with radiculopathy.
  • World Health Organization (2023) — Consensus guideline on chronic low back pain stressing active education and self-management over passive strategies, together with core stabilisation, ergonomics and weight management.
  • Fersum et al. (2013) — Randomised trial showing that classification-based cognitive functional therapy produced superior, clinically important improvements in disability and pain compared with manual therapy plus exercise in chronic low back pain.
  • Petersen et al. (2011) — Randomised trial in 350 patients with low back pain and centralisation or peripheralisation showing the McKenzie method was slightly more effective than spinal manipulation when added to information and advice, supporting directional-preference exercise for discogenic pain.

6References

  2. McKenzie R, May S. The Lumbar Spine: Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy. (syllabus reference 24) — derangement, centralisation, extension principle.
  3. Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System. — lumbar spine mechanics and loads (Nachemson data).
  4. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. F.A. Davis — posture chapter and spinal stabilisation/segmental stability sections.
  5. Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology. Elsevier — motor functions and postural control of the nervous system.
  6. Danazumi MS, et al. Effects of spinal manipulation or mobilization as an adjunct to neurodynamic mobilization for lumbar disc herniation with radiculopathy: a randomized clinical trial. J Man Manip Ther. 2023;31(6):408–420.

Question 7 · 10 marks

Q7. Define Gait. Describe the determinants of gait with examples.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit 8 — Gait and function (gait cycle, biomechanical analysis of gait, energy expenditure and gait)

★ Memory hook — Gait: stance 60 : swing 40; phases IC → LR → MSt → TSt → PSw | ISw → MSw → TSw; the six determinants exist to flatten the COM curve.

1Introduction

Gait is the manner or style of walking — the pattern of locomotion produced by the cyclic, coordinated movement of body segments. One gait cycle = heel strike of one foot to the next heel strike of the same foot: a stance phase (60%) and a swing phase (40%) — the two together spanning the eight phases of the cycle from initial contact through terminal swing (IC → LR → MSt → TSt → PSw | ISw → MSw → TSw).

2Physiology

If the legs were rigid struts and the pelvis fixed, the body's centre of mass would travel in a series of arcs as high as each leg length step-over, wasting enormous energy lifting and dropping the body ~7–8 cm twice each step. The six determinants of gait (Saunders, Inman & Eberhart) are the pelvic and lower-limb movements that flatten these arcs, cutting vertical COM displacement to about 5 cm (2 inch) and horizontal sway to ~2.5 cm — conserving energy.

3Pathophysiology

Pathological gait is, in the classic formulation, the exaggeration or loss of one or more determinants. Trendelenburg lurch follows abductor (gluteus medius) weakness — the stance-side pelvic drop is no longer controlled. Circumduction and vaulting compensate for a stiff or fused knee (the limb becomes a long lever). Hip-hiking substitutes for lost knee flexion in swing (e.g., rectus femoris spasticity or post-operative arthrofibrosis). An ankle equinus or calcaneus destroys the foot–ankle rockers and forces hip substitution. A wide-based gait or coxa vara increases lateral sway and raises the energy cost per metre. In each case the COM path is no longer flattened and the metabolic cost of walking rises — the clinical signature of a lost determinant.

4Answer

  1. Pelvic rotation — the pelvis rotates ~4° forward on the swing side (total ~8°) in the transverse plane at initial contact. This lengthens the step and flattens the arc's base. Example: loss of rotation after hip fusion forces the patient to "square-off" and circumduct — gait looks stiff and costlier.
  2. Pelvic tilt (obliquity) — the pelvis drops ~4–5° on the swing side (controlled eccentrically by the stance-side hip abductors — gluteus medius), lowering the apex of the COM arc. Example: weakness of abductors (safe-side Trendelenburg pattern) produces an exaggerated drop and lateral lurch.
  3. Knee flexion in stance — after loading response the knee stays flexed ~15–18° until mid-stance; it shortens the stance limb exactly when the COM would otherwise be highest. Example: after knee fusion/arthrodesis the leg becomes a long lever and the patient vaults on the sound side to clear it.
  4. Foot and ankle mechanisms — from heel strike (ankle plantarflexed with the heel as rocker) to foot-flat, then the ankle rocker, then heel-off with the forefoot rocker: a smooth rolling radius instead of a point pivot. Example: ankle equinus/calcaneus deformity after trauma destroys the rockers and substitutes hip circumduction.
  5. Knee mechanisms — the knee's linked flexion with the ankle rockers at the start and end of stance: since the ankle plantarflexes while the knee flexes (and vice versa), the combined limb length stays nearly constant, again smoothing the COM path. Example: a stiff-knee gait (rectus femoris spasticity/post-op arthrofibrosis) produces compensatory hip-hiking in swing.
  6. Lateral pelvic displacement — the pelvis (and COM) shifts ~2.5 cm over the weight-bearing limb in the frontal plane, with a functional genu valgum at the knee keeping the COM near the supporting foot. Example: coxa vara or wide-based gait increases sway and the energy cost of walking.
Fig 7.1 — The red dashed line is the COM path without determinants (rigid struts); the green line is the real, flattened trajectory (~5 cm) that the six determinants buy us.

The six determinants therefore act as an energy-saving system: each one flattens part of the COM trajectory, and the reciprocal (pathological) gait deviations we treat in clinic — Trendelenburg lurch, circumduction, vaulting, hip hiking — are simply the loss of one or more determinants. Quantify them clinically with observant video/10-metre walk analysis; the underlying principle is minimisation of energy expenditure (a 10-mark answer must close on this sentence).

The word "Saunders/Inman" attached to the determinants earns credit; so does stating the purpose (flattening the COM arc → energy conservation). Most students list the six correctly and forget the VALUES (4°, 4–5°, 15–18°, ~2.5 cm) — those numbers are what distinguish a first-class script. Also write 60:40 stance-to-swing — even though it's "defining gait" territory.

5Recent advances

  • Prisco et al. (2024) — Systematic review of wearable inertial sensors confirming that IMU-based systems now allow quantitative gait analysis outside the laboratory, a mobile gait lab capturing spatiotemporal and kinematic parameters in real clinical and community settings.
  • Tesio and Rota (2019) — Review re-examining centre-of-mass motion with modern three-dimensional methods, describing the bow-tie figure-eight trajectory and inverted-pendulum energy exchange that explain walking economy better than the classic determinant model.
  • Hof et al. (2005) — Introduction of the extrapolated centre of mass (XCoM) and margin-of-stability model, which, with the inverted-pendulum model, has largely displaced the six determinants for analysing and controlling bipedal locomotion.
  • Rynne et al. (2022) — Systematic review and meta-analysis showing that gait retraining improves knee adduction moment and WOMAC outcomes in knee osteoarthritis, with real-time biofeedback the strongest method for changing walking biomechanics.
  • Silva et al. (2022) — Systematic review and meta-analysis showing that neuromuscular gait-modification strategies (ipsilateral trunk lean, toe-out, toe-in) can reduce indicators of medial knee joint load in medial knee osteoarthritis, with dose-response effects.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT-MSK 2020 Ordinance & Syllabus, Paper II Unit 8 — Gait and function (gait cycle, biomechanical analysis, energy expenditure).
  2. Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System. — locomotion/gait analysis chapter.
  3. Levangie PK, Norkin CC. Joint Structure and Function. F.A. Davis — the walking chapter (determinants of gait).
  4. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. F.A. Davis — gait assessment and pathological gait patterns (syllabus reference 10).
  5. Preatoni E, et al. Present and future of gait assessment in clinical practice: towards the application of novel trends and technologies. Front Med Technol. 2022;4:901331.
  6. Cavagna GA, et al. The motion of body center of mass during walking. Front Neurol. 2019;10:999.
Question 8 · 10 marks

Q8. Explain the various theories of pain in detail.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit 9 — Pain (definition, pathways, physiology and pathophysiology; theories and models of pain)

★ Memory hook — Pain fibres: Aδ = fast & sharp (first pain), C = slow & dull (second pain). Gate theory: large-fibre input closes the gate on small-fibre traffic.

1Introduction

Pain, per the International Association for the Study of Pain, is "an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with, or resembling that associated with, actual or potential tissue damage." The pathway in one line: nociceptors → Aδ and C fibres → dorsal horn (substantia gelatinosa) → decussation → lateral spinothalamic tract → thalamus → somatosensory cortex & limbic centres. Theories of pain explain how this raw signal becomes the experience we treat.

2Physiology

Four classical theories trace how nociception becomes the experience of pain; each corrects the weakness of the one before it.

1. Specificity theory (von Frey, 1895 — descended from Descartes' idea of a dedicated pain pathway). Pain is a dedicated modality with its own receptors, dedicated Aδ and C afferents and a specific line to a "pain centre" in the brain, exactly as vision has its own line. Strength: it correctly predicted specialised nociceptors and labelled lines (Aδ = sharp, fast, first pain; C = dull, slow, second pain). Weakness: it cannot explain phantom limb pain, chronic pain without ongoing tissue damage, or the modulation of pain by emotion and attention.

2. Intensity theory (Erb; Goldscheider — also called the pattern-of-stimulus theory). Pain is not a special sense but simply excessive stimulation of any sensory receptor — strong touch or heat becomes pain. Largely of historical value: it is disproved because intense stimulation of non-nociceptive receptors does not reliably produce pain.

3. Pattern theory (Nafe; Sinclair and Weddell). Pain is a pattern of neural firing — intense, frequent, temporally patterned discharge from any receptor is decoded centrally as pain. Strength: it introduced the crucial idea of central processing and temporal summation (the ancestor of wind-up and central sensitisation). Weakness: it underplayed the genuine specificity of nociceptors.

4. Gate control theory (Melzack and Wall, 1965 — the single most examinable theory). A "gate" in the dorsal horn (substantia gelatinosa, lamina II) regulates transmission from peripheral afferents to transmission (T) cells that project up the spinothalamic tract:

  • Large-diameter Aβ (touch/mechanoreceptor) fibres excite the T cells but ALSO excite the substantia gelatinosa (SG) interneurons, which inhibit transmission → gate closes.
  • Small-diameter Aδ/C (nociceptive) fibres excite T cells and inhibit the SG interneurons → gate opens → pain ascends.
  • Central control: descending fibres from the brain (periaqueductal grey, raphe magnus — serotonergic/noradrenergic) can bias the gate — the physiology behind attention, anxiety, expectation and placebo changing pain.
Fig 8.1 — Gate control theory (Melzack & Wall, 1965). Draw the gate as a shaded box in substantia gelatinosa with Aβ closing and Aδ/C opening it.

Clinical applications physiotherapists use daily: TENS (large-fibre stimulation closing the gate), rubbing a knock, and cognitive reassurance reducing descending facilitation. Limitation: pain is more than a spinal gate — the theory gives no account of chronic plasticity or emotional colour, which the neuromatrix (below) supplies.

3Pathophysiology

Phantom limb pain in people without peripheral input forced the next leap: the brain contains a body-self neuromatrix — a widespread network (somatosensory, limbic, thalamic, parietal) that continuously generates the experience of the body. Pain is the output of this matrix shaped by sensory, cognitive-evaluative and emotional-motivational dimensions — the neuroscientific scaffold of the biopsychosocial model we now use for chronic MSK pain, and the justification for pain neuroscience education, graded activity and cognitive-behavioural methods (which sit in RGUHS Paper IV, Unit 2c).

4Answer

Present the theories as a progression, and give each one a physiotherapy application — that pairing is what separates a physiotherapy answer from a history essay:

Theory (author, year)Core claimPhysiotherapy application
Specificity (von Frey, 1895)Dedicated pain receptors and pathwaysBasis of nociceptor-targeted care; explains first and second pain
Intensity (Erb; Goldscheider)Excess stimulation of any receptorHistorical only — superseded
Pattern (Nafe; Sinclair)Temporal pattern of firing decoded centrallyAncestor of wind-up and central-sensitisation concepts
Gate control (Melzack & Wall, 1965)Dorsal-horn gate modulated by Aβ input and descending controlTENS, massage, heat, movement, distraction
Neuromatrix (Melzack, 1999)Pain is the brain's body-self output (neurosignature)Pain neuroscience education, graded exposure, graded motor imagery
Biopsychosocial modelBiological + psychological + social factors interactCognitive functional therapy, yellow-flag screening, pacing

Conclusion. Each theory is partly right: specificity gave us nociceptors, pattern gave us central processing, gate control gave us modulation (and TENS), and the neuromatrix gives us the modern biopsychosocial treatment of persistent pain. For the examiner, name the theory with its author and date, then link each to one intervention you actually use.

5Recent advances

  • Kosek et al. (2021) — IASP taskforce paper setting out the clinical criteria and grading system for nociplastic pain, the third mechanistic descriptor alongside nociceptive and neuropathic pain introduced in 2017.
  • Woolf (2011) — Review establishing central sensitisation as the major mechanism of nociplastic pain and a well-established feature of chronic low back pain, osteoarthritis, fibromyalgia and post-surgical pain, supporting a shift from tissue-targeted to CNS-focused, biopsychosocial care.
  • Fitzcharles et al. (2021) — Lancet review standardising central-sensitisation and nociplastic-pain terminology for clinicians to improve recognition and precision pain medicine.
  • Louw et al. (2016) — Systematic review of randomised trials showing that pain neuroscience education reduces pain, improves function, lowers disability and improves pain knowledge in chronic musculoskeletal pain, supporting cognitive reconceptualisation as a physiotherapy tool.
  • Moseley (2004) — Randomised trial showing that graded motor imagery (laterality recognition, imagined movements, mirror therapy) produced large reductions in pain and swelling in long-standing complex regional pain syndrome, a landmark for cortical-targeted pain therapy.

6References

  3. Melzack R, Wall PD. Pain mechanisms: a new theory. Science 1965;150(3699):971–9. (primary source, cited for examiner-level completeness)
  4. Melzack R. From the gate to the neuromatrix. Pain 1999;Suppl 6:S121–6.
  5. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. F.A. Davis — pain assessment and management chapters (syllabus reference 10).
  6. Kosek E, Clauw D, Nijs J, et al. Chronic nociplastic pain affecting the musculoskeletal system: clinical criteria and grading system. Pain. 2021;162(11):2629–2634.
  7. Nijs J, et al. Nociplastic pain and central sensitization in patients with chronic pain conditions: a terminology update for clinicians. Braz J Phys Ther. 2023;27(3):100518.
Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. Write the biophysical effects of heat on various systems in the body.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit 10 — Electro Physics (biophysical effects of heat and cold; clinical decision making in electro-modalities)

★ Memory hook — Heat rule: stretch while hot, hold while cooling — that is what makes the collagen gain permanent.

1Introduction

Heat is a physical agent that produces its effects by raising tissue temperature. The biophysical effects of heat are the predictable physiological changes that follow this rise in temperature, and they act on several body systems at once — vascular, neuromuscular, metabolic and connective-tissue. Understanding these effects system by system lets the physiotherapist choose the right modality, dose and timing, and avoid harm.

2Physiology

Raising tissue temperature produces four effect families, each with a physiotherapy use, and the magnitude of each depends on how much the tissue temperature rises and for how long.

  • Vascular effects: vasodilatation with increased cutaneous and muscle blood flow, improved oxygen and nutrient delivery, and faster clearance of metabolites. Superficial heating raises skin and subcutaneous temperature; deep heating (shortwave, ultrasound) reaches muscle and joint capsule.
  • Metabolic effects: tissue metabolic rate rises roughly 10–13% for every 1 degree Celsius of temperature rise, accelerating enzymatic activity, healing and the inflammatory resolution that follows the acute phase.
  • Neuromuscular effects: warmth alters nerve conduction velocity, raises the pain threshold through the gate mechanism (large-fibre thermal input closing the gate on small-fibre pain), reduces muscle spasm by quietening muscle-spindle and gamma activity, and increases the extensibility of muscle and connective tissue.
  • Connective-tissue effects: heated collagen becomes more extensible, and elongation produced while the tissue is hot is retained after cooling — the basis of the clinical rule "stretch while hot, hold while cooling".

Numbers to quote: therapeutic heating aims to raise tissue temperature to about 40–45 degrees Celsius; superficial agents heat to a depth of 1–2 cm, while 1 MHz ultrasound and shortwave diathermy heat at 3–5 cm — the depth of the joint capsule and deep muscle.

3Pathophysiology

The same physics that makes heat therapeutic makes it harmful when misapplied. Applied during the acute inflammatory phase (first 24–48 hours), heat increases vasodilatation and capillary permeability, worsening oedema, bleeding and pain — so heat is contraindicated in fresh injury. Excessive or prolonged heating raises tissue temperature above the safe range and can cause burns, especially over insensate skin (as in diabetic or post-stroke patients) and over areas of impaired circulation. Heat over a region with acute infection, malignancy, deep-vein thrombosis or a bleeding disorder can spread infection, accelerate tumour growth, dislodge thrombus or provoke haemorrhage; shortwave diathermy is additionally avoided over cardiac pacemakers, metal implants and the pregnant uterus. The therapist's task is therefore to match the agent and dose to the tissue, the depth and the healing phase.

4Answer

The biophysical effects of heat, organised by body system, are as follows.

1. Circulatory system

  • Local vasodilatation and increased blood flow, with a rise in tissue temperature and oxygen delivery.
  • Improved clearance of metabolites and reduced tissue fluid stasis; a generalised vasodilatation and sweating if the whole body is heated.

2. Neuromuscular system

  • Analgesia through the gate mechanism, and a rise in the pain threshold.
  • Reduced muscle spasm and tone, from decreased spindle and gamma-motor activity.
  • Increased nerve conduction velocity and improved tissue extensibility of muscle and tendon.

3. Metabolic and connective-tissue systems

  • Increased metabolic rate and enzymatic activity, accelerating repair after the acute phase.
  • Increased collagen extensibility, so heated tissue stretches further with less force and retains more of the gain.
  • Reduced joint stiffness and increased range of motion when combined with stretching.

4. Clinical applications

  • Subacute and chronic pain, muscle spasm, joint stiffness and contracture; pre-stretch preparation before mobilisation and exercise.
  • Superficial agents (hot packs, paraffin wax, infrared) for superficial tissue; deep agents (shortwave diathermy at 27.12 MHz, 1 MHz ultrasound) for muscle, tendon and joint capsule.
  • Dosage: superficial heat for 15–20 minutes with adequate towelling; check skin in insensate or diabetic patients.
SystemPrincipal biophysical effect of heat
VascularVasodilatation, increased blood flow
MetabolicMetabolic rate rises ~10–13% per degree C
NeuralAnalgesia, reduced spasm, faster conduction
Connective tissueIncreased collagen extensibility, retained stretch

Indian-practice context: hot packs and paraffin wax are cheap, widely used and effective for chronic musculoskeletal pain and stiff hands; in patients with diabetic neuropathy or vascular disease, skin checks and shorter application times prevent burns, a real hazard in Indian OPDs.

Conclusion: heat works through vasodilatation, raised metabolism, analgesia and increased collagen extensibility — effects that help in subacute and chronic conditions but harm in the acute phase — so the physiotherapist must match the agent, depth and dose to the tissue and the healing phase.

5Recent advances

  • Nakamura et al. (2023) — Elastography study showing hot-pack application raises range of motion largely by increasing stretch tolerance, with only a transient fall in muscle shear modulus rather than a permanent stiffness change.
  • Nakano et al. (2012) — Systematic review and meta-analysis showing that heat applied with stretch increases range of motion more than stretch alone, and that multiple treatments produce more sustained gains, the evidence base for the clinical rule of stretching while hot.
  • Clijsen et al. (2021) — Systematic review and meta-analysis showing that local heat application gives immediate pain relief, improves physical function and increases range of motion in acute and chronic musculoskeletal disorders, supporting heat as an adjunct in physiotherapy.
  • Peres et al. (2002) — Trial showing that pulsed shortwave diathermy combined with prolonged long-duration stretching increased ankle dorsiflexion range of motion more than identical stretching without diathermy, demonstrating deep-heat enhancement of stretch.

6References

  3. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. F.A. Davis — thermal agents and connective-tissue stretching sections.
  4. Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology. Elsevier — body-temperature regulation, local and systemic responses to heat.
  5. Synergistic effects of heating and traction during fibrous tissue elongation. J Biomech Sci Eng. 2023;18(2):22-00379.
  6. Unravelling the molecular mechanism of collagen flexibility during physiological warm-up using molecular dynamics simulation and machine learning. 2023.
Question 10 · 10 marks

Q10. Explain the pathomechanics following TA rupture.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit 6 — Mechanics and Pathomechanics of Joints (lower extremity joints, soft tissues); Unit 8 — pathological gait

★ Memory hook — TA rupture: loss of push-off with hip-flexor compensation, positive Thompson's test, destroyed gait phase = terminal stance–pre-swing.

1Introduction

The tendo-Achilles (TA) is the thickest and strongest tendon in the body and the final common pathway of the triceps surae. Rupture of the TA — commonest in the 30–50-year-old "weekend athlete" — removes the calf's ability to transmit force to the calcaneus, with consequences at the ankle and, more importantly for the examiner, at the level of gait. This answer moves from normal mechanics, through the mechanism of rupture, to the pathomechanics at the ankle and in gait, and closes with rehabilitation significance.

2Physiology

The triceps surae (gastrocnemius + soleus) converges into the tendo-Achilles, the thickest, strongest tendon in the body (withstands ~4000 N in walking), inserting on the calcaneal tuberosity. As the prime plantarflexor, it:

  • generates the propulsive push-off (terminal stance–pre-swing) — the A2 plantarflexor-knee power burst that vaults the body over the stance foot;
  • works eccentrically after heel strike to control tibial advancement (ankle dorsiflexion) — the soleus is postural, active through most of stance;
  • contributes to the windlass mechanism and shock absorption through mid-stance, and to venous return via the calf pump.
Fig 10.1 — The calcaneal lever with the Achilles pull intact vs retracted after rupture. Redraw with the arrow of the calf's force literally "cut".

3Pathophysiology

Typical injury is in the 30–50-year-old "weekend athlete": a sudden, violent eccentric contraction on a dorsiflexing ankle — landing from a jump or push-off burst — often in a degenerated, hypovascular mid-tendon (watershed 2–6 cm above insertion). Patients report being "hit in the calf by a stone". Thompson's test (Simmonds') is positive: absent ankle plantarflexion on calf squeeze.

  • Loss of plantarflexion torque: the calf's force is not transmitted to the calcaneus → plantarflexion strength is profoundly reduced and isolated plantarflexion is performed only by the long toe flexors, peroneals, tibialis posterior and plantaris (if present).
  • Loss of eccentric control: after initial contact the unrestrained tibia advances on the talus, so dorsiflexion is excessive and uncontrolled — the foot slaps into a flatter loading pattern.
  • Heel-cord insufficiency: the calcaneus loses its posterior tether and rides slightly anteriorly/proximally; if treated non-operatively with a gap, the tendon heals elongated → permanent weakness; with malalignment the calcaneus assumes a more vertical position because the plantarflexor pull line is lost (the "calcaneus-type" deformity in chronic neglected rupture).
  • Arch and shock absorption: diminished triceps surae contribution to the longitudinal arch mechanism alters mid-foot load sharing, increasing forefoot and medial-arch stress.
  • Absent push-off / flat-foot gait: no heel rise, no terminal-stance plantarflexion power (loss of the A2 burst) — the affected step is shorter, with reduced or absent ankle plantarflexion at pre-swing.
  • Compensatory pattern: hip flexion and hip-hiking with a shorter contralateral step; the patient "walks through" the limb rather than over it; often an ipsilateral trunk lean and early hip-extensor substitution — the classic shift of propulsion from ankle to hip strategy.
  • Stance-phase effects: decreased terminal stance ankle plantarflexion moment, excessive dorsiflexion, reduced knee-extension moment → genu recurvatum avoidance patterns and increased demand on knee extensors; walking speed and cadence drop, and energy cost per metre rises (losing a gait determinant-like mechanism).
  • Functional losses: inability to do a single-limb heel raise, difficulty with stairs, running and jumping; altered venous return (calf-pump loss) → distal oedema risk.

4Answer

Pathomechanics dictates the protocol: the aim is to restore push-off power while the healing tendon regains tensile strength.

PhaseBiomechanical goalKey interventions
Protection (0–2 weeks)Hold tendon ends apposed; prevent elongationEquinus cast/orthosis or functional brace; non- to partial weight-bearing as allowed
Early loading (2–6 weeks)Controlled tension to stimulate collagen without creating a gapProtected weight-bearing in a rocker-bottom/heel-raise boot; gentle range in the permitted arc; avoid passive stretch
Strengthening (6–12 weeks)Rebuild soleus–gastrocnemius strength and the calf pumpIsometric → concentric → eccentric (heel raises); stationary cycling; proprioception
Return to function (3–6 months)Restore push-off power and plyometric capacitySingle-limb heel raises, hopping, running progression, push-off and plyometric drills before sport

Key clinical points. (i) The destroyed gait phase is terminal stance–pre-swing, so the first functional goal is a pain-free heel raise. (ii) A heel-raise wedge or orthosis offloads the tendon early while still allowing the calf pump. (iii) Tendon elongation — the chief cause of persistent weakness — is minimised by protecting against early passive dorsiflexion stretch. (iv) Accelerated functional rehabilitation (early weight-bearing and controlled motion) gives outcomes similar to operative repair, so the conservative and post-operative pathways converge.

Conclusion. TA rupture removes the calf's lever and the gait's push-off; the resulting hip-dominant, flat-footed, shortened-step pattern is the body's intelligent compensation. Rehabilitation is staged to protect the repair, then progressively reload the triceps surae until push-off power and plyometric capacity return.

5Recent advances

  • Hansen et al. (2022) — Gait analysis after Achilles tendon rupture showing a persistent deficit in peak ankle plantarflexor power at push-off (about 14% at 6 months, improving to about 7% at 12 months), with tendon elongation of roughly 18-19 mm versus the uninjured side.
  • Pečjak and Kozinc (2023) — Review showing triceps surae atrophy and tendon elongation persist for 4 years and beyond, regardless of operative or conservative treatment, with calf strength deficits of roughly 10-30%.
  • Stäudle et al. (2021) — Study showing muscle-tendon remodelling (a longer, stiffer tendon with shorter fascicles and greater pennation) shifts peak force production to a more dorsiflexed ankle angle and leaves an approximately 31% plantarflexion moment deficit.
  • Wenning et al. (2021) — EMG study showing neuromechanical activation remains altered up to 3.5 years after repair, with higher gastrocnemius activation during push-off and reduced tibialis anterior pre-activation before ground contact.
  • Willits et al. (2010) — Multicentre randomised trial showing that with accelerated functional rehabilitation (early weight-bearing and early range of motion) nonoperative and operative treatment of acute Achilles rupture gave clinically similar outcomes, and that accelerated functional rehabilitation is safe and effective.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT-MSK 2020 Ordinance & Syllabus, Paper II Unit 6 (lower extremity joints, soft tissues) and Unit 8 (normal and pathological gait).
  2. Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System. — biomechanics of the ankle-foot complex.
  3. Levangie PK, Norkin CC. Joint Structure and Function. F.A. Davis — ankle-foot complex chapter.
  4. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. Elsevier — lower leg, ankle and foot assessment (Thompson/Simmonds test) (syllabus reference 4).
  5. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. F.A. Davis — Achilles tendon rupture rehabilitation sections.
  6. Aufwerber S, Naili JE, Grävare Silbernager K, Ackermann PW. No effects of early functional mobilization on gait patterns after acute Achilles tendon rupture repair. J Orthop Res. 2022;40(8):1932–1942.
  7. Long-term deficits in muscle composition, performance and quality of movement after Achilles tendon rupture: a review. BioMed (MDPI). 2023;3(1):12.
