Question 1 · 10 marks

Q1. Explain the structure and functions of the neuro-muscular system.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 1a — Basic concepts of the musculoskeletal system: anatomy and physiology of the neuro-muscular system

★ Memory hook — Final Common Pathway: Structure → Function → Lesion. Say “motor unit”, “size principle”, “alpha–gamma co-activation” and “final common pathway” once each.

1Introduction

The neuro-muscular system is the functional marriage of the nervous system with skeletal muscle — Sherrington's final common pathway through which every intention to move becomes force on bone. Structure first, then map every structure onto a function: that is exactly how the marking pattern runs, so do not write two pages of fibre biochemistry and forget the loop back to movement.

2Physiology

The structural unit is the motor unit: one anterior horn cell, its axon, and every muscle fibre it supplies. Fine-control muscles such as the extraocular muscles have a handful of fibres per unit; postural giants such as gastrocnemius may have over a thousand — the CNS trades precision for power by choosing unit size. Muscle fibres are typed I (slow, oxidative, fatigue-resistant, postural), IIa (fast oxidative-glycolytic) and IIx (fast glycolytic, fatiguable). On the sensory side sit the muscle spindle (length and rate of length change; intrafusal fibres; Ia and II afferents), the Golgi tendon organ (tension; Ib afferent), and joint, skin and vestibular receptors feeding the same loop. The wiring is closed: command travels down, information about length and tension travels back.

Force production and grading: force is raised by recruitment obeying Henneman's size principle (small units first) and by rate coding of discharge. Posture and tone: alpha–gamma co-activation keeps the spindle sensitive while the muscle shortens, so the antigravity muscles hold a steady background tone. Protection: the myotatic stretch reflex, the withdrawal (flexor) reflex and the crossed extensor reflex guard the limb within milliseconds. Proprioception: the same afferents give the cortex its map of joint position — the raw material for movement re-education.

Fig 1 — The motor unit drawn as a closed loop. Label the anterior horn cell, the axon, the fibres it supplies, and the spindle afferent looping back: four labels that map directly onto the marks.

3Pathophysiology

Where the wiring is disturbed, function fails in predictable ways. Immobilisation and disuse switch the muscle down: motor-unit discharge rates fall, oxidative enzymes drop and type II fibres drift toward the fast-fatiguable end, so strength declines faster than bulk in the first weeks. Pain adds reflex guarding and arthrogenic inhibition — the joint’s effusion inhibits its own motor drive — and the deep stabilisers are inhibited first, a pattern that long outlives the original injury. Fibre transformation is slow in both directions: the endurance-to-power shift of detraining takes months to reverse, which is why rehabilitation is measured in weeks but remodelling in months.

4Answer

Every physiotherapy tool speaks this language. Manual muscle testing interrogates the motor output; the Ashworth scale interrogates tone; progressive resistance training works because recruitment and rate coding respond to load within weeks, while fibre transformation takes months. Lower motor neuron lesions waste the muscle and abolish reflexes; upper motor neuron lesions do the opposite — knowing the wiring tells them apart at the bedside. In one sentence: the neuro-muscular system converts electrical intention into graded mechanical force and reports back, and every assessment and treatment we give is read or written through that loop.

5Recent advances

  • Stevens-Lapsley et al. (2012) — a randomised controlled trial showed that adding neuromuscular electrical stimulation to standard rehabilitation from 48 hours after total knee arthroplasty attenuated quadriceps strength loss and improved functional performance through one year, a landmark for NMES in orthopaedic rehabilitation.
  • Maddocks et al. (2016) — a double-blind placebo-controlled trial found that home-based NMES improved six-minute walk distance in patients with severe COPD who could not exercise, confirming NMES as a substitute when voluntary training is not possible.
  • Borzuola et al. (2025) — neuromuscular electrical stimulation superimposed on voluntary contractions (NMES+) acutely raised motor-unit discharge rate and the proportion of common synaptic input and improved force steadiness, giving a mechanism for its use in rehabilitation.
  • Duchateau & Hainaut (1990) — classic immobilisation studies showed that disuse suppresses firing preferentially in low-threshold motor units while higher-threshold neuromuscular junctions are more prone to disruption, a selective, threshold-specific weakness.

6References

  1. Guyton and Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — motor unit and reflex physiology.
  2. Lehmkuhl and Smith, Brunnstrom's Clinical Kinesiology — muscle structure and fibre types.
  3. Hislop, Montgomery, Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing — clinical application of motor output.
  4. Motor unit discharge behavior in human muscles throughout force gradation: a systematic review and meta-analysis with meta-regression. 2025 (systematic review).
  5. Thomas ACQ, Stead CA, Burniston JG, Phillips SM. Exercise-specific adaptations in human skeletal muscle: molecular mechanisms of making muscles fit and mighty. Free Radical Biology and Medicine 2024;223:341–356.
Question 2 · 10 marks

Q2. How would you analyze, using the various anthropometry methods, to differentiate normal and abnormal curvature of the spine?

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 2a — Anthropometry: tools of measurement, body size, shape and proportion

★ Memory hook — Plumb line, then the sagittal trio 20–40 / 20–45 / 40–60°, then five methods, then the two thresholds: 5–7° scoliometer, 10° Cobb.

1Introduction

Anthropometry is the radiation-free way to separate normal from abnormal spinal curvature: it does not diagnose, it quantifies asymmetry and tells you when to reach for a radiograph. Before any measurement, state the standard you will judge against — the plumb line and the normal sagittal ranges — because the whole answer is a comparison against that standard.

2Physiology

Begin by defining the standard you will judge against. In the coronal plane the spine is straight, and a plumb line dropped from the external auditory meatus should pass through the shoulder, the greater trochanter, just behind the knee and the lateral malleolus. In the sagittal plane there are three gentle curves — cervical lordosis about 20–40 degrees, thoracic kyphosis about 20–45 degrees and lumbar lordosis about 40–60 degrees. State these numbers; examiners award the definition marks for reference values, not for adjectives.

Fig 2 — The spine in side view against a plumb line, with the three sagittal reference ranges. Drawing this anchors the whole answer: judge every measurement against these numbers.

3Pathophysiology

Coronal plane: any measurable lateral curvature is suspicious; scoliosis as a diagnosis is reserved radiologically for a Cobb angle of 10 degrees or more, so your anthropometric job is to find the asymmetry that predicts it — trunk rotation above about 5–7 degrees, a positive plumb deviation, or unequal shoulder or iliac crest levels by more than about 1 cm. Sagittal plane: kyphosis beyond about 45–50 degrees, a lumbar lordosis outside roughly 40–60 degrees, or a C7 plumb line falling well ahead of the sacrum signals abnormal curvature — postural kyphosis versus Scheuermann or a flat-back, for example. Progressive loss of sitting-height gain in a growing child flags a worsening curve.

4Answer

First, observation with a plumb line and a marked grid: shoulder level, scapular and iliac crest levels, skin folds at the waist, head tilt — free, repeatable, and the backbone of any school-screening camp in India. Second, the flexible ruler (flexicurve): mould it along the spinous processes from C7 to the sacrum, trace it on paper, and measure the kyphosis angle or the lateral deviation index on the tracing. Third, the inclinometer and scoliometer: with the patient in Adam's forward-bend position, the angle of trunk rotation is read at the apex; an angle of about 5–7 degrees or more is the accepted referral threshold. Fourth, goniometric inclinometry in standing for sagittal curves — two inclinometers over T12–L1 and the sacrum give a lumbar lordosis angle. Fifth, stature anthropometry: standing height, sitting height and arm span, which expose growth-related changes and track progression in adolescent deformity; a rib hump can be quantified with callipers or a level and ruler in centimetres.

Observe with plumb line and levels; if asymmetry is found, flexicurve and scoliometer quantify it; if the scoliometer reads above the threshold or the curve progresses on serial measurement, refer for radiographic Cobb measurement, which remains the gold standard. Anthropometry gives you a cheap, radiation-free way to screen, document and follow up — that sentence is a fitting conclusion and earns the application mark.

5Recent advances

  • Schreiber et al. (2016) — an assessor-blinded randomised controlled trial found Schroth physiotherapeutic scoliosis-specific exercises added to standard care reduced the largest Cobb angle compared with standard care alone in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, the first rigorous exercise trial for scoliosis.
  • Schreiber et al. (2017) — a secondary analysis of that trial reported a number needed to treat of about 4 for Schroth exercises to prevent one curve progression over six months, showing the effect is clinically important, not just statistically significant.
  • Negrini et al. (2018) — the SOSORT 2016 guidelines recommend physiotherapeutic scoliosis-specific exercises, used alone or with bracing, to limit progression, reduce pain and delay surgery for curves under 45°.
  • Rohde et al. (2025) — a multicentre prospective validation study found a smartphone-based surface-topography app detected clinically significant scoliosis (major curve ≥ 20°) with 96.4% sensitivity versus 50% for the scoliometer, offering a radiation-free screen for field and clinic.
  • Bertsch et al. (2025) — a systematic review and meta-analysis found surface topography and ultrasonography the most studied and most promising radiation-free alternatives to repeated radiographs for scoliosis monitoring.

6References

  1. Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment — posture and spinal alignment assessment.
  2. Nordin and Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — spinal curvatures and loads.
  3. Levangie and Norkin, Joint Structure and Function — vertebral column mechanics.
  4. Rohde MS, et al. Smartphone-based surface topography app accurately detects clinically significant scoliosis. Spine Deformity 2025;13(4):1051–1057.
  5. Exploring radiation-free scoliosis monitoring: systematic review and meta-analysis of non-ionizing methods. BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders 2025.
Question 3 · 10 marks

Q3. Explain the concepts of energetics in chronic osteoarthritis of knee.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 3c — Biomechanics: energetics, efficiency and metabolic energy cost

★ Memory hook — Energetics = Work ÷ Energy: define work, energy, efficiency and oxygen cost; then apply them to OA, name the deconditioning spiral, then treat the budget.

1Introduction

Movement costs fuel. Mechanical work is the product of force moving through displacement, divided into internal work (moving limb segments against each other) and external work (moving the body against gravity and ground). Metabolic energy is the fuel bill, paid in oxygen — roughly five kilocalories per litre of oxygen consumed. Efficiency links the two: mechanical work divided by metabolic cost; for level walking the body manages only about 25–30 percent, and the oxygen cost of walking is expressed per kilogram per metre walked.

2Physiology

In health, walking is an energy bargain. Mechanical work splits into internal work — moving the limb segments relative to one another — and external work against gravity, and the body performs it at only about 25–30 percent efficiency; the rest is lost as heat. The pendulum-like exchange of kinetic and potential energy in swing, the storage and return of energy in the Achilles tendon, and the smooth path of the centre of gravity under Saunders’ determinants all hold the oxygen cost of walking near its minimum — which is why the body spontaneously chooses a self-selected speed that is the most economical per metre.

3Pathophysiology

Pain and effusion drive co-contraction — simultaneous quadriceps and hamstring activation that splints the joint. Protection has a price: a stiff, co-contracted knee does not swing freely, so internal work rises. Cartilage loss and varus alignment shift the ground reaction force medially, enlarging the knee adduction moment, so the same step demands more muscle force at the knee. The patient responds with a slower, shorter-stride, more flexed-knee gait — comfortable per second, but costlier per metre, because the energetic optimum for walking is near the self-selected speed that OA now forces them to abandon. Add quadriceps weakness — partly arthogenic inhibition — and each newton of support costs a larger fraction of the available muscle, which means higher relative intensity for the same stroll to the bus stop.

Because walking feels expensive, the patient walks less; walking less lowers cardiovascular fitness; lower fitness makes the same walk a higher percentage of maximum capacity — breathlessness, fatigue, then still less activity. This spiral is the energetics of chronic OA stated as a clinical course, and naming it earns the analysis mark.

Fig 3 — A two-bar comparison is enough: normal versus OA energy cost per metre, with the mechanism arrow between them. The examiner wants the reasoning, not an elaborate graph.

4Answer

Indirect calorimetry from expired gases gives oxygen cost per metre. When a metabolic cart is unavailable — the usual Indian OPD reality — the physiological cost index approximates it: heart rate while walking minus resting heart rate, divided by walking speed. Either way, document speed too, because cost per metre without speed is half a story.

Everything we do for knee OA can be read energetically. Aerobic and strengthening training raise the efficiency of the engine; weight loss shrinks the load — every kilogram of body weight transmits roughly three to four kilograms of force through the knee during stairs and squats; a cane in the opposite hand unloads the medial compartment and trims the adduction moment; pacing and energy conservation spread the budget across the day. State it as one chain: OA raises the cost of walking, and our job is to lower the cost, raise the capacity, or both.

5Recent advances

  • Uhlrich et al. (2025) — a randomised controlled trial in Lancet Rheumatology showed that personalised foot-progression-angle gait retraining cut medial knee pain and the knee adduction moment peak over one year, a non-surgical physiotherapy option for medial compartment OA.
  • Holden et al. (2023) — an OARSI international consensus produced 54 recommendations for delivering therapeutic exercise in knee and hip OA, covering assessment, dosing, progression and adherence to standardise physiotherapy practice.
  • Skou & Roos (2017) — the GLA:D programme showed that structured patient education plus supervised neuromuscular exercise delivered by physiotherapists nationwide improved pain and function in knee and hip OA, closing the guideline-to-practice gap.
  • Fransen et al. (2015) — a Cochrane review confirmed that land-based therapeutic exercise reduces knee OA pain and improves physical function, with benefit sustained for at least two to six months after treatment.
  • Wang et al. (2021) — a meta-analysis of foot-progression-angle modification found toe-out gait lowers the second knee adduction moment peak and angular impulse in medial knee OA, while toe-in lowers the first peak.

6References

  1. Nordin and Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — work, energy and efficiency of gait.
  2. ACSM's Resource Manual for Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription — oxygen cost and training implications.
  3. O'Sullivan and Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation — functional training and energy conservation in chronic disease.
  4. Personalised gait retraining for medial compartment knee osteoarthritis: a randomised controlled trial. The Lancet Rheumatology 2025.
  5. Wang S, et al. How foot progression angle affects knee adduction moment and angular impulse in patients with and without medial knee osteoarthritis: a meta-analysis. Arthritis Care & Research 2021;73(12):1763–1776.
Question 4 · 10 marks

Q4. Discuss the changes in gait in older adults.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 4b — Biomechanics across the lifespan: gait changes in older adults

★ Memory hook — Older gait: Shorter stride (not slower steps), Double support 18→26%, ankle push-off down, and 0.8 m/s as the danger line.

1Introduction

Gait in older adults is best read as a negotiated compromise: the mature pattern is quietly re-tuned to buy stability with speed. To describe the change you must first fix the baseline — normal mature gait and the determinants that make it economical — and then measure every deviation against it.

2Physiology

Mature gait is free, reciprocal and economical: self-selected speed near 1.3 metres per second in healthy younger adults, stride length about one and a half times leg length, stance phase 60 percent and swing 40 percent of the cycle, and smooth arm swing opposite the legs. Saunders' classic determinants — pelvic rotation, tilt, knee flexion in stance, foot and ankle mechanisms, and lateral pelvic displacement — flatten the path of the centre of gravity and minimise the metabolic cost of transport. Name the baseline; every change you list is measured against it.

3Pathophysiology

Older adults walk slower — nearer 1.0 metre per second by the seventies — and the reduction is driven mainly by shorter stride length rather than slower steps; cadence changes little or even rises slightly. Stance phase lengthens, and double support time grows from about 18 percent of the cycle in youth toward 26 percent and beyond. Both feet on the ground longer means the body spends less time balancing on one leg — the biomechanical signature of trading speed for safety. Base of support widens slightly, and step-to-step variability increases, which is a better falls predictor than slow speed alone.

The consistent finding is a reduced ankle plantarflexor burst at push-off (the A2 power peak), with compensation at the hip — a hip strategy gait. Ankle range falls, knee flexion in stance may be slightly reduced, arm swing diminishes, and the head-and-trunk path oscillates a little more, so the determinants that once smoothed the ride work less efficiently and oxygen cost per metre rises. Fear of falling adds co-contraction of the shank muscles — the older person carries a stiffer, more guarded leg — and sarcopenia of the plantarflexors removes the engine.

Fig 4 — Two gait-cycle bars with the double-support ends shaded. One glance carries the whole answer: stance lengthens, swing shortens, balance improves, speed and economy fall.

4Answer

Slowing alone is an adaptation, not a disease; what should alarm the clinician is a speed below about 0.8 metres per second (the rough threshold for independent community ambulation), marked variability, a Parkinsonian or hemiplegic pattern, or a new widening of the base. Assessment combines observation, the timed up-and-go, and 10-metre walk timing; treatment is strength and balance training, challenge to the balance systems under supervision, and management of vision, vestibular function and foot-wear. The message for the exam: the older gait is a negotiated compromise between mobility and stability, and our job is to keep the negotiation from tipping into falls.

5Recent advances

  • Sherrington et al. (2019) — a Cochrane review of 108 trials (23,407 participants) found exercise reduces the rate of falls in community-dwelling older adults by 23%, with balance and functional training the most effective and greater effects when delivered by a physiotherapist.
  • Adam et al. (2023) — a 12-month decline in gait speed predicted falls in community-dwelling older adults regardless of cognitive status, a fall risk that rises even before the conventional 1.0 m/s threshold.
  • Neira Álvarez et al. (2024) — wearable-sensor gait parameters stratified older adults by frailty and fall history, supporting sensor-based assessment alongside the timed up-and-go and 10-metre walk.
  • Verghese et al. (2009) — increased step-to-step variability remained a better falls predictor than slow speed alone, so variability should be measured, not just average speed.

6References

  1. Saunders, Inman and Eberhart, JBJS 1953 — the major determinants of gait.
  2. Nordin and Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — gait kinetics and kinematics.
  3. O'Sullivan and Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation — gait assessment and balance training in older adults.
  4. Change in gait speed and fall risk among community-dwelling older adults with and without mild cognitive impairment: a retrospective cohort analysis. BMC Geriatrics 2023.
  5. Predictors of fall risk in older adults using the G-STRIDE inertial sensor: an observational multicenter case-control study. BMC Geriatrics 2023.
Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. Explain the adaptation of different systems during an exercise program.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 5c — Physiological basis of movement: adaptations of different systems

★ Memory hook — Adaptation order: Neural (weeks 1–4) → Cardiovascular/metabolic (weeks 4–8) → Structural tissue (months). Overload, specificity, reversibility.

1Introduction

Every single session produces acute responses — heart rate climbs, ventilation rises, muscle burns substrate — which subside within hours. A program is repeated, progressive doses, and chronic adaptation is the body rebuilding itself between sessions in the direction of the imposed demand. The overload principle decides the direction, specificity the system, and reversibility the fate of anyone who stops — all three words should appear in your first paragraph.

2Physiology

Resting heart rate falls because stroke volume rises — a larger, more compliant ventricle filling better through an expanded plasma volume. Submaximal heart rate for a given workload drops, cardiac output at max rises, capillary density and mitochondrial density in trained muscle increase, and endothelial function improves with a modest fall in resting blood pressure. This is why the post-MI or post-arthroplasty patient who could barely walk the ward corridor ends up comfortably walking to the market within months.

The lungs change little structurally in healthy adults, but ventilation becomes more efficient — lower breathing frequency at a given workload, better coordination, and improved lactate buffering through adaptations in muscle. Neuromuscular adaptation is the early superstar: in the first two to four weeks, strength rises out of proportion to any visible muscle growth because the nervous system learns — better recruitment, higher discharge rates, less antagonist co-activation, refined motor unit synchrony. That is why the frail elderly patient on the ward doubles her sit-to-stand score in week two, long before hypertrophy could account for it.

Insulin sensitivity improves within days of a single session's effect on GLUT4 translocation and persists with training; oxidative enzymes multiply; fat oxidation becomes a larger share of the fuel mix. Bone follows Wolff's law — it thickens where the load is imposed, which is why weight-bearing and resistance exercise, not just tablets, are part of osteoporosis management. Tendon and ligament gain tensile strength slowly, weeks behind muscle, a timing mismatch the prescribing therapist must respect. Sleep quality, mood and pain thresholds also shift — worth one line, because our musculoskeletal patients notice these first.

Fig 5 — The adaptation staircase: neural first, cardiovascular and metabolic next, structural last. One timeline drawn this way answers "adaptation of different systems" and doubles as a progression-planning chart in the clinic.

3Pathophysiology

The same systems fail in reverse when the stimulus is withdrawn or the dose is wrong. Detraining reverses the gains within weeks — plasma volume falls, resting heart rate climbs back toward baseline and oxidative enzymes retreat — which is why a patient who stops after six good weeks slides back. Overload applied faster than tissue can remodel produces injury rather than adaptation: tendon and bone lag muscle by weeks, so maximal loading in week one of a program tears what a graded program would have strengthened. Chronic overtraining adds a maladaptive systemic picture — persistent fatigue, disturbed sleep and blunted hormonal responses — the mirror image of healthy adaptation.

4Answer

Adaptation is predictable and time-sequenced: neural in the first month, cardiovascular and metabolic across the first two months, structural tissue over months to a year. A program that ignores this sequence — maximal loads to a tendon in week one — invites injury; a program that respects it turns a deconditioned MSK patient into a functioning one.

5Recent advances

  • Schoenfeld et al. (2017) — a systematic review and meta-analysis found a graded dose-response between weekly resistance-training volume and muscle hypertrophy, with each additional weekly set adding roughly 0.37% greater growth, guiding loading in strengthening programmes.
  • Schoenfeld et al. (2016) — a meta-analysis showed that training each muscle group at least twice a week, at equal volume, produces superior hypertrophy to once a week, informing strength-training frequency.
  • Kongsgaard et al. (2007) — the first study to report tendon hypertrophy after resistance training, showing 12 weeks of heavy knee-extension training increased patellar tendon cross-sectional area and stiffness while light training did not, linking load to connective-tissue adaptation.
  • Bohm et al. (2015) — a systematic review and meta-analysis showed mechanical loading raises tendon stiffness and modulus, with high-strain resistance protocols producing the greatest adaptation, a basis for loading in tendinopathy.
  • Wisløff et al. (2007) — a randomised trial found high-intensity interval training produced greater cardiovascular and skeletal-muscle adaptation than moderate continuous training in heart failure, reshaping aerobic exercise prescription.

6References

  1. ACSM's Resource Manual for Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription — systemic adaptations to training.
  2. Guyton and Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — cardiovascular and metabolic responses.
  3. Kisner and Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — progression and tissue-healing timelines.
  4. Exercise metabolism and adaptation in skeletal muscle. Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology 2023;24.
  5. A primer on global molecular responses to exercise in skeletal muscle: Omics in focus. 2025 (review).
Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. Explain the mechanics and pathomechanics of non-specific neck pain.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 6c — Mechanics and pathomechanics of the spine: cervical region

★ Memory hook — Text-neck is a lever problem: every cm the head moves forward multiplies the extensor force; creep → deep flexor inhibition → “non-specific” pain.

1Introduction

“Non-specific” is the operative word: the tissues are normal, the load they receive is not. The answer runs as a chain — normal cervical mechanics, the load imposed by sustained postures, and the pathomechanical consequence — and stops short of naming fracture, tumour or radiculopathy, because those are specific and out of scope.

2Physiology

The cervical spine is a lordotic mobile column carrying a head of about four and a half to five kilograms. The lordosis is not decoration: it places the compressive load closer to the axes of the posterior muscles and the uncovertebral joints, distributing stress. Functionally it is two regions — the craniovertebral complex for nodding and rotation, and the mid and lower cervical segments for combined movements. Side-flexion in the mid and lower cervical spine is classically coupled with rotation to the same side, a rule broken only at the craniovertebral joints, where rotation is coupled with slight opposite side-flexion. Motion segments each contribute roughly 13–23 degrees of flexion-extension on in-vivo studies, with the mid-cervical levels (C4–C5/C5–C6) among the most mobile — which is why degeneration shows there first.

In neutral, the head's centre of mass sits almost over the cervical column and the extensor moment arm is small. Every centimetre the head drifts forward lengthens the horizontal moment arm of that five-kilogram head, and the extensor force must multiply to balance it — the familiar biomechanics of the computer-and-mobile posture of our OPD patients, who now include young adults with text-neck patterns. The flexion moment also loads the posterior elements, capsules and intervertebral discs eccentrically.

3Pathophysiology

Sustained static flexion imposes a constant load on viscoelastic tissue, and creep follows: ligaments and the posterior annulus lengthen under a load they were built to carry only briefly, and recovery lags minutes to hours behind the insult. Repeated daily, microstrain accumulates in poorly vascularised tissue. The deep neck flexors — longus capitis and colli — become inhibited while the superficial sternocleidomastoid and upper trapezius take over, so the segment loses its fine local control. Proprioception from fatigued cervical muscles degrades, and the patient now holds posture by passive structures rather than active control. Nociception from ligament, disc and muscle triggers protective spasm and referred pain over the scapula. Nothing here is structurally "specific" — no fracture, no tumour, no radiculopathy — yet the mechanics fully explain the pain, which is precisely why the exam question says non-specific.

Fig 6 — The forward head as a first-class lever problem: one circle, one dashed gravity line, one arrow for the growing moment arm. This drawing IS the pathomechanics of non-specific neck pain.

4Answer

Treatment therefore reverses the chain: posture re-education shrinks the moment arm, micro-breaks every 20–30 minutes outlast creep recovery, deep neck flexor training restores the local control the superficial muscles stole, and McKenzie's assessment of directional preference — often retraction and extension in postural syndromes — tests which movement re-centres the segment. Conclude with the one-liner the examiner wants: non-specific neck pain is a load-management problem — the tissues are normal, the dose they receive is not.

5Recent advances

  • Blanpied et al. (2017) — the APTA/JOSPT clinical practice guideline classifies neck pain and recommends manual therapy plus mixed cervicoscapulothoracic exercise (coordination, strengthening, endurance) as first-line physiotherapy, the benchmark for evidence-based neck-pain management.
  • Tsiringakis et al. (2020) — a systematic review and meta-analysis found motor control training of the deep neck flexors with pressure biofeedback improves pain and disability in neck pain and is superior to strength-endurance training of the cervical muscles.
  • Martín Gómez et al. (2019) — a systematic review and meta-analysis showed craniocervical flexion exercise outperforms other treatments for chronic non-specific neck pain, confirming the deep-flexor retraining rationale.
  • Falla et al. (2004) — better deep cervical flexor performance correlates with reduced superficial sternocleidomastoid activity, the motor-control reversal that treatment targets.

6References

  1. McKenzie and May, The Cervical and Thoracic Spine: Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy — directional preference and postural syndromes.
  2. Levangie and Norkin, Joint Structure and Function — cervical coupled motion and loading.
  3. Butler and Jones, Mobilisation of the Nervous System — mechanosensitivity in persistent pain.
  4. Martin-Gomez C, et al. Motor control using cranio-cervical flexion exercises versus other treatments for non-specific chronic neck pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Musculoskeletal Science and Practice 2019;42:52–59.
  5. Motor control training of deep neck flexors with pressure biofeedback improves pain and disability in patients with neck pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Musculoskeletal Science and Practice 2020;50:102220.
Question 7 · 10 marks

Q7. How would you distinguish the mechanics and pathomechanics of the anterior cruciate ligament of the knee?

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 6d — Mechanics and pathomechanics of the lower extremity: the knee

★ Memory hook — ACL: 85% of anterior restraint; AM bundle tight in flexion, PL bundle tight in extension; Lachman most sensitive, Pivot shift most specific.

1Introduction

“Distinguish” is the verb: the examiner wants mechanics (how the intact ligament behaves) set against pathomechanics (how the knee misbehaves once it fails), and then the bedside tests that separate the two. Structure, bundle behaviour, the injury mechanism and its consequences form one continuous argument.

2Physiology

The ACL runs from the posteromedial aspect of the lateral femoral condyle down to the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia, an oblique course that makes it the primary restraint to anterior tibial translation — it provides about 85 percent of that restraint — and a secondary restraint to rotation and hyperextension. Mechanoreceptors within it feed the CNS (Hilton's law), which is why ACL injury damages not just stability but reflex control. Anatomically it behaves as two functional bundles: the anteromedial bundle, taut in flexion, and the posterolateral bundle, taut in extension — reciprocal tensioning that keeps some fibres loaded throughout the arc. Within terminal extension lives the screw-home mechanism: as the knee locks, the tibia externally rotates on the femur, and the ACL winds up and tightens.

Fig 7 — Femur, tibia, and the two bundles crossing from the tibial plateau to the lateral condyle, with the flexion-arc arrows. Label AM and PL and their tension states — that pairing is the "mechanics" half of the answer in one drawing.

3Pathophysiology

The classic non-contact mechanism is deceleration with the foot planted: the femur internally rotates and adducts over a fixed tibia with the knee near 20 degrees of flexion — valgus collapse. The lateral tibial plateau subluxes anteriorly under the lateral femoral condyle and reduces with a clunk as the knee extends: the pivot shift episode, often remembered by the patient as "it went out and came back". Hyperextension injuries and direct blows, as on a two-wheeler, tear it by other routes. A partial tear leaves the checkrein intact; a complete tear removes anterior restraint, so the quadriceps — pulling up the slope of the tibial plateau — now drags the tibia forward on every attempted extension under load.

Episodes of giving way on pivoting, Indian-style squatting and cross-legged sitting, stairs and uneven roads; secondary meniscal and chondral damage from repeated subluxation; arthrogenic inhibition weakening the quadriceps; accelerated osteoarthritis; and lost proprioceptive acuity delaying protective reflexes further. The ligament does not heal to functional competence because synovial fluid bathes the torn ends — a one-line justification for why conservative care must build muscle instead of waiting for the ligament.

4Answer

The Lachman test — knee near 30 degrees, anterior drawer of the tibia — is the most sensitive clinical test and should be named first; the pivot-shift test is the most specific though hardest to elicit in a guarded patient; the instrumented arthrometer quantifies the translation. Distinguish mechanism from pathomechanics in your answer: mechanism is how it tore, pathomechanics is how the knee misbehaves afterwards — that distinction is exactly what the question is testing.

5Recent advances

  • Waldén et al. (2012) — a cluster randomised controlled trial in 4564 adolescent female footballers found a 15-minute neuromuscular warm-up (core stability, balance, knee alignment) reduced the rate of ACL injury by 64%, the strongest evidence for exercise-based prevention.
  • Silvers-Granelli et al. (2017) — a cluster randomised controlled trial in collegiate male soccer showed the FIFA 11+ warm-up reduced ACL injuries about four-fold, extending prevention evidence to male players.
  • Grindem et al. (2016) — the Delaware-Oslo ACL cohort showed that delaying return to sport until quadriceps strength and hop-test symmetry criteria are met reduced reinjury risk by 84%, establishing objective return-to-sport testing.
  • Sundberg et al. (2025) — a systematic review of 62 studies and 5612 ACL injury situations classified sport-specific mechanisms into four patterns — change of direction, landing, direct contact and gear-induced — tailoring prevention to each sport.
  • Wojtys et al. (2016) — growing evidence shows the ACL can fail from repeated submaximal loading cycles (fatigue failure), challenging the dogma that non-contact tears are always a single supramaximal overload.

6References

  1. Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment — Lachman, pivot shift and arthrometer testing.
  2. Nordin and Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — ACL restraint and knee kinematics.
  3. Donatelli and Wooden, Orthopaedic Physical Therapy — rehabilitation after ACL injury.
  4. Della Villa F, et al. Systematic video analysis of ACL injuries in professional male football: injury mechanisms, situational patterns and biomechanics in 134 consecutive cases. British Journal of Sports Medicine 2020;54(23):1423–1432.
  5. Sport-specific injury mechanisms and situational patterns of ACL injuries: a comprehensive systematic review. Sports Medicine 2025.
Question 8 · 10 marks

Q8. Explain the mechanism of control of posture.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 7b — Posture: control of posture

★ Memory hook — Postural control = Input → Integration → Output; latencies 30–50 / 100–150 / 200+ ms; feed-forward before feedback.

1Introduction

Postural control is the continuous regulation of the body's centre of mass over its base of support — in standing, an inverted pendulum that would topple were it not corrected several times a second. The continual small corrections appear as postural sway, and sway itself is the measurable proof that control exists: perfectly rigid posture would mean falling, not standing. Distinguish static control (quiet standing) from dynamic control (maintaining equilibrium while moving) — the second is the one our MSK and neurological patients struggle with most.

2Physiology

Visual input supplies a stable external reference, though an inaccurate one when the environment itself moves. Vestibular input gives head position and acceleration. Somatosensory input — pressure on the soles, joint and muscle afferents — is the dominant stream on firm ground. The CNS weights the three according to context: on a compliant bus floor the somatosensory stream lies, so weighting shifts toward vision and the labyrinth; in the dark, vision is withdrawn and the remainder must cope. This sensory re-weighting is why the Romberg's test works: remove vision, and a somatosensory or vestibular deficit is unmasked.

Spinal circuits generate the fastest, crudest corrections; the brainstem — vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts — manages the antigravity set against perturbation; the cerebellum calibrates and updates them; the basal ganglia select the strategy; the cortex overrides everything for voluntary, anticipatory control. Latency tells the hierarchy apart: spinal reflexes act within roughly 30–50 milliseconds, long-loop corrections within about 100–150, and voluntary corrections beyond 200. Knowing these orders of magnitude earns analysis marks and is clinically useful in interpreting delayed balance reactions after stroke.

Anticipatory (feed-forward) postural adjustments prepare the body before movement: lift your arm and the trunk and leg muscles fire before the deltoid does. Reactive (feedback) strategies correct unexpected displacement, and scale with the size of the threat: the ankle strategy for small sway on a firm surface, the hip strategy for larger or faster displacement, and a step or a grasping arm when the base itself is exceeded. Older adults, neuropathic feet and post-operative patients drift from ankle toward hip and stepping strategies — which is the physiological story behind the falls that fill our OPDs.

Fig 8 — The inverted pendulum below, the sensorimotor loop above: input box, integration box, strategy box, arrows between. This is the whole answer as one diagram — sensors, processor, actuators.

3Pathophysiology

Postural control fails predictably when any link in the loop is damaged. Loss of a sensory stream — diabetic peripheral neuropathy, vestibular hypofunction, visual impairment — forces the CNS to reweight onto the remaining inputs, and if it cannot reweight fast enough the person sways more and steps late. Ageing slows sensory conduction and the long-loop latencies, shifts the strategy from ankle toward hip and stepping, and adds fear of falling, which stiffens the body with co-contraction. The clinical endpoint is the same in every case: sway that exceeds the base of support — a fall.

4Answer

Assessment maps to the mechanism: quiet stance with eyes open and closed on firm and compliant surfaces (the clinical sensory-organisation test), limits-of-stability and reaction to external perturbation. Training follows the same map — challenge each sensory stream, then train each strategy under progressively harder conditions. Posture control is a closed sensorimotor loop, and every fall we prevent is a loop we repaired.

5Recent advances

  • Mansfield et al. (2015) — a systematic review and meta-analysis found perturbation-based balance training, which repeatedly challenges postural reactions, reduced the number of falls by about 46% and the proportion of fallers in older adults and people with Parkinson's disease.
  • Li et al. (2018) — a randomised clinical trial in JAMA Internal Medicine found therapeutic Tai Ji Quan reduced falls more than a multimodal exercise programme in older adults at high fall risk, supporting mind-body training for postural control.
  • Cui et al. (2024) — long-term Tai Chi practice is associated with faster, more flexible sensory reweighting and better postural stability under multisensory perturbation in older adults.
  • Sung & Lee (2025) — sensory analysis scores detected trial-by-trial sensory reweighting more sensitively than equilibrium indices, identifying visual reliance as a modifiable rehabilitation target.

6References

  1. Nordin and Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — standing posture and equilibrium.
  2. Guyton and Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — vestibular and motor control hierarchy.
  3. O'Sullivan and Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation — balance assessment and training.
  4. Is It Me or the Train Moving? Humans Resolve Sensory Conflicts with a Nonlinear Feedback Mechanism in Balance Control. Journal of Neuroscience 2025;45(29).
  5. Sensory reweighting and self-motion perception for postural control. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience 2024;18:1482752.
Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. Discuss the specific pain states and syndromes in musculoskeletal conditions.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 9c — Pain: specific pain states and syndromes

★ Memory hook — Three mechanisms: Nociceptive, Neuropathic, Nociplastic. Mechanism, not region, dictates treatment.

1Introduction

Pain in musculoskeletal practice divides by mechanism, not by body part. Nociceptive pain arises from actual or threatened tissue damage — the sprained ankle, the arthritic knee — and is usually proportional, mechanical and well localised. Neuropathic pain arises from a lesion or disease of the nervous system itself — radicular pain, peripheral neuropathy. Nociplastic pain arises from altered nociception without clear tissue or nerve damage: the nervous system has turned its own gain up. Gate control theory (Melzack and Wall, 1965) and Melzack's later neuromatrix (1999) explain how modulation — spinal gating, descending inhibition, brain-body maps — lets the same input hurt differently in different people; cite both, briefly, and you have the theoretical frame examiners look for.

2Physiology

Normal nociception is a protective, well-behaved system. A noxious stimulus depolarises free nerve endings, the signal travels by A-delta and C fibres to the dorsal horn, ascends the spinothalamic tract, and is modulated on the way up and down. Melzack and Wall’s gate control (1965) showed that large-fibre input and descending inhibition from the brainstem can close the gate on small-fibre pain, and Melzack’s later neuromatrix (1999) explained how the brain’s own body-map shapes the final experience. In a healthy system, pain is proportional to damage and switches off when healing completes.

3Pathophysiology

Acute pain is protective, time-limited and proportional; it resolves with healing. Chronic pain — beyond three months — outlives healing and has become, in the International Association for the Study of Pain's framing, a disorder in its own right. Inflammatory pain announces itself with rest and night pain, morning stiffness over about an hour and swelling — think rheumatoid, not osteoarthritis. Ischaemic pain — claudication — is brought on by walking and relieved by standing still in under ten minutes, and must not be confused with night cramps. Referred pain is felt remote from its source but non-dermatomal and deep — a hip referring to the knee; radicular pain follows a dermatome and often lancinating qualities — a C6 or L5 root. Recognising these patterns is the analysis core of this answer.

4Answer

Myofascial pain syndrome: a taut band with a focal trigger point that reproduces the patient's pain on pressure and refers in a characteristic pattern, with a local twitch response on snapping palpation. Fibromyalgia: widespread pain for over three months with fatigue and non-restorative sleep, diagnosed on widespread distribution and symptom severity, commonly accompanied by central sensitisation — allodynia, hyperalgesia and spread beyond any tissue story. Complex regional pain syndrome: disproportionate regional pain with sensory, vasomotor (colour and temperature change), sudomotor (sweating, oedema) and motor or trophic findings, classically after a minor limb injury or immobilisation — a familiar complication of an over-cautiously splinted Colles fracture. Whiplash-associated disorder sits in the same spectrum of persistent MSK pain with sensitisation features.

Screen every persistent MSK patient for the pattern: pain disproportionate to findings, spread beyond one region, allodynia, poor response to tissue-directed treatment, and distress (the yellow flags of fear-avoidance and catastrophising). Pain drawings and simple questionnaires document it. Treatment must then match the mechanism: nociceptive pain responds to tissue-directed manual therapy and graded loading; neuropathic to pharmacological co-management and desensitisation; nociplastic and syndromic pain to pain neuroscience education, graded activity and exercise in dosages that do not flare the system. Conclude with the examiner's sentence: we classify pain by mechanism because the mechanism, not the region, dictates the treatment.

Fig 9 — A three-branch tree with one example under each branch and the treatment rule at the bottom. The tree IS the classification, and classification is what the question means by "specific pain states".

5Recent advances

  • Louw et al. (2016) — a systematic review of 13 randomised controlled trials found pain neuroscience education reduces pain, improves function, lowers disability and reduces catastrophising in chronic musculoskeletal pain, a core physiotherapy approach for nociplastic pain.
  • Wood & Hendrick (2019) — a systematic review and meta-analysis showed that adding pain neuroscience education to usual physiotherapy improves short-term pain and disability in chronic low back pain, though long-term effects are unproven.
  • Geneen et al. (2017) — a Cochrane overview found that physical activity and exercise reduce pain severity and improve function in adults with chronic pain, with few adverse events.
  • IASP (2017, 2021) — the IASP adopted "nociplastic pain" as a third mechanistic descriptor in 2017, and in 2021 published criteria for "possible" and "probable" nociplastic pain in the musculoskeletal system.
  • Freynhagen et al. (2019) — the "mixed pain" phenotype now recognises that nociceptive, neuropathic and nociplastic mechanisms commonly coexist — for example in fibromyalgia and chronic low back pain.

6References

  1. Melzack R, Wall PD. Pain mechanisms: a new theory. Science 1965.
  2. Melzack R. From the gate to the neuromatrix. Pain 1999.
  3. Butler and Jones, Mobilisation of the Nervous System — neuropathic and sensitisation states.
  4. O'Sullivan and Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation — chronic pain management.
  5. Nociplastic pain: towards an understanding of prevalent pain conditions. The Lancet 2021.
  6. The concept of nociplastic pain — where to from here? Pain 2024.
Question 10 · 10 marks

Q10. Explain the biophysical effects of heat in adhesive capsulitis.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 10a — Biophysical effects of physical agents: heat

★ Memory hook — Heat is the assistant, not the hero: heat 15–20 min → stretch at the barrier; heated collagen keeps the length it gains.

1Introduction

Heat is a physical agent used to change tissue, not a cure for a joint. The answer moves from the biophysics of heating tissue, to choosing a modality that can reach the capsule, to the sequence that actually gains range in adhesive capsulitis, and closes with dosage, precautions and an honest conclusion.

2Physiology

Raising tissue temperature produces four effect families, each with a physiotherapy use. Vascular effects: vasodilatation and increased blood flow, which improves nutrition and clears metabolites. Metabolic effects: tissue metabolic rate rises roughly 10–13 percent for every degree Celsius — healing and enzymatic repair accelerate. Neural effects: warmth alters nerve conduction and, through the gate mechanism of Melzack and Wall, produces analgesia — large-fibre thermal input closing the gate on small-fibre pain; muscle spindle and gamma activity quietens, so muscle spasm eases. Connective tissue effects: heated collagen becomes more extensible, and — the effect that matters in this question — elongation produced while the tissue is heated is retained after cooling, where the same stretch applied to cold tissue largely recoils.

3Pathophysiology

Adhesive capsulitis is, at tissue level, a capsular contracture: synovial inflammation gives way to fibrosis of the glenohumeral capsule and coracohumeral ligament, which shorten and thicken so the joint loses volume and external rotation first. The disease runs through painful, freezing and thawing phases, and the capsule — not the muscle — is the structure that must be lengthened. This pathophysiology explains the biophysics: a contractured, densely cross-linked collagen needs heat to become extensible, and a pain-guarded joint needs analgesia before it will allow the stretch — which is why heat is applied before mobilisation rather than as a stand-alone cure.

4Answer

Superficial agents — hot packs, paraffin wax, infrared — heat skin and subcutaneous tissue to about 1–2 centimetres, warming the shoulder mostly by conduction from the surface. Because the glenohumeral capsule lies deeper, deep heating is traditionally preferred: shortwave diathermy at 27.12 MHz and therapeutic ultrasound (which heats at the 3–5 centimetre depth of the capsule and can be focused on the coracohumeral ligament and anterior capsule). In the thawing or frozen stage, where the capsule is the contractured tissue, the depth of the agent is the first clinical decision.

Adhesive capsulitis is, mechanically, a capsular contracture with pain-guarded loss of external rotation and abduction. Heat is used as the preparation, not the cure: heat the capsule for 15–20 minutes, then apply grade II–IV mobilisations and sustained stretching to the barrier in the restricted directions — external rotation, abduction, internal rotation behind the back. Heated collagen lengthens under less force, so the same stretch gains more and holds it; analgesia and reduced spasm raise the patient's tolerance, letting you work closer to the true barrier. Controlled comparisons of combined heat-and-stretch programmes report better range gain than stretch alone — Lehmann's classic principle that tissue heated before stretch retains its elongation is the sentence to quote here.

Hot packs: 15–20 minutes, adequate towel layers, checking skin in insensate or diabetic patients — a real concern in Indian OPDs where diabetic frozen shoulders abound. Deep agents: ultrasound at about 1 MHz for the deeper capsule, avoiding direct bone contact, and shortwave not used over cardiac pacemakers, metal implants, malignancy, pregnancy or acute inflammation with shortwave. The conclusion the examiner wants: heat does not melt a frozen shoulder; it lowers the pain cost and raises the tissue's willingness to be stretched — the stretch and the exercise still do the mechanical work. Prescribed that way, heat is a valuable assistant, not the hero.

Fig 10 — Two curves: elongation retained when tissue is heated before stretch versus when it is not. This single graph carries the whole "biophysical effect" argument in adhesive capsulitis — draw it and label the vertical gap as retained range.

5Recent advances

  • Teytelbaum et al. (2024) — a randomised controlled trial found an at-home high-intensity stretching device matched or beat traditional physiotherapy for adhesive capsulitis in range of motion and shoulder scores.
  • Page et al. (2014) — a Cochrane review of 32 trials found that manual therapy combined with exercise is a safe physiotherapy option for adhesive capsulitis, though glucocorticoid injection may give faster short-term relief.
  • Sung et al. (2022) — a systematic review and meta-analysis of ultrasound deep heat therapy concluded that ultrasound as a co-intervention with exercise improves pain in adhesive capsulitis, though not range of motion.
  • Amin et al. (2025) — a trial of the Spencer muscle energy technique (with a hot pack before mobilisation) reduced pain and disability more than conventional physiotherapy in adhesive capsulitis.

6References

  1. Kisner and Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — thermal agents and stretching of connective tissue.
  2. O'Sullivan and Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation — physical agents in rehabilitation.
  3. Donatelli and Wooden, Orthopaedic Physical Therapy — management of the stiff shoulder.
  4. The effectiveness of ultrasound deep heat therapy for adhesive capsulitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. 2022.
  5. Frozen shoulder: a narrative review of current treatment. 2025.
Last-Hour Sheet · Paper II

QP 8130 · 12-Nov-2025 · the 60-minute sheet — one line per idea, the night before the exam. Cover a column and test yourself.

1Neuro-muscular system

  • Motor unit = anterior horn cell + axon + all its fibres; Henneman: small units recruited first.
  • Fibre types I, IIa, IIx — oxidative to glycolytic, fatigue-resistant to fatiguable.
  • Spindle senses length (Ia/II), GTO senses tension (Ib); alpha–gamma co-activation keeps spindles sensitive.
  • Functions: graded force, tone, protective reflexes, proprioception. Sherrington: final common pathway.

2Spinal curvature by anthropometry

  • Plumb line: ear–shoulder–trochanter–lateral malleolus.
  • Sagittal normals: cervical 20–40°, thoracic 20–45°, lumbar 40–60°.
  • Flexicurve tracing; scoliometer on Adam's test — refer above about 5–7° ATR.
  • Cobb 10° or more = scoliosis (radiographic gold standard).

3Energetics of knee OA

  • Efficiency = mechanical work / metabolic energy; walking is about 25–30 percent efficient.
  • OA: co-contraction, larger adduction moment, slower gait — cost per metre rises.
  • PCI = (walking HR − resting HR) / speed.
  • Treat the budget: aerobic training, weight loss, cane in opposite hand, pacing.

4Gait in older adults

  • Speed 1.3 to about 1.0 m/s; shorter stride, not slower steps.
  • Double support 18 percent to about 26 percent.
  • Reduced ankle push-off (A2), hip compensation; more variability = falls risk.
  • Below 0.8 m/s: community ambulation threatened.

5Exercise adaptations

  • Neural gains weeks 1–4; cardiovascular and metabolic by weeks 4–8; tissue months 2–6+.
  • Stroke volume up, resting HR down, capillary and mitochondrial density up.
  • Insulin sensitivity improves within days; bone follows Wolff's law.
  • Overload, specificity, reversibility — say all three.

6Non-specific neck pain

  • Head about 5 kg; every cm forward lengthens the extensor moment arm.
  • Sustained flexion → creep in ligament and disc; recovery lags.
  • Deep neck flexor inhibition, superficial takeover, scapular referral.
  • Treat: posture re-education, micro-breaks every 20–30 min, deep flexor training, McKenzie directional preference.

7ACL mechanics

  • Primary restraint to anterior tibial translation (~85%); secondary to rotation.
  • AM bundle tight in flexion, PL bundle tight in extension; screw-home winds it in terminal extension.
  • Injury: non-contact deceleration, femur internally rotates over fixed tibia — pivot shift.
  • Lachman most sensitive, pivot shift most specific; arthrometer quantifies.

8Control of posture

  • Postural control = COM over base of support; sway is the visible proof.
  • Three inputs — visual, vestibular, somatosensory — weighted to context.
  • Latencies: spinal 30–50 ms, long loop 100–150 ms, voluntary 200+ ms.
  • Feed-forward (anticipatory) versus feedback (ankle, hip, step strategies).

9Pain states and syndromes

  • Three mechanisms: nociceptive, neuropathic, nociplastic.
  • Inflammatory = rest and night pain, morning stiffness over an hour; claudication relieved by standing.
  • Syndromes: myofascial (trigger point, twitch response), fibromyalgia (widespread, 3 months+, fatigue), CRPS (sensory + vasomotor + sudomotor + motor).
  • Gate control 1965, neuromatrix 1999; mechanism dictates treatment.

10Heat in adhesive capsulitis

  • Metabolic rate up about 10–13 percent per °C; vasodilatation; gate-mediated analgesia.
  • Heated collagen stretched retains its elongation — heat before stretch.
  • Capsule is deep: ultrasound or shortwave, not just a hot pack.
  • Sequence: heat 15–20 min → grade II–IV mobilisation and sustained stretch at the barrier.
keep-if-nothing-else: motor unit + plumb line values + double support 18 to 26 percent + AM/PL bundles + nociceptive-neuropathic-nociplastic + heat before stretch. Six lines that can rescue a whole paper.
