Question 1 · 10 marks

Q1. Describe the factors affecting mobility during aging.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 4a — Biomechanics across the lifespan: aging

★ Memory hook — Mobility in ageing = the four pillars fall together: Joint (thin cartilage, stiff capsule), Muscle (sarcopenia → dynapenia), Nerve (slow reflexes, poor balance) and Behaviour (fear of falling). Anchor line: “mass falls 3–5% a decade, but strength and power fall 2–5 times faster.”

1Introduction

Mobility is the capacity to change and control joint position and to move the body through space — a joint-range, strength, and motor-control package. Aging does not damage one system; it quietly taxes all four pillars at once: articular, muscular, neural, and behavioural. The examiner wants you to say this framing sentence before listing factors, because it shows you understand the integrated nature of the problem.

2Physiology

Articular cartilage thins and loses water and proteoglycans, so its shock-absorbing capacity falls; joint surfaces that once glided now protest. The joint capsule and ligaments become fibrotic and less extensible through cross-linking of collagen, so capsular restriction reduces range of motion, especially at the shoulder and hip. Synovial fluid volume and viscosity change, reducing lubrication. The net result: stiffer joints with less terminal range, and a slower response to load.

The headline term is age-related loss of muscle mass and strength. Muscle mass declines roughly 3 to 5 percent per decade from the third decade, accelerating after the seventh, so that an average 80-year-old retains only about 80 percent of young-adult mass. Crucially, strength and power fall two to five times faster than mass — this quality loss is called dynapenia — because of preferential atrophy of fast type II fibres and reduced neural drive. Loss of power (force times velocity) matters most for mobility tasks: rising from a chair, climbing a bus step, catching a trip. Tendons also stiffen and lose elasticity, and their reduced compliance lowers the energy returned during gait, raising the metabolic cost of walking. Sustained connective-tissue loading produces time-dependent creep, and aged tissue recovers it more slowly, so posture-related deformities and stiffness accumulate.

Reaction time lengthens, motor-unit firing rates fall, and there is a progressive loss of motor units with reinnervation that leaves larger, clumsier units. Proprioceptive acuity declines at the joint and muscle-spindle level, vestibular hair cells degenerate, and vision loses acuity and contrast sensitivity. Standing balance therefore deteriorates, postural sway increases, and protective stepping reactions slow — which is why falls, not stiffness, are the first presenting complaint in many older Indian patients who walk barefoot on wet floors.

3Pathophysiology

Pain from osteoarthritis reduces voluntary movement; fear of falling produces self-imposed inactivity; deconditioning then accelerates sarcopenia — a vicious cycle. Comorbidities (diabetic neuropathy, stroke, cardiopulmonary limitation), medication effects, decreased skin elasticity, foot deformities, and unsafe footwear (chappals rather than supported shoes) all chip away at mobility. Bone loss (osteopenia/osteoporosis) makes falls costlier, which feeds the fear again.

4Answer

Because the decline is multifactorial, so is the management. Progressive resistance training attacks sarcopenia, but it is power training — fast, forceful movement — that most restores chair-rise, bus-step climbing and trip-recovery, because power falls faster than strength. Balance and gait retraining, review of footwear and home hazards, analgesia for osteoarthritic pain, correction of visual and vestibular deficits, and control of comorbidities and polypharmacy all help break the fear-of-falling / deconditioning cycle. The one line to remember: it is not mass but power, and not strength alone but balance, that keeps the older adult mobile.

Fig 1 — Draw three inputs (joint, muscle, nerve) funnelling into one output box (mobility down, falls risk up) with the inactivity feedback loop. This shows the examiner systems-level thinking in ten seconds.
Examiner's tip: the phrase "strength is lost two to five times faster than mass — dynapenia" is a marks magnet. Also mention power (not just strength) for chair-rise and fall-recovery; most answers stop at mass.

5Recent advances

  • Chen et al. (2023) — network meta-analysis of 50 RCTs (4,085 older adults with sarcopenia or dynapenia) confirming that resistance training, with or without nutrition, improves muscle strength and physical performance, and that moderate-to-vigorous intensity produced greater gains in muscle mass, leg-press strength and gait speed than low-intensity training.
  • Hurst et al. (2022) — set out the evidence-based resistance-exercise prescription for sarcopenia: at least two sessions weekly of 1–3 sets of 6–12 repetitions at a high degree of effort with progressive overload, noting that lower-load and resistance-band training can also build strength and mass in older adults.
  • Sayer et al. (2024) — the Global Leadership Initiative in Sarcopenia (GLIS) consensus reframing sarcopenia diagnosis around muscle strength rather than mass alone, giving physiotherapists a functional, testable target (grip strength, chair-stand, gait speed) for exercise prescription in older adults.
  • Robertson et al. (2002) — meta-analysis of the four Otago Exercise Programme trials showing that a physiotherapist-led home programme of leg strengthening and balance retraining reduced falls and fall-related injuries by about 35% in community-dwelling older adults.
  • Bull et al. (2020) — the WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour give a strong recommendation that older adults perform varied multicomponent physical activity emphasising functional balance and strength training on 3 or more days a week to enhance capacity and prevent falls.

6References

  1. Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — biomechanics of aging chapters.
  2. Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — aging, sarcopenia and exercise in older adults.
  3. Hislop, Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing — strength changes with age.
  4. Kirk B, et al. The conceptual definition of sarcopenia: Delphi consensus from the Global Leadership Initiative in Sarcopenia (GLIS). Age Ageing. 2024;53:afae052.
  5. Shen Y, et al. Exercise for sarcopenia in older people: a systematic review and network meta-analysis. J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle. 2023;14:1199–1211.
Question 2 · 10 marks

Q2. Describe the role of fascia in the musculoskeletal system.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 1c — Basic concepts: fascia

★ Memory hook — “Structure → mechanics → sensation → clinic.” Fascia is one continuous collagen–hyaluronan web that packages, transmits force sideways (myofascial force transmission), stores elastic energy and senses (Ruffini, Pacinian, myofibroblasts). Treat the glide, not just the muscle.

1Introduction

Fascia is the three-dimensional continuous web of connective tissue — mostly collagen with elastin and a hydrated ground substance rich in hyaluronan — that invests every muscle, organ, nerve and vessel. Classically it is divided into superficial fascia (subcutaneous, carrying fat and vessels), deep fascia (dense envelopes such as fascia lata, crural fascia and the thoracolumbar fascia) and visceral fascia. Modern terminology treats it as one interconnected tensional network rather than isolated sleeves.

2Physiology

Fascia serves four roles in the musculoskeletal system.

  • Packaging: it separates muscles into compartments, allows glide between them through sliding layers, and retains muscle shape so fibres contract efficiently without bulging sideways.
  • Force transmission: because connective tissue links muscle to tendon, bone and neighbouring muscle, tension generated in one belly is distributed laterally to its neighbours — myofascial force transmission. Force therefore reaches the skeleton by paths other than the classic origin–insertion tendon line, which partly explains why isolated single-muscle exercises still load wide regions.
  • Elastic energy storage: the fascia lata, plantar fascia, Achilles tendon and thoracolumbar fascia store and release elastic energy, so muscle fibres can contract almost isometrically while the "spring" oscillates — economical movement. Tensegrity describes how local tension is spread globally through this continuous web.
  • Sensation: fascia is one of the richest sensory organs of the body, densely innervated by free nerve endings and mechanoreceptors (Ruffini, Pacinian, interstitial receptors) and containing contractile myofibroblasts. It contributes substantially to proprioception and interoception, and its nociceptors are implicated in myofascial pain and trigger-point tenderness.

3Pathophysiology

When fascia is injured, immobilised or overloaded, its matrix changes and function is lost. Hyaluronan thickens and layers lose their glide, so fibrosis and adhesion follow surgery, burns, trauma or prolonged bed rest, limiting range and raising injury risk. The thoracolumbar fascia stiffens in chronic low back pain, altering load transfer between the trunk and limbs. In the deep compartments of the leg, swelling within an unyielding fascial envelope raises intracompartmental pressure and can progress to acute compartment syndrome — a surgical emergency. Repetitive strain produces myofascial trigger points and sensitised nociceptors, while post-surgical scars act as irritable anchors in the tensional web, changing distant mobility. Because fascia is continuous, a local change is rarely a local problem.

4Answer

The role of fascia in the musculoskeletal system can be summarised as packaging, force transmission, elastic energy storage and sensation, with clinical consequences at every level.

1. Structural role

  • Invests and compartmentalises muscles, tendons, nerves and vessels, permitting gliding between layers.
  • Forms retinacula, septa and the deep envelopes (fascia lata, crural fascia, thoracolumbar fascia) that guide and stabilise muscle action.

2. Mechanical role

  • Transmits force laterally (myofascial force transmission) and forms functional chains, so movement is integrated rather than single-muscle.
  • Stores and returns elastic energy, improving movement economy, and distributes load through tensegrity.

3. Sensory role

  • Richly innervated, contributing to proprioception, interoception and nociception; myofibroblasts give it a limited active contractile capacity.

4. Clinical role

  • Loss of fascial glide after injury or immobilisation causes stiffness, adhesion and pain; fascial mobilisation, stretching and early movement aim to restore glide.
  • Scars behave as irritable anchors, so releasing them can restore distant mobility.
RoleMechanical/sensory basis
PackagingCompartmentalisation and gliding layers
Force transmissionMyofascial force transmission, chains
Elastic storageFascia lata, plantar fascia, Achilles, thoracolumbar fascia
SensationRuffini, Pacinian, interstitial receptors, myofibroblasts

Indian-practice context: the demands of floor-sitting, squatting, carrying loads and barefoot walking place high strain on the plantar fascia and thoracolumbar fascia, making fascial mobility and loading advice clinically relevant in daily Indian life.

Conclusion: fascia is not inert packing — it packages, transmits force sideways, stores elastic energy and senses — so treating "the glide, not just the muscle" is the practical implication of its true role.

5Recent advances

  • Zügel et al. (2018) — British Journal of Sports Medicine consensus statement confirming myofascial force transmission between synergists and along myofascial chains, and noting that fascial stiffness can be modified by fluid content, crosslinks and myofibroblast activity — the rationale for fascial mobilisation and myofascial release techniques.
  • Ajimsha et al. (2015) — systematic review of RCTs on myofascial release concluding that the evidence, though mixed in quality, is encouraging and that myofascial release is emerging as a manual-therapy strategy with a solid evidence base for pain and function.
  • Overmann et al. (2024) — meta-analysis in Physiotherapy of 10 RCTs (549 patients) finding that myofascial release significantly reduced chronic neck pain and improved right rotation and lateral flexion versus other treatments, although pressure-pain threshold did not change.
  • Wiewelhove et al. (2019) — meta-analysis of 21 studies showing self-myofascial release (foam rolling) used before exercise improves flexibility (~4%) and sprint performance, and used after exercise reduces muscle soreness (~6%) — supporting its role as a warm-up and recovery tool in rehabilitation.

6References

  1. Lehmkuhl & Smith, Brunnstrom's Clinical Kinesiology — fascia and connective tissue structure.
  2. Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — connective tissue mechanics.
  3. Schleip — fascial research, Fascial Fitness articles, Journal of Bodywork and Movement Therapies.
  4. Schleip R, et al. Fascial tissue research in sports medicine: from molecules to tissue adaptation, injury and diagnostics (consensus statement). Br J Sports Med. 2018;52:1497–1505.
  5. Chan DD, Guilak F, Sah RL, Calve S. Mechanobiology of hyaluronan: connecting biomechanics and bioactivity in musculoskeletal tissues. Annu Rev Biomed Eng. 2024;26:25–47.
Question 3 · 10 marks

Q3. Elaborate on the kinetics and kinematics of the shoulder following rotator cuff repair.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 6c — Mechanics and pathomechanics: shoulder

★ Memory hook — “Move it, don’t load it.” Keep kinematics (geometry of motion — guarded arcs, scapulohumeral rhythm, stiffness) separate from kinetics (forces — deltoid up, cuff compresses = concavity compression). Restore rhythm first, force couple second.

1Introduction

A rotator cuff repair re-approximates torn cuff tendon (most often supraspinatus) to the greater tuberosity, by anchors and sutures. The repaired tendon-to-bone interface is weakest early: healing passes through inflammatory, proliferative and remodelling phases, and tendon strength does not approach normal for months. Every kinematic and kinetic statement below flows from this one biological fact — the repair must be moved enough to prevent stiffness but not loaded enough to fail.

2Physiology

Normally the shoulder runs on two linked mechanisms. Kinematically, arm elevation obeys a scapulohumeral rhythm of roughly 2:1 — every 3° of elevation is shared as 2° glenohumeral and 1° scapulothoracic — so the scapula must upwardly rotate and the humeral head must stay centred for the arm to clear the acromion. Kinetically, that centring depends on a force couple: in the coronal plane the deltoid’s upward pull is balanced by the inferior stabilizing pull of the intact cuff (subscapularis anteriorly, infraspinatus posteriorly), which presses the humeral head into the glenoid — concavity compression. This is the normal reference against which the post-repair changes are read.

3Pathophysiology

Kinematics — the geometry of motion. Kinematics changes in three ways after cuff repair. First, passive range is deliberately restricted in the early phase: abduction and external rotation are the guarded arcs, because both maximally strain the supraspinatus footprint. Second, scapulohumeral rhythm is altered — pain, inhibition and cuff deficiency increase scapular upward rotation and the use of scapulothoracic substitution, so the patient "hikes" the shoulder to reach overhead and the normal 2:1 glenohumeral-to-scapular ratio becomes more scapular. Third, postoperative stiffness is the signature complication: capsular contracture reduces glenohumeral rotation, and an internal-rotation deficit shifts mechanics further. Because the deltoid is preserved and active while the cuff is protected, the joint's instantaneous centre of rotation can translate upward if the cuff's stabilising pull is late to return.

Kinetics — the study of forces. Immediately after repair the cuff side of the coronal and transverse force couples is surgically silenced, so unopposed deltoid force would drive superior humeral-head translation and jam the healing footprint under the acromion. The intact subscapularis and infraspinatus must therefore be protected but activated early, because they supply the "seatbelt" that keeps the head centred and shares load with the deltoid. Passive forces matter too: immobilisation shortens the capsule, and friction at the repaired footprint raises the torque needed for the first degrees of motion. Above all, the tensile strength of the repair itself is weakest in the first weeks, so the magnitude and direction of every applied load must be graded to the phase of healing.

4Answer

Rehabilitation is applied kinetics and kinematics: early gentle passive motion to glide the surfaces and limit adhesion (unless the tear was massive, where conservative immobilization may be chosen), avoidance of active abduction against gravity in the first weeks, progressive activation of the scapular stabilizers to restore rhythm, and later resisted external rotation and scapular retraction before deltoid-dominant lifting. Conclusion: after repair the shoulder moves differently (kinematics) and is loaded differently (kinetics) because a healing, temporarily non-contractile cuff lets deltoid dominate; successful therapy restores rhythm first and the force couple second.

Fig 3 — Circle for the humeral head, one upward arrow (deltoid), two converging green arrows (cuff compression into the glenoid). Label it "coronal force couple" — that label alone is worth a mark.
Examiner's tip: open with "the repair must be moved but not loaded" and the whole answer writes itself. Distinguish kinematics (motion geometry, rhythm, stiffness) from kinetics (forces, couples, compression) in your subheadings — examiners specifically check whether you know the difference.

5Recent advances

  • Hao et al. (2025) — meta-analysis of 11 RCTs finding that early exercise after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair improved shoulder flexion, abduction, internal and external rotation and reduced postoperative stiffness (risk ratio 0.34) versus brace fixation, with no significant increase in pain or re-tear rate.
  • Nikpay et al. (2025) — randomised trial (n=120) reporting that supervised early passive motion begun within 24 hours gave lower pain, higher UCLA scores and less stiffness than 6 weeks of immobilisation, with no difference in re-tear rate, but that large tears (>3 cm) with Goutallier grade ≥3 fatty infiltration remained a high-risk subgroup needing cautious, individualised rehabilitation.
  • Hu et al. (2023) — systematic review of 13 RCTs (1,082 patients) finding that both early passive and early active motion improved range of motion over delayed protocols and were safe for small-to-large tears, with no difference in re-tear rate.
  • Sheps et al. (2019) — RCT (n=206) showing early active motion gave better early flexion and abduction but no long-term advantage in range, pain, strength, quality of life or repair integrity at 24 months compared with sling immobilisation.

6References

  1. Levangie & Norkin, Joint Structure and Function — shoulder complex mechanics.
  2. Donatelli & Wooden, Orthopaedic Physical Therapy — rotator cuff rehabilitation.
  3. Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — post-repair protocols and force couples.
  4. Sheps DM, et al. Early active motion versus sling immobilization after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair: a randomized controlled trial. Arthroscopy. 2019;35(3):749–760.
  5. Early versus delayed mobilization for arthroscopic rotator cuff repair: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Musculoskelet Disord. 2023;24:944.
Question 4 · 10 marks

Q4. Describe the various physiological adaptations seen in muscles during endurance training.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 5a — Physiological basis of movement: exercise and training

★ Memory hook — “Endurance training buys quality, not bulk”: more mitochondria (PGC-1α), more capillaries, more myoglobin, more oxidative enzymes, glycogen sparing — and the lactate threshold shifts right. Write hypertrophy and you have written the resistance-training answer by mistake.

1Introduction

Endurance training is repeated, sustained, predominantly aerobic exercise — typically large-muscle rhythmic activity at moderate intensity performed three to five times a week for weeks. The muscles adapt to delay fatigue: they learn to generate the same force for longer, using oxygen more efficiently and sparing their limited carbohydrate fuel.

2Physiology

The dominant change is mitochondrial biogenesis: mitochondrial volume density rises by roughly 25 to 100 per cent with training — in humans largely enlargement of existing mitochondria rather than new ones — driven by PGC-1alpha signalling, so aerobic ATP production capacity rises. Capillary density increases (more capillaries per fibre, smaller diffusion distances), improving oxygen and substrate delivery and metabolite removal. Myoglobin content rises, storing and ferrying oxygen inside the fibre. Oxidative enzymes of the Krebs cycle, electron transport chain and beta-oxidation pathways increase in activity, so fat — an abundant fuel — is oxidized faster. The net result: a rightward shift of the lactate threshold, meaning the same work is done with less lactate accumulation and less fatigue.

Type I (slow oxidative) fibres hypertrophy modestly and become even more oxidative; type IIa fibres shift their myosin heavy-chain profile toward a more oxidative type IIa phenotype (with possible IIx-to-IIa conversion), so the fast population becomes fatigue-resistant. There is little wholesale conversion of type II to type I in humans, and no dramatic hypertrophy — that is the resistance-training answer, not the endurance one. Intramuscular triglyceride storage increases as a local fuel depot.

Trained muscle spares muscle glycogen by oxidizing more free fatty acids at any given submaximal intensity; the "crossover" shifts so carbohydrate is preserved for later effort. Resting glycogen storage capacity itself increases, phosphocreatine depletion at a given load is less, and buffering and lactate-shuttle capacity improve so lactate can be cleared and used as fuel by other fibres and the heart.

3Pathophysiology

Read against the untrained state, the adaptations make sense as corrections of fatigue. In the untrained muscle, submaximal work is limited by a low mitochondrial and capillary density, so anaerobic glycolysis is recruited early; the resulting lactate and H+ accumulation, phosphocreatine depletion and rapid muscle-glycogen use are what the patient feels as fatigue and breathlessness. Endurance training reverses precisely this profile — the same absolute work is done with less lactate accumulation (the lactate threshold shifts right), phosphocreatine depletion at a given load is less, and buffering and lactate-shuttle capacity improve so lactate is cleared and reused as fuel by other fibres and by the heart. Detraining reverses these gains within weeks, which is why the adaptations must be maintained.

4Answer

Although the question is about muscle, one line on the whole-body context earns completeness: stroke volume rises, resting and submaximal heart rate fall, and muscle blood flow extraction (arteriovenous oxygen difference) improves. Functionally, the trained muscle can sustain walking, cycling or occupational activity longer, fatigue resistance being the single most practical outcome for physiotherapy patients in cardiac, pulmonary and deconditioned populations.

Fig 4 — One big fibre box, six blue dots for mitochondria, three parallel lines for capillaries, and an arrow labelled "lactate threshold shifts right". Thirty seconds to draw, and it carries the answer's whole logic.
Examiner's tip: the commonest error is writing hypertrophy and neural-gain adaptations from strength training. State explicitly: "endurance training increases quality (oxidative machinery), not bulk." Quote PGC-1alpha once, then stop — depth beats name-dropping.

5Recent advances

  • Abrego-Guandique et al. (2025) — systematic review and meta-analysis confirming that endurance exercise significantly raises PGC-1α, the master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis (pooled Hedge’s g = 1.17), with interval and continuous training producing similar large effects.
  • Mølmen et al. (2024) — meta-regression pooling 353 studies (5,973 participants) finding mitochondrial content rose about 23% with endurance training and about 27% with high-intensity or sprint interval training, with larger gains at higher training frequency (6 > 4 > 2 sessions/week).
  • Wisløff et al. (2007) — landmark randomised trial showing aerobic interval training produced far greater gains in peak oxygen uptake (46% vs 14%) and reversed left-ventricular remodelling in heart-failure patients, reshaping high-intensity exercise prescription in cardiopulmonary physiotherapy.
  • Mølmen et al. (2024) — the same analysis showed capillary density per fibre increased about 15% with endurance training, but gains occurred mainly in the first 4 weeks and only in untrained-to-moderately-trained people — a useful caution about expectations for exercise prescription.

6References

  1. Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — sports physiology and muscle adaptation.
  2. ACSM's Resource Manual for Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription — endurance training adaptations.
  3. Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — aerobic endurance training principles.
  4. Dent JR, Stocks B, Campelj DG, Philp A. Transient changes to metabolic homeostasis initiate mitochondrial adaptation to endurance exercise. Semin Cell Dev Biol. 2023;143:3–16.
  5. Effects of exercise training on mitochondrial and capillary growth in human skeletal muscle: a systematic review and meta-regression. Sports Med. 2024.
Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. Describe the changes in the mechanics of the elbow following fixed flexion deformity of the elbow.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 6c — Mechanics and pathomechanics: elbow

★ Memory hook — “The arc does not shrink, it shifts.” A fixed flexion deformity relocates the elbow’s range into flexion, removes the locked extended position for weight-bearing, effaces the carrying angle, and throws the extra work onto the shoulder and wrist.

1Introduction

The elbow is a trochleoulnar (hinge) plus radiohumeral (pivot) joint: flexion-extension occurs at the ulnohumeral articulation, pronation-supination at the proximal radioulnar joint. The flexion axis runs through the epicondyles; full extension ends in a slight valgus carrying angle — roughly 11 degrees in men and 13 degrees in women — which lets the forearm clear the hip in carrying objects. Flexion is guided by the coronoid and olecranon fitting the trochlea, giving the joint its intrinsic bony stability.

2Physiology

Normally the elbow works within a functional arc of roughly 100° of flexion–extension — about 30° to 130° carries most daily activity — together with a pronation–supination arc of about 100°, some 50° each way (Morrey). Full extension is the close-packed, locked position: the coronoid and olecranon are maximally congruent in the trochlea, load is distributed over the largest contact area, and the limb can bear weight through the extended arm. The small valgus carrying angle (about 11° in men and 13° in women) lets the forearm clear the hip. These are the reference values for reading the deformity.

3Pathophysiology

A fixed flexion deformity (FFD) means the joint cannot reach terminal extension — the olecranon is blocked by anterior capsular contracture, biceps tightening, or bony impingement (as in malunited distal humerus fractures, rheumatoid arthritis, or post-burn scar contracture common in Indian practice). The functional arc of motion shifts upward: total range is preserved in many cases but is displaced into flexion. The close-packed, locked position of full extension is lost, so the arm that would have transmitted load through a congruent, maximally contact-distributed joint now loads the posterior trochlea and radial head even at rest. The carrying angle is effectively reduced or abolished in extension because there is no extension; the deformity is often accompanied by pronation contracture, eating into the roughly 100-degree functional pronation-supination arc (about 50 degrees each way, Morrey).

Functionally, roughly 100 degrees of flexion-extension (from about 30 to 130 degrees) carries most daily activity, so a small FFD of 15 to 20 degrees is surprisingly well tolerated. What matters is reach: the patient cannot push open a door, cannot reach the far end of a table, cannot do a press-up or support body weight on an extended limb, and cannot put the hand flat under the thigh when sitting. Reaching the back pocket or combing hair is affected only when flexion contracture is combined with pronation loss.

Compensation comes from the shoulder (increased abduction and medial rotation to make the hand meet the midline or the table) and the wrist (hyperextension to flatten the hand). These substitutions overload adjacent structures: the shoulder abductors fatigue, and the wrist is forced into end-range postures. The elbow itself now moves through its flexed arc against contracted soft tissue, so the extensor mechanism (triceps) works at a shortened, mechanically disadvantaged length, and the joint reaction force is directed through a smaller contact area posteriorly — encouraging cartilage wear over time.

4Answer

Assess and record the FFD with a goniometer and the functional arc, then decide: postural and night extension splinting, prolonged low-load stretch, joint mobilizations (especially posterior glides to regain extension), and management of the cause (scar release in post-burn patients, pain control in arthritis). Conclusion: FFD does not merely subtract degrees — it relocates the entire arc, removes the locked extended position for weight-bearing, changes the carrying angle and joint reaction forces, and shifts work to shoulder and wrist, and therapy must address all of these.

Fig 5 — Two bones at an open angle, the elbow circle, an arc labelled "30 degrees lost", and a small arrow showing where extension should lie. The examiner instantly sees you understand arc relocation.
Examiner's tip: write the sentence "the arc does not shrink, it shifts." Then give the functional arc values (30-130 degrees does most daily tasks) — numbers anchor an otherwise descriptive answer and show clinical sense.

5Recent advances

  • Santacaterina et al. (2025) — systematic review of RCTs concluding that conservative measures such as muscle-energy technique give short-term pain and function gains for mild-to-moderate post-traumatic stiffness, while open arthrolysis followed by early structured rehabilitation is preferred for severe or refractory cases.
  • Op de Coul et al. (2022) — randomised trial in children with brachial-plexus elbow flexion contractures (≥30°) finding that a night-worn dynamic orthosis and serial casting gave comparable one-year contracture reduction, with serial casting faster over the first 20 weeks — evidence that prolonged low-load orthotic stretch works.
  • Veltman et al. (2015) — systematic review of 232 patients showing that static-progressive and dynamic splinting each add about 36–37° of elbow motion in post-traumatic stiffness, supporting non-operative bracing continued for up to 12 months before surgery is considered.
  • Chen et al. (2017) — systematic review of 10 clinical trials concluding that static-progressive orthoses significantly improve elbow range of motion in contracture, though evidence quality remains low and optimal protocols are still undefined.

6References

  1. Levangie & Norkin, Joint Structure and Function — elbow complex mechanics.
  2. Lehmkuhl & Smith, Brunnstrom's Clinical Kinesiology — elbow and forearm joints.
  3. Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment — elbow contracture assessment.
  4. Onggo JR, et al. Clinical outcomes following surgical management of post-traumatic elbow contractures in the pediatric age group: a meta-analysis and systematic review. J Hand Surg Am. 2024.
  5. Op de Coul LS, et al. Elbow flexion contractures in neonatal brachial plexus palsy: a one-year comparison of dynamic orthosis and serial casting. Clin Rehabil. 2023;37(4):493–503.
Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. Describe the various changes seen in forward head posture on the body.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 7b — Posture: abnormal postures and deformities

★ Memory hook — “Upper cervical extension, lower cervical flexion — so the eyes stay level.” Then the crossed pattern: tight upper trapezius, levator, suboccipitals and pecs; weak deep neck flexors and lower trapezius. End on the trigeminocervical link to headache.

1Introduction

Forward head posture (FHP) is an anterior translation of the head relative to the trunk, so the external auditory meatus falls ahead of the shoulder instead of aligning with it. It rides on thoracic kyphosis, and its causes are our daily furniture: prolonged smartphone and laptop use, poor bench and pillow ergonomics, and weak endurance of the deep cervical flexors. Every centimetre of forward translation adds effective load on the cervical extensors, multiplying the moments the neck must sustain.

2Physiology

Normal upright posture keeps the external auditory meatus vertically over the shoulder, so the head’s centre of mass sits near the body’s line of gravity and the cervical extensors carry only a small moment arm. Balance between the deep cervical flexors (longus colli and capitis) and the cervical extensors holds this position, while the scapular stabilizers (middle and lower trapezius with serratus anterior) keep the scapula flat against the thorax so the neck muscles are not recruited to carry the head. The craniovertebral angle — the angle between a line from the C7 spinous process to the tragus and the horizontal — quantifies how far the head has translated forward, and normal values are higher than those seen in forward head posture.

3Pathophysiology

The spine adapts in a see-saw: upper cervical segments extend (the head must stay level to look forward, hence upper cervical extension) while lower cervical segments flex. The natural cervical lordosis first accentuates, then with disc degeneration and posterior soft-tissue creep may flatten or reverse. Sustained flexion loads the cervical discs posteriorly, stretches the posterior ligaments and capsular structures, and shortens the anterior structures. The craniovertebral angle decreases, and the suboccipital region is held in chronic extension, compressing the upper cervical facet joints and the trigeminocervical nucleus territory.

FHP is the facial expression of upper crossed syndrome: tightness of the upper trapezius, levator scapulae, suboccipitals and pectorals; weakness and inhibition of the deep neck flexors (longus colli, capitis) and the lower and middle trapezius with serratus anterior. The scapulae abduct, tilt anteriorly and elevate — a protracted, rounded-shoulder thorax. Trigger points flourish in the upper trapezius and levator because they hold the head statically for hours.

The rounded chest restricts rib excursion, so breathing becomes more apical and accessory-muscle driven, reducing chest-wall expansion. Subacromial space narrows with scapular protraction and downward rotation, predisposing to shoulder impingement. The protracted mandible stresses the temporomandibular joint, encouraging disc displacement and bruxism. Sustained suboccipital extension and upper cervical facet loading refer pain via the trigeminocervical complex into tension-type headaches. The whole kinetic chain leans: increased thoracic kyphosis, lumbar compensation, and a higher energy cost of upright posture. Swallowing and voice are subtly affected in severe cases.

4Answer

Assess by plumb-line and craniovertebral angle from a lateral photograph, pectoral and suboccipital length, deep-neck-flexor endurance (chin-tuck hold), and scapular position. Treatment is the mirror image of the cause: lengthen the tight (pectoral, upper trapezius, suboccipitals), strengthen the weak (deep flexors, lower trapezius, serratus anterior), and re-engineer the environment — screen at eye level, lumbar support, and regular postural resets.

Fig 6 — A dashed vertical plumb line, a head circle sitting in front of it, a curved neck, and two boxes: "tight" and "weak". This IS the upper-crossed pattern drawn honestly in under a minute.
Examiner's tip: the phrase "upper cervical extension with lower cervical flexion — so the eyes stay level" is what separates an A-grade answer from a list of complaints. Always end with the trigeminocervical link to headaches; it is a favourite viva follow-up.

5Recent advances

  • Sheikhhoseini et al. (2018) — systematic review and meta-analysis of 7 RCTs (627 participants) finding therapeutic exercise produces large improvements in the craniovertebral angle (odds ratio 6.7) and moderate reduction in neck pain in forward head posture — level 1a evidence.
  • Heydari et al. (2022) — randomised clinical trial in 103 students with forward head posture establishing a minimal clinically important difference for correction: the craniovertebral angle should increase by at least 1.40° and the shoulder angle by 1.34° after an eight-week corrective exercise programme.
  • Elsayed & Alowa (2024) — randomised controlled trial finding that a cervicothoracic correction programme improved the craniovertebral angle and neck disability index, and that adding a lumbopelvic component gave a greater short-term reduction in neck pain and disability than the cervicothoracic programme alone.
  • Titcomb et al. (2023) — four-arm randomised trial in young adults showing that corrective exercise (self-myofascial release with stretching, with or without strengthening) improved the craniovertebral angle more than postural education alone.

6References

  1. Lehmkuhl & Smith, Brunnstrom's Clinical Kinesiology — posture and spinal curves.
  2. Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — posture impairment syndromes and Janda's crossed syndromes.
  3. Donatelli & Wooden, Orthopaedic Physical Therapy — shoulder girdle and posture relationships.
  4. Corrective exercises for forward head posture: minimal clinically important difference for the craniovertebral and shoulder angles. BMC Pediatr. 2022;22:230.
  5. Postural education versus corrective exercise for forward head posture in young adults: a four-arm randomized controlled trial. Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2023;20:6468.
Question 7 · 10 marks

Q7. Describe the role of equilibrium following ankle injuries.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 6d — Mechanics and pathomechanics: ankle injuries and balance

★ Memory hook — Balance = three inputs (somatosensory, vestibular, visual) and three strategies (ankle, hip, stepping); the body is an inverted pendulum on the ankle. A sprain tears the mechanoreceptors (Freeman: articular reflex failure) — so treat equilibrium, not just range and strength.

1Introduction

Equilibrium is the state in which the body's centre of mass stays over its base of support. Postural control achieves it by integrating three sensory inputs — somatosensory (joint and muscle receptors, richest at the ankle), vestibular, and visual — and by grading three motor strategies: the ankle strategy for small slow sways on a firm wide surface, the hip strategy for larger disturbances, and the stepping strategy when the base is exceeded. Static equilibrium holds a position; dynamic equilibrium maintains control during movement.

2Physiology

In standing, the ankle is the fulcrum of the inverted pendulum of the body. Mechanically, its ligaments and the calf-peroneal muscle group correct each sway in the sagittal and frontal planes; sensorily, the ankle ligaments, capsule and muscle spindles deliver the earliest warning that the ground relationship has changed. The lateral ligament complex in particular carries mechanoreceptors that fire at the end-ranges where a sprain actually happens.

3Pathophysiology

A lateral ankle sprain tears ligament and with it the mechanoreceptors, degrading joint position sense and reflex latency. The classical chain: damaged receptors give degraded afferent input, delayed or reduced protective reflexes, increased postural sway especially with eyes closed (sensory reweighting onto vision), recurrent episodes of the ankle "giving way", and finally chronic ankle instability. Freeman described this as articular reflex failure; later work confirmed increased sway and poor single-leg balance in unstable ankles, including deficits on the uninjured side, implying a central reweighting component. Strength loss of the peroneal muscles compounds the mechanical side, and every re-sprain re-damages the afferent field.

4Answer

Assess single-leg stance time with eyes open versus closed (a large eyes-closed drop flags sensory reliance), the Star Excursion Balance Test or SEBT for dynamic reach, joint position sense reproduction, and peroneal strength and reaction time. Instrumented force plates quantify sway and time-to-boundary in research settings, but clinical tests detect the same signal.

Balance training is the treatment and the prevention: progressive single-leg work on unstable surfaces, wobble-board and perturbation training, hopping and sport-specific agility. In a classic randomized trial of acute sprains, supervised rehabilitation emphasizing balance training cut re-injury at one year from about 29 percent to 7 percent, and systematic reviews report roughly a one-third reduction in sprains among athletes. Conclusion: after ankle injury, restoring equilibrium — not merely range and strength — is the difference between recovery and a lifetime of a "weak ankle".

Fig 7 — A dot (centre of mass) on a line (body) over a small ankle circle on a base line, with two curved sway arrows. Add the words "inverted pendulum" and "damaged receptors" and the mechanism is complete.
Examiner's tip: quote the Holme 1999 trial numbers (re-injury 29 percent without balance training versus 7 percent with) — one number pair turns a descriptive answer into an evidence-based one. Mention Freeman by name for the mechanoreceptor concept.

5Recent advances

  • Tang et al. (2024) — meta-analysis of the dosage of balance training (20 studies, 682 participants) recommending the optimal prescription for chronic ankle instability as three sessions per week, 20–30 minutes each, for 4–6 weeks to improve self-reported function and dynamic balance.
  • Yang et al. (2024) — network meta-analysis of 44 RCTs ranking a combination of balance and strengthening exercises, augmented with manual therapy or dry needling, as the most effective for function and pain, while tai chi emerged as the most promising single intervention for improving stability.
  • Guo et al. (2024) — meta-analysis confirming that balance training significantly improves Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool scores, Star Excursion Balance Test reach and Foot and Ankle Ability Measure sports scores compared with no training, and improves functional scales more than strength training alone.
  • Su et al. (2024) — systematic review and meta-analysis finding that a combination of strength and balance training produced the greatest improvement in patient-reported outcomes, whereas balance training alone gave the greatest improvement in dynamic balance.

6References

  1. Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — postural equilibrium.
  2. Levangie & Norkin, Joint Structure and Function — ankle complex and stability.
  3. Freeman and Wyke — articular reflexes at the ankle joint, 1967 (primary).
  4. Holme et al 1999, Scandinavian Journal of Medicine and Science in Sports — supervised rehabilitation after ankle sprain (primary).
  5. Mollà-Casanova S, Inglés M, Serra-Añó P. Effects of balance training on functionality, ankle instability, and dynamic balance outcomes in people with chronic ankle instability: systematic review and meta-analysis. Clin Rehabil. 2021;35:1694–1709.
  6. Dosage of balance training on ankle function and dynamic balance ability in patients with chronic ankle instability: a meta-analysis. BMC Musculoskelet Disord. 2024;25:696.
Question 8 · 10 marks

Q8. A 50-year-old man is unable to dorsiflex his right foot following an intramuscular injection in his right gluteal region. Describe his pathological gait.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 8b — Gait: abnormal and pathological gait

★ Memory hook — Injection palsy = sciatic nerve, peroneal division (lateral, less protected): dorsiflexors and evertors out, plantar flexion spared. Contact → foot slap; swing → steppage. Manage with an ankle-foot orthosis while the nerve recovers.

1Introduction

A gluteal-region intramuscular injection that immediately produces dorsiflexion loss has injured the sciatic nerve — the classic injection palsy of Indian outpatient practice. The sciatic nerve runs through the middle of the buttock deep to piriformis; a needle placed medial or inferior to the safe upper-outer quadrant strikes it. Within the nerve the common peroneal division is lateral, less protected by connective tissue and relatively tethered, which is exactly why the peroneal division is injured far more often than the tibial division. This man therefore most likely has a peroneal-division lesion: loss of the ankle dorsiflexors and evertors (tibialis anterior, extensors, peroneals), with relative sparing of plantar flexion and inversion — a picture of steppage gait. Sensory loss affects the anterolateral leg and dorsum of the foot; pain and paraesthesia in a sciatic distribution are common early.

2Physiology

Normal gait depends on the ankle dorsiflexors at two points. At initial contact and loading response, the tibialis anterior contracts eccentrically to lower the forefoot gently (the first rocker) and the foot rolls heel-to-toe; in swing, the same muscle contracts concentrically to clear the ground while the hip and knee flex through a small arc. The ankle thus contributes both shock absorption in stance and toe clearance in swing, and its plantar-flexors provide push-off at terminal stance. Remove the dorsiflexors and both the stance and the swing halves of the cycle are destabilised.

3Pathophysiology

At initial contact the affected foot, hanging in equinovarus, cannot be held in neutral, so it strikes either flat and slaps — foot slap as eccentric control of dorsiflexors is lost — or lands toes-first with the forefoot. During loading response the ankle remains plantarflexed, so the tibialis anterior silence removes the first rocker shock absorption and the stance limb accepts weight abruptly. In mid-stance and terminal stance the ankle stays in relative equinus; push-off is only mildly weak if the tibial division is spared, but ankle stability is poor on uneven ground. The characteristic problems are in swing: with no dorsiflexors the foot would drag, so toe clearance is the patient's single biggest engineering problem, solved by compensation.

The textbook compensation is exaggerated hip and knee flexion of the swing limb to lift the dropped foot high — steppage gait, often with the classical foot slap on descent. Alternative or additional patterns include circumduction (swinging the leg outward in an arc), hip hiking (elevating the pelvis on the swing side), and contralateral vaulting (rising on the sound toes to create clearance). Watch an Indian patient walking on a wet floor in chappals and you will see trunk lean toward the sound side and widened base as well — safety overrides elegance.

4Answer

Clearance strategies raise the metabolic cost of walking and can overload the hip and lumbar spine. Persistent equinus predisposes to ankle plantar-flexion contracture, calf tightness and, if sensory loss is significant, unnoticed injuries and ulceration over the dorsum of the foot. On examination, look for gluteal and hamstring weakness if the whole sciatic nerve is involved (then knee flexion is weak too), a diminished or intact Achilles reflex depending on tibial sparing, and confirm with nerve conduction studies, which typically show the peroneal division far more affected.

Early management: an ankle-foot orthosis or dorsiflexion spring splint to hold the foot neutral in swing and give lateral stability in stance, gait training with the orthosis, electrical stimulation and strengthening of any partially active dorsiflexors, tendon-transfer considerations in permanent lesions, stretching to prevent equinus contracture, sensory protection education, and careful follow-up — many injection palsies show partial spontaneous recovery over months. Conclusion: this is a preventable, iatrogenic high peroneal-pattern sciatic lesion producing foot drop; its gait is the body's intelligent solution to one missing function — ankle dorsiflexion — and the physiotherapist restores clearance with an orthosis while awaiting and supporting nerve recovery.

Fig 8 — A horizontal timeline arrow with three boxes: foot slap at contact, abrupt loading in stance, hip-and-knee hyperflexion in swing, plus a caption listing the substitute clearances. This maps deviation to phase, which is what a 10-marker demands.
Examiner's tip: candidates lose marks by narrating anatomy without connecting to gait phases. For every deviation, force the sentence pattern "because X muscle is silent at Y phase, the patient does Z." Mention the AFO explicitly — it is the management action the examiner is silently waiting for.

5Recent advances

  • Smith et al. (2026) — review in Muscle & Nerve concluding that electrical modalities in peripheral nerve injury remain incompletely established: transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation may help pain in the acute phase and surface EMG biofeedback shows promise for motor relearning, but robust evidence for routine neuromuscular electrical stimulation is lacking.
  • González-Graniel et al. (2024) — systematic review of sensing and control in functional electrical stimulation for foot drop finding inertial measurement units (45%) and biopotential electrodes (37%) the commonest sensors, and that closed-loop control now dominates research, though most commercial devices still use open-loop strategies.
  • Prenton et al. (2018) — meta-analysis of 7 RCTs (464 participants) showing functional electrical stimulation and ankle-foot orthoses produce equivalent improvements in walking speed in foot drop from stroke, so device choice can be guided by patient preference, convenience and cost.
  • Kottink et al. (2008) — randomised trial of an implantable peroneal nerve stimulator versus an ankle-foot orthosis in chronic stroke with foot drop finding no functional gain in walking speed but increased voluntary tibialis anterior and gastrocnemius output, suggesting training-related plasticity.

6References

  1. O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation — pathological gait analysis.
  2. Lehmkuhl & Smith, Brunnstrom's Clinical Kinesiology — nerve injuries and gait.
  3. Saunders, Inman and Eberhart, JBJS 1953 — the major determinants of gait (primary).
  4. Reviews of sciatic nerve injection injury (Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine / International Journal of Surgery case reports, primary).
  5. Surgical management of peroneal nerve injuries. Acta Neurochir (Wien). 2023;165:2571–2580.
  6. Functional outcomes of different surgical treatments for common peroneal nerve injuries. BMC Surg. 2024;24:57.
Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. Describe the changes in male and female body structure and composition.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 2a — Anthropometry: body composition and sex differences

★ Memory hook — Two-component model first: fat mass + fat-free mass = body mass. Women carry more fat (essential fat 12–15% vs 3–5%; total 20–30% vs 12–20%), men more lean mass — but per kilogram of lean mass the strength gap narrows. Pelvic subpubic angle 80–85° vs 50–60°; the larger Q angle links to female knee injury.

1Introduction

On average, men are taller (roughly 12 to 13 centimetres globally) and heavier, with broader shoulders and narrower hips; women have a lower shoulder-to-hip ratio, a relatively wider pelvis, shorter limbs relative to trunk, and more subcutaneous fat distributed in the gluteofemoral (pear) pattern versus the male abdominal (apple) pattern. The female centre of gravity sits lower, and the carrying angle of the forearm is about 2 degrees greater in women.

2Physiology

The essential difference is in the two-component model. Women carry substantially more body fat: healthy young women average roughly 20 to 30 percent fat against 12 to 20 percent in men, and essential fat is about 12 to 15 percent in women versus about 3 to 5 percent in men — the female body banks fat for reproductive function. Conversely, fat-free mass — muscle, bone, water — is absolutely and relatively greater in men: men have about 40 percent more muscle mass in the upper body and 25 to 33 percent more in the lower body, larger muscle fibre cross-sectional areas (especially type II), greater bone mineral density and less total body water percentage-wise. Men therefore generate higher absolute strength and power; when strength is expressed per kilogram of lean mass the gap narrows considerably, which is the examiner's favourite nuance.

Testosterone drives male muscle mass, haemoglobin concentration and visceral fat deposition; oestrogen directs female fat to the gluteofemoral depot, supports bone density, and its menopausal withdrawal reverses both fat distribution and bone protection. This is why the sex differences in strength are largely, though not completely, hormonal.

3Pathophysiology

The female pelvis is adapted for childbearing: a wider and shallower pelvis, rounder inlet, broader subpubic angle (80 to 85 degrees versus 50 to 60 degrees in men), and a greater inclination of the femur with a larger Q angle at the knee — the mechanical link to the higher female incidence of patellofemoral pain and anterior cruciate ligament injury. Men have larger, denser, more robust long bones with more prominent muscle attachments; women have lighter bones and, after menopause, accelerated bone loss with higher osteoporosis and fracture risk.

4Answer

Functionally, male anatomy favours absolute power; female anatomy favours endurance and flexibility (greater joint laxity). Clinically, the physiotherapist reads these tables with care: female Q angle and ligament laxity inform knee rehabilitation, gluteofemoral fat and the lower centre of gravity alter balance training, female lower lean mass means lower absolute strength benchmarks and slower basal metabolic rates, and postmenopausal bone loss demands early weight-bearing and resistance exercise. Sex-specific normative values — never unisex ones — should be used when interpreting skinfold, body mass index and strength data.

Fig 9 — Two stacked bars: the male bar mostly green (lean) with a thin yellow cap; the female bar with a taller yellow cap. One arrow says "more fat-free mass". Any examiner marking composition can mark this figure in five seconds.
Examiner's tip: always include the two-component model (fat mass + fat-free mass = body mass) before giving numbers, and finish with "per kilogram of lean mass the strength gap narrows" — that one sentence shows you think, not memorize. The Q-angle link to the female knee converts this from anatomy to physiotherapy.

5Recent advances

  • EWGSOP & AWGS (2024) — consensus guidance positioning dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) as the reference method for body composition, with appendicular lean mass divided by height squared (ALM/height²) recommended as the primary indicator of low muscle mass.
  • Hewett et al. (2005) — landmark review and meta-analysis showing female athletes have a 4–6 times higher anterior cruciate ligament injury rate than males, and that neuromuscular training programmes significantly reduce ACL injury incidence — the evidence base for sex-specific injury-prevention exercise.
  • Shojaa et al. (2020) — systematic review and meta-analysis of 75 studies (5,300 postmenopausal women) showing exercise training produces significant, though modest, improvements in bone mineral density at the lumbar spine, femoral neck and total hip.
  • Kim & Won (2022) — systematic review of sex-different changes in body composition in ageing finding that older men have larger skeletal muscle mass while older women have larger fat mass, and that muscle mass is more strongly favourable for physical function, bone density and falls risk in men.

6References

  1. Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — anthropometry and sex differences.
  2. Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — body composition, metabolism and hormonal regulation.
  3. ACSM's Resource Manual — body composition assessment and normative values.
  4. American Health Foundation roundtable, American Journal of Clinical Nutrition — healthy body fat percentages (primary).
  5. Nuzzo JL. Narrative review of sex differences in muscle strength, endurance, activation, size, fiber type, and strength training participation rates, preferences, motivations, injuries, and neuromuscular adaptations. J Strength Cond Res. 2023;37(2):494–536.
  6. Use of dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry for body composition analysis in sarcopenia. J Clin Prev Cardiol. 2024;6:e13.
Question 10 · 10 marks

Q10. Describe the effects of thermal agents on soft tissue repair.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 10a — Biophysical effects of physical agents: thermal agents

★ Memory hook — Match the agent to the phase: cold in inflammation (days 0–6), gentle heat in proliferation (weeks 1–3), heat plus deep heating before stretch in remodelling (months). Thermal agents manage the environment; movement directs the repair.

1Introduction

Soft tissue repair runs through three overlapping phases: the inflammatory phase (roughly days 0 to 6: haemostasis, vasodilation, exudation, phagocytosis), the proliferative phase (weeks 1 to 3 or so: fibroblast proliferation, collagen synthesis, angiogenesis, granulation), and the remodelling phase (months up to a year: collagen reorganization along lines of stress, gradual strength gain to perhaps 80 percent of original). Every thermal agent earns its place by speeding, slowing or reshaping one of these phases.

2Physiology

Heating to 40 to 45 degrees Celsius produces vasodilation and increased blood flow, raising oxygen and nutrient delivery and accelerating metabolic rate locally — helpful for resolution in the late inflammatory and proliferative phases. It increases collagen extensibility, so heated tissue stretches further with less risk — the basis of heating before stretch in contracture and scar work. It decreases pain (gate control plus later endorphin effects), reduces muscle spasm and decreases joint stiffness; useful in subacute and chronic low back pain, before mobilization. Applied in the acute inflammatory phase it would worsen oedema and pain, which is the classic caution.

Cold is the acute-phase agent. It causes vasoconstriction, limiting bleeding and oedema formation in the first 24 to 48 hours; it reduces metabolic rate and secondary hypoxic injury; it slows nerve conduction velocity, raising the pain threshold and providing analgesia; and it reduces muscle spasm by cooling muscle spindles. Applied correctly — with protection of the skin and careful timing — it shortens the painful acute window, and early controlled motion on a numb, less swollen joint begins healing in a better mechanical environment. Cold should not be used over ischaemic tissue or poor circulation, and excessive duration risks nerve injury (watch the ulnar nerve at the elbow and the peroneal nerve at the fibular head).

Ultrasound (typically 1 megahertz for 3 to 5 centimetres depth) heats collagen-rich tissue selectively — tendon, ligament, joint capsule — from within. It increases extensibility for stretching of dense connective tissue, raises blood flow, and (at non-thermal intensities) promotes cellular activity: proposed stimulation of fibroblast proliferation and protein synthesis, aiding the proliferative and early remodelling phases. It should be avoided over acute inflammation, malignancy, the pregnant uterus, growth plates and cemented implants.

3Pathophysiology

Applied against the wrong phase, any thermal agent becomes harmful rather than helpful. Heat during the acute inflammatory phase would increase vasodilatation and capillary permeability and so worsen oedema, bleeding and pain. Cold over ischaemic or poorly perfused tissue risks further injury, and excessive or prolonged cold over superficial nerves (the ulnar nerve at the elbow, the peroneal nerve at the fibular head) can itself cause nerve injury. Ultrasound must be avoided over the tissues and circumstances listed above. The therapist's task is therefore not simply to apply an agent but to match the agent's biophysics to the healing phase, the tissue depth, and the patient's vascular and sensory status.

4Answer

The examination answer is a timetable: cold in the inflammatory phase, heat and gentle ultrasound in the proliferative phase, and heat plus deep heating before stretching and strengthening in remodelling. Combined with early graded movement — the real driver of organized collagen — thermal agents manage the environment while mechanotransduction directs the repair. Conclusion: thermal agents do not heal tissue themselves; cold buys time in the acute phase by controlling oedema and pain, and heat plus deep energy later increase circulation and extensibility so that movement can do its work — they are assistants to, not substitutes for, therapeutic exercise.

Fig 10 — A timeline arrow with three phase boxes, each tagged COLD or HEAT, and a curve showing collagen strength rising over months. The one-line caption is the entire clinical message of this answer.
Examiner's tip: structure the whole answer around the three healing phases and you cannot drift. The sentence "thermal agents manage the environment; movement directs the repair" is a memorable closer. Learn the contraindication trio for each agent — viva examiners love asking heat over acute inflammation and cold over ischaemic skin.

5Recent advances

  • Racinais et al. (2024) — critical review in the British Journal of Sports Medicine finding no human evidence that cryotherapy limits secondary injury or improves tissue regeneration; it recommends cold within the first 6 hours of injury for pain (and possibly haematoma) control, with caution beyond 12 hours because animal studies suggest it may delay healing.
  • R. Chen et al. (2024) — network meta-analysis (57 studies, 1,220 participants) ranking cryotherapy best for relieving delayed-onset muscle soreness and for neuromuscular recovery, and contrast water therapy best for clearing creatine kinase after exercise-induced muscle damage.
  • J. Chen et al. (2025) — Bayesian network meta-analysis of physical modalities for delayed-onset muscle soreness finding photobiomodulation (low-level laser) superior to placebo at 24 and 48 hours, whereas cryotherapy and ultrasound were not significant.
  • Best et al. (2016) — systematic review of low-intensity therapeutic ultrasound finding it improves tendon tensile strength and collagen alignment and aids muscle, ligament and tendon-bone healing, being most effective when started early in the repair process.

6References

  1. Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — thermal agents and tissue healing.
  2. O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation — physical agents in rehabilitation.
  3. Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — local blood flow and temperature regulation.
  4. Levangie & Norkin, Joint Structure and Function — connective tissue injury and repair.
  5. Cryotherapy for treating soft tissue injuries in sport medicine: a critical review. Br J Sports Med. 2024;58:1215–1224.
  6. Comparison between cryotherapy and photobiomodulation in muscle recovery: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Lasers Med Sci. 2022;37(3):1655–1664.
Last-Hour Sheet · Paper II

QP 8130 · 30-May-2024 · the 60-minute sheet — one line per idea, the night before the exam. Cover a column and test yourself.

1Aging and mobility

  • Muscle mass: 3-5% lost per decade from the 30s; strength and power fall 2-5 times faster than mass (dynapenia).
  • Four pillars shrink together: joint (cartilage, capsule), muscle (sarcopenia), nerve (reaction time, proprioception), behaviour (fear of falling).
  • Power loss matters most for chair-rise and fall recovery — mention it for extra marks.

2Fascia

  • One continuous collagen-hyaluronan web: packages, transmits force laterally (myofascial force transmission), stores elastic energy.
  • Richest sensory organ — mechanoreceptors plus myofibroblasts; source of myofascial pain.
  • Treat the glide, not just the muscle: slow stretch, movement, scar release.

3Shoulder after cuff repair

  • Protect the healing tendon-bone interface: moved, not loaded.
  • Kinematics: guarded abduction and external rotation, altered scapulohumeral rhythm (more scapular), stiffness is the big complication.
  • Kinetics: deltoid unopposed upward versus cuff compression — concavity compression; restore rhythm first, force couple second.

4Muscle in endurance training

  • Mitochondria 2-3 times more, capillary density up, myoglobin up, oxidative enzymes up.
  • Type I hypertrophy modest; IIx toward IIa; no big bulk — quality, not size.
  • Glycogen sparing, lactate threshold shifts right; fatigue resistance is the outcome.

5Elbow fixed flexion deformity

  • The arc does not shrink, it shifts into flexion; carrying angle effectively lost.
  • Functional arc 30-130 degrees does most tasks; small FFD tolerated, but no pushing, no weight-bearing lock, no flat reach.
  • Compensation: shoulder and wrist — they overload. Treat with extension splinting, low-load stretch, posterior glides.

6Forward head posture

  • Upper cervical extension with lower cervical flexion, so the eyes stay level; craniovertebral angle decreases.
  • Upper crossed syndrome: tight upper trapezius, levator, suboccipitals, pecs; weak deep neck flexors, lower trapezius.
  • Remote effects: apical breathing, impingement, TMJ stress, tension-type headache via trigeminocervical nucleus.

7Equilibrium after ankle injury

  • Three inputs (somatosensory, vestibular, visual) plus three strategies (ankle, hip, stepping); body is an inverted pendulum on the ankle.
  • Torn ligament means torn mechanoreceptors — Freeman: articular reflex failure, sway up, eyes closed worse, chronic instability.
  • Balance training cut re-injury from 29% to 7% (Holme 1999) — quote it.

8Injection foot drop

  • Sciatic nerve, peroneal division (lateral, less protected): dorsiflexors and evertors out; plantar flexion relatively spared.
  • Contact: foot slap or toe strike; stance: abrupt loading; swing: steppage — hip and knee hyperflexion.
  • Alternatives: circumduction, hip hiking, vaulting; manage with AFO, stimulation, contracture prevention.

9Male versus female structure

  • Fat: women 20-30% versus men 12-20%; essential fat 12-15% versus 3-5%; fat-free mass higher in men.
  • Upper body muscle about 40% more in men; strength gap narrows per kilogram of lean mass.
  • Pelvis: subpubic angle 80-85 degrees versus 50-60; larger Q angle links to female knee problems.

10Thermal agents and repair

  • Three phases: inflammatory days 0-6, proliferative weeks 1-3, remodelling months to a year.
  • Cold in inflammation: vasoconstriction, less oedema, analgesia, slower nerve conduction.
  • Heat 40-45 degrees later: blood flow, collagen extensibility before stretch; ultrasound heats deep collagen. Match agent to phase; movement directs the repair.
keep-if-nothing-else: the minimum cargo for the exam hall.

Question 1 · 10 marks

Q1. Explain the various classification of joints.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit I — Arthrology, joint structure & function

★ Memory hook — "Structure names the tissue, Function names the freedom, and the two maps always agree."

1Introduction

A joint, or articulation, is the region where two or more bones meet. It is the structural solution that reconciles two competing demands of the skeleton: stability, so that load can be transmitted and organs protected, and mobility, so that movement can occur. Because joints must serve both roles in different proportions, anatomists, biomechanists and clinicians have developed several complementary ways of classifying them. In musculoskeletal physiotherapy the classification of joints is not a matter of taxonomy for its own sake — it predicts how much motion a joint can give, how much load it can bear, and therefore which joints are vulnerable to which pathology and which movement strategies are safe to prescribe.

2Physiology

Every classification rests on the normal structure of a joint. A fibrous joint unites bones by dense fibrous connective tissue and has no joint cavity; a cartilaginous joint unites bones by hyaline cartilage or fibrocartilage; and a synovial joint has a fluid-filled joint cavity separating the articulating surfaces. A synovial joint is a composite structure: a fibrous articular capsule continuous with the periosteum; a synovial membrane that secretes synovial fluid for lubrication and nutrition; hyaline articular cartilage covering each bony surface; and, in some joints, intra-articular discs or menisci. This architecture gives synovial joints an extremely low coefficient of friction and the capacity to transmit loads several times body weight. Crucially, the amount of movement a joint permits is inversely related to its stability: the more mobile the joint, the more it depends on ligaments, capsule and muscles for its integrity.

3Pathophysiology

Joint type governs pathomechanics. A synovial joint that loses articular cartilage (osteoarthritis) or that is immobilised (adhesive capsulitis) loses its defining property — free, near-frictionless motion. A cartilaginous joint such as an intervertebral disc degenerates by losing its hydrated, pressurised nucleus, shifting load onto the annulus and facets. A fibrous joint such as a syndesmosis can be disrupted by a divisive force (ankle syndesmotic sprain). Ankylosing spondylitis converts mobile, diarthrodial and amphiarthrodial spinal joints into rigid synarthroses by ossification, abolishing segmental movement and dramatically changing the mechanics of the whole column. Thus the classification directly frames the mechanical consequences of disease.

4Answer

(A) Structural (histological) classification — based on the tissue uniting the bones:

  • Fibrous joints: Sutures (skull, immovable), Gomphoses (tooth in socket), Syndesmoses (tibiofibular, radioulnar — slightly movable).
  • Cartilaginous joints: Primary (synchondroses) — hyaline cartilage, e.g. first sternocostal joint, growth plates; Secondary (symphyses) — fibrocartilage, e.g. pubic symphysis, intervertebral discs.
  • Synovial joints: a joint cavity with synovial fluid; the most mobile and most numerous joints.

(B) Functional classification — based on the amount of movement:

  • Synarthrosis — immovable (sutures).
  • Amphiarthrosis — slightly movable (symphyses).
  • Diarthrosis — freely movable (all synovial joints).

(C) Classification of synovial joints by shape and axes:

SubtypeAxes / movementExample
Plane (gliding)Non-axialIntercarpal, facet joints
HingeUniaxial (flexion–extension)Elbow, knee
PivotUniaxial (rotation)Atlantoaxial, proximal radioulnar
CondyloidBiaxialMetacarpophalangeal, wrist
SaddleBiaxialFirst carpometacarpal
Ball & socketMultiaxialShoulder, hip

(D) Biomechanical classification — by degrees of freedom (1, 2 or 3 DOF), by number of articulating surfaces (simple — two surfaces; compound — three or more, e.g. elbow; complex — with an intra-articular disc/meniscus, e.g. knee), and by articular surface geometry (flat, concave, convex, trochlear).

5Recent advances

  • Malfait et al. (2017) — The 2017 international classification of the Ehlers–Danlos syndromes recognises 13 subtypes and revises the clinical criteria for the hypermobile type, giving physiotherapists a standard way to classify symptomatic joint hypermobility (Beighton score ≥5) and separate it from other joint-laxity disorders.
  • Castori et al. (2017) — Proposed the "hypermobility spectrum disorders" framework that classifies symptomatic joint hypermobility as generalised, peripheral, localised or historical — a clinically useful, physiotherapy-facing taxonomy that complements the classical structural and functional classification of joints.
  • Liaghat et al. (2022) — Randomised trial in BJSM showed that high-load shoulder strengthening gave greater functional gains than low-load training in people with hypermobile shoulders, guiding exercise prescription once a joint is classified as hypermobile.
  • Reychler et al. (2021) — Systematic review found therapeutic exercise and proprioceptive/motor-function training improve pain and proprioception in hypermobile EDS, showing that classifying a joint as hypermobile directly changes physiotherapy management.

Question 2 · 10 marks

Q2. Describe how body size influence musculoskeletal disorder.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit — Biomechanics of load, body composition & musculoskeletal risk

★ Memory hook — "Weight loads the joint; fat inflames it too — so body size hits bone twice."

1Introduction

Body size — captured clinically as body mass index (BMI), body mass, and fat distribution — is one of the strongest modifiable determinants of musculoskeletal health. Excess body size acts on the musculoskeletal system through two broad mechanisms: a biomechanical mechanism (greater load and altered movement), and a metabolic/systemic mechanism (low-grade inflammation from adipose tissue). Understanding both is essential because it explains why obesity is linked not only to load-bearing joint disease such as knee osteoarthritis but also to conditions at non-weight-bearing sites.

2Physiology

Normal joint mechanics are scaled to body mass. During walking the knee and hip transmit forces that are multiples of body weight; the ground reaction force is distributed between compartments according to alignment and the external moment arms. Greater body mass increases both the magnitude of the ground reaction force and the muscle forces required to control it, because muscle force scales with the moment that must be generated. Heavier individuals also adopt a wider stride, spend longer in double support, and show increased ankle and knee muscle co-contraction to stabilise the loaded limb. Body fat distribution matters: android (abdominal) and gynoid (hip/thigh) patterns produce different neuromuscular adaptations and different lever arms about the joint.

3Pathophysiology

Biomechanically, higher body mass raises articular cartilage contact stress. Subject-specific musculoskeletal and finite-element models show that obesity significantly increases muscle activation, ligament stress and cartilage contact stress at the knee, particularly at the first and second peak loading instances of stance, with a disproportionate rise on the medial plateau. This drives medial compartment cartilage loss and varus progression. Systemically, adipose tissue is metabolically active, releasing adipokines (leptin, IL-6, CRP) that create a chronic low-grade inflammatory state which degrades cartilage independently of load — explaining why obesity also associates with hand and shoulder disease. At the spine, obesity raises L5–S1 compression and shear during reaching and lifting, and postural adjustment alone does not compensate for the extra load, increasing low back pain and disc degeneration risk.

4Answer

Body size influences musculoskeletal disorders through the following pathways:

  • Increased joint loading — greater compressive, shear and patellofemoral forces at the knee, hip and ankle; higher L5–S1 compression and shear in the spine.
  • Altered gait and alignment — wider stride, longer double support, increased knee adduction moment and varus alignment, medialising load.
  • Increased muscle work — higher muscle activation and co-contraction to move and stabilise a heavier limb; earlier fatigue, reduced balance, greater fall risk.
  • Metabolic / inflammatory effects — adipokine-driven low-grade inflammation degrades cartilage and sensitises pain pathways, including at non-weight-bearing joints.
  • Structural consequences — accelerated knee and hip osteoarthritis, meniscal tears, plantar heel pain, altered foot posture, tendinopathy, and disc degeneration.
  • Rehabilitation implications — higher surgical risk, greater prosthetic and orthotic demands, and greater need for load-reduction strategies (weight management, aquatic therapy, gait retraining).

Epidemiologically, high BMI is estimated to account for tens of millions of prevalent cases of osteoarthritis and low back pain worldwide, with substantial disability and economic burden. Clinically, even modest weight reduction lowers knee joint compressive force, so body-size management is a first-line musculoskeletal intervention.

5Recent advances

  • Messier et al. (2013) — The IDEA randomised trial (JAMA) showed that diet-induced weight loss (≥10%) plus exercise lowered knee compressive force and inflammation and improved pain and function more than exercise alone in obese knee OA, making weight management a core physiotherapy target.
  • Bannuru et al. (2019) — The OARSI guidelines make structured land-based exercise, with or without dietary weight management, a "core treatment" for knee OA, translating the body-size–load link into first-line physiotherapy practice.
  • Fransen et al. (2015) — Cochrane review confirmed that land-based exercise reduces pain and improves physical function in knee OA, supporting exercise even before significant weight reduction is achieved.
  • Maktouf et al. (2024) — Gait study showed body-fat distribution (android vs gynoid) alters ankle muscle co-contraction in obese individuals, refining individualised load-reduction and gait advice.

6References

  2. Levangie PK, Norkin CC. Joint Structure and Function. 6th ed. FA Davis.
  3. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. 7th ed. FA Davis.
  4. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. 8th ed. FA Davis.
