Question 3 · 10 marks

Q3. Describe the Kinetic & Kinematic change following Patellectomy.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit — Knee biomechanics & the extensor mechanism

★ Memory hook — "Lose the patella, lose the pulley — the quadriceps must work harder for less."

1Introduction

Patellectomy is the surgical removal of the patella, historically performed for comminuted fractures, severe patellofemoral arthritis or tumours. The patella is not a redundant sesamoid: it is the key mechanical element of the knee extensor mechanism. Its removal predictably alters both the kinematics (movement) and the kinetics (forces) of the knee, producing weakness, altered tracking and a characteristic functional deficit. Understanding these changes explains why patellectomy is now rare and why, when unavoidable, it is followed by focused rehabilitation.

2Physiology

Normally the patella functions as a mobile pulley. It increases the moment arm of the quadriceps about the knee joint centre, so for a given quadriceps force it produces a larger extension moment. It also centralises the pull of the quadriceps, protects the femoral articular surface, and shares load with the femoral trochlea through the patellofemoral joint. The patellofemoral contact force rises steeply with knee flexion — during squatting it can exceed three times body weight — and depends on patellar thickness, position and tracking. The extensor mechanism is thus a lever-and-pulley system whose efficiency depends on the patella being present, centred and at correct height.

3Pathophysiology

When the patella is removed, the quadriceps tendon is repaired directly to the patellar tendon. The lever arm of the extensor mechanism is reduced by roughly the thickness of the patella (about 2–3 cm), so the quadriceps must generate substantially more force for the same extension moment — a mechanical disadvantage estimated at 15–30% loss of extension torque. The tendon repair lengthens the extensor mechanism and alters the tendon–joint angle, reducing efficiency further and predisposing to extensor lag. Loss of the patella also removes anterior protection and centralisation, so the residual quadriceps vector can deviate and produce abnormal tracking. Over time the altered mechanics increase stress at the tibiofemoral joint and the repair site.

4Answer

Kinematic changes (movement):

  • Reduced active knee extension range and a terminal extensor lag — the knee cannot be actively straightened fully, especially against gravity or resistance.
  • Altered sagittal plane motion: the extensor mechanism's changed length–tension relation produces a weaker and more variable extension arc.
  • Loss of normal patellar tracking (the patella no longer glides in the trochlea), removing a stabilising element of knee motion.
  • Compensatory gait adaptations: reduced knee flexion moment, shorter step and slower speed, and increased hip and ankle work to compensate for the weak knee.

Kinetic changes (forces):

  • Reduced quadriceps moment arm → increased quadriceps force required for any given knee extension moment (mechanical disadvantage).
  • Lower peak knee extension torque (strength deficit), most marked in extension near full range.
  • Increased stress at the tibiofemoral articulation because the extensor load is redistributed without the patellofemoral load-sharing.
  • Altered patellofemoral contact mechanics in the resurfaced/reconstructed knee; where patellar reconstruction or component is used, thickness and position strongly affect contact force.

Functional consequence: difficulty with stair climbing, rising from a chair, and walking on inclines, with measurable strength loss and a higher complication rate if later total knee arthroplasty is required.

VariableNormal patellaAfter patellectomy
Quadriceps moment armLongReduced
Extension torqueFullReduced 15–30%
Active terminal extensionCompleteExtensor lag
Patellofemoral load-sharingPresentAbsent

5Recent advances

  • Gibson & Scott (1991) — Isokinetic study in Physiotherapy found quadriceps isometric force about 21–30% and peak torque about 33% lower years after patellectomy despite hypertrophy, because the patellar moment arm is lost — so rehabilitation must target sustained quadriceps strengthening.
  • Ziran et al. (1994) — Cybex testing after patellectomy with cruciform extensor-mechanism repair showed extensor torque was never fully restored and quadriceps function remained moderately reduced, with altered extensor-to-flexor ratios that guide realistic rehabilitation goals.
  • Asopa et al. (2015) — A tension-preserving patellectomy technique reported that the best long-term outcomes followed an intensive physiotherapy programme (early assisted range of motion, then closed- to open-chain strengthening), emphasising that rehabilitation, not surgery alone, drives recovery.

6References

  2. Levangie PK, Norkin CC. Joint Structure and Function. 6th ed. FA Davis.

Question 4 · 10 marks

Q4. Role of equilibrium following Total Hip Replacement.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit — Hip biomechanics, joint stability & balance

★ Memory hook — "A hip replacement is only as stable as the balance of forces around it."

1Introduction

Total hip replacement (THR) restores a pain-free, mobile hip, but its long-term success depends on equilibrium — the balance of forces, moments and postural control acting across the new joint. Equilibrium here has two linked meanings: the mechanical equilibrium of joint reaction forces and moments that keeps the prosthetic head seated in the cup, and the postural equilibrium (balance) that keeps the patient upright and stable during function. Both are central to preventing the commonest early complication, dislocation, and to restoring confident gait.

2Physiology

The normal hip is a multiaxial ball-and-socket joint stabilised by bony congruence, the labrum, a strong capsule and ligaments, and the abductor muscles. During single-leg stance, the abductors generate a force that balances the body-weight moment about the hip; the resultant joint reaction force is several times body weight and acts through the femoral head into the acetabulum. Posturally, the hip is a key balance strategy — the "hip strategy" moves the centre of mass by flexing or extending at the hip, complementing the ankle strategy. Proprioceptors in the capsule and muscles provide the sensory input for this control. Correct cup inclination and anteversion, restoration of offset and leg length, and adequate abductor tension together define the "safe zone" in which the hip remains mechanically stable.

3Pathophysiology

After THR the stabilising structures are altered: the capsule is cut, the labrum removed, and the native head–neck geometry replaced. Stability now depends heavily on implant design and position. Impingement — between the femoral neck and the acetabular rim or liner — is the mechanical precursor to dislocation; it occurs most in flexion–internal rotation and in extension–external rotation. Component malposition (excessive or insufficient anteversion, wrong inclination) lowers the "safety factor" and concentrates stress at the anterosuperior and posterosuperior acetabular quadrants. Posturally, pain, weakness of the abductors and altered proprioception impair balance, and patients with prior spinal fusion or neuromuscular disease are at higher dislocation risk because their lumbopelvic balance is already compromised.

4Answer

(A) Mechanical equilibrium — joint stability:

  • Jump distance: the lateral translation of the head needed to dislocate; increases with larger effective head diameter, giving a greater margin before dislocation.
  • Impingement-free arc of movement: larger heads and dual-mobility designs widen the arc before neck–cup impingement.
  • Component position: cup inclination about 40–45° and anteversion about 15–20°, restored offset and leg length, maintain the balance of forces and a high safety factor.
  • Abductor tension and soft-tissue repair: restoring the capsule and abductors re-establishes the moment balance that seats the head in the socket.
  • Dual-mobility bearings: a small head within a large mobile liner increases both jump distance and the impingement-free arc, reducing dislocation.

(B) Postural equilibrium — balance:

  • Balance is restored through the ankle and hip strategies; THR patients lean more on the hip strategy as hip control returns.
  • Abductor and extensor strengthening restores pelvic control during single-leg stance (the Trendelenburg mechanism).
  • Proprioceptive and gait retraining improve the sensory integration needed for dynamic balance.
  • Precautions (avoiding combined flexion, adduction and internal rotation) protect the mechanical equilibrium while soft tissues heal.

(C) Clinical importance: good equilibrium prevents dislocation, improves gait symmetry and weight-bearing confidence, and reduces fall risk — the outcome the patient values most.

5Recent advances

  • Jogi et al. (2015) — Randomised trial showed that adding balance exercises to standard post-operative rehabilitation after total hip arthroplasty significantly improved Berg Balance Scale and Timed Up and Go scores versus routine exercise alone.
  • Trudelle-Jackson & Smith (2004) — An 8-week late-phase programme emphasising weight-bearing and postural stability improved hip and knee strength and single-leg postural stability by about 37% in patients 4–12 months after total hip arthroplasty.
  • Labanca et al. (2021) — Systematic review found balance and proprioception deficits persist for up to 5 years after total hip arthroplasty with increased fall risk, but structured balance training is effective in every rehabilitation phase — justifying routine equilibrium retraining.

6References

  1. Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System. 5th ed. Wolters Kluwer.
  2. Levangie PK, Norkin CC. Joint Structure and Function. 6th ed. FA Davis.
  3. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. 8th ed. FA Davis.
  4. Dutton M. Dutton's Orthopaedic Examination, Evaluation and Intervention. 5th ed. McGraw Hill.
  5. Dual mobility versus standard cups in total hip replacement for displaced femoral neck fractures (Duality): an international randomised controlled superiority trial. The Lancet. 2026.
  6. Hip stability parameters with dual mobility and fixed bearing in THA: an analytical evaluation. BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders. 2022.
Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. Describe the changes seen in gait following Osteoarthritis knee.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit — Gait analysis & knee pathomechanics

★ Memory hook — "The knee shifts load inward, so the patient shifts time, speed and stance to cope."

1Introduction

Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a mechanically driven disease, and gait is where its mechanics are most visible. Because OA changes joint structure, alignment and pain, it alters every level of gait — spatiotemporal parameters, kinematics and kinetics. Recognising these gait changes is central to physiotherapy assessment and to designing load-modifying interventions.

2Physiology

Normal level walking has a stance phase of about 60% and a swing phase of about 40% of the cycle. At the knee, the joint is near full extension at heel strike, flexes slightly through loading (a "shock-absorbing" wave), extends in midstance and flexes again for toe clearance. The knee has a normal valgus alignment (Q angle) and load is shared between medial and lateral compartments. The external knee adduction moment (KAM) — the tendency of the ground reaction force to rotate the knee into varus — is the standard surrogate for medial compartment load, and its first and second peaks during stance describe the load pattern.

3Pathophysiology

In medial knee OA the joint loses cartilage and meniscus, the limb drifts into varus, and the mechanical axis shifts so that the ground reaction force passes further from the knee centre — increasing the KAM and loading the medial compartment further. Kinetic conversion occurs early: even at mild (grade 2) disease the relative contribution of the knee flexion moment falls while the KAM rises, before gross varus deformity appears. As severity increases, a fixed flexion contracture develops, the knee cannot fully extend, and the trunk flexes forward during gait to keep the centre of mass over the foot — a sagittal-plane compensation. Pain and quadriceps weakness further reduce the patient's tolerance for normal loading, so they adopt protective, energy-inefficient strategies.

4Answer

Spatiotemporal changes:

  • Reduced walking speed and cadence; shortened step and stride length.
  • Increased stance time on the affected side or, with pain, a shorter painful stance (antalgic pattern) with longer double-support.
  • Wider step width to improve frontal-plane stability.

Kinematic changes:

  • Reduced knee flexion during loading (loss of the shock-absorbing wave) and reduced peak knee flexion in swing.
  • Flexion contracture → inability to reach terminal extension; reduced overall knee range.
  • Varus thrust during loading — a dynamic bowing of the knee.
  • Compensatory trunk forward flexion and reduced pelvic/hip excursion.
  • Altered foot progression angle (often toe-out) as a load-reducing strategy.

Kinetic changes:

  • Elevated external knee adduction moment (both peaks), the hallmark of medial compartment overload.
  • Reduced knee flexion moment and a shift in the relative moment contribution (kinetic conversion) from flexion to adduction dominance.
  • Reduced knee extensor (quadriceps) moment and power; increased hip and ankle compensation.
  • Lower vertical ground reaction force peaks and a prolonged, flattened loading response.

Clinical translation: these changes explain why gait retraining (foot progression angle modification, increased step width, trunk modification) is used to reduce the KAM and offload the medial compartment, alongside strengthening and load management.

5Recent advances

  • Wang et al. (2021) — Meta-analysis in Arthritis Care & Research found toe-out gait reduces the second knee adduction moment peak and knee adduction impulse in knee osteoarthritis.
  • Uhlrich et al. (2022) — Personalised gait modification reduced the larger knee adduction moment peak in a greater proportion of patients than uniform toe-in or toe-out instructions.
  • Rynne et al. (2022) — Systematic review and meta-analysis in Gait & Posture showed gait retraining with real-time biofeedback significantly reduced the knee adduction moment and improved WOMAC scores in knee osteoarthritis.
  • Cottmeyer et al. (2023) — Systematic review in Clinical Biomechanics found exercise interventions can reduce the external knee adduction moment during gait, supporting strengthening and gait work alongside load-reduction strategies.

6References

  1. Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System. 5th ed. Wolters Kluwer.
  2. Levangie PK, Norkin CC. Joint Structure and Function. 6th ed. FA Davis.
  3. Perry J, Burnfield JM. Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function. 2nd ed. Slack.
  4. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. 7th ed. FA Davis.
  5. Assessing knee joint biomechanics and trunk posture according to medial osteoarthritis severity. Scientific Reports. 2023.
  6. Wang S, et al. How foot progression angle affects knee adduction moment in medial knee OA: a meta-analysis. Arthritis Care & Research. 2021.
Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. Write in detail about various methods of energy conservation following below knee amputation.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit — Amputee biomechanics, gait & energy cost

★ Memory hook — "Walk less, walk better, walk lighter — conserve the energy the missing ankle used to give."

1Introduction

After a below-knee (transtibial) amputation the energy cost of walking rises, because the prosthetic ankle cannot replace the powerful push-off and energy-return of the biological ankle. The metabolic cost of ambulation may be 20–40% higher than in non-amputees and rises further with proximal amputation level, poor fitness and comorbidity. Energy conservation is therefore a core rehabilitation goal: it protects the cardiovascular system, reduces fatigue and secondary joint overload, and improves the patient's ability to participate in daily life.

2Physiology

In normal gait the ankle plantarflexors generate the largest single burst of power in the cycle — the push-off that accelerates the body forward — and the Achilles tendon stores and returns elastic energy. The prosthetic limb, whether an energy-storing-and-return (ESAR) foot or a microprocessor-controlled ankle, can only partly reproduce this. Additional energy is then drawn from the hip and knee of both limbs, and the patient uses compensatory movements (vaulting, hip hiking, circumduction, lateral trunk lean) that themselves cost energy. The result is a higher physiological cost of walking and a tendency to fatigue early.

3Pathophysiology

Loss of the ankle’s push-off means the residual limb cannot generate normal trailing-limb positive work, so the intact limb must do more — raising intact-limb loading, knee adduction moment and long-term osteoarthritis risk. Reduced ankle proprioception and altered balance increase the muscular work needed for stability. Higher prosthetic mass distally increases the energy cost of swing (each additional 0.5 kg at the ankle raises metabolic rate). Compensatory gait deviations, while protecting against falling, add to the overall energy demand, creating a vicious cycle of fatigue, reduced activity, deconditioning and still greater relative effort.

4Answer

Energy-conservation methods fall into prosthetic, gait-training, fitness, activity and environmental strategies:

(A) Prosthetic and orthotic optimisation:

  • Prescribe a lightweight, well-aligned prosthesis with an appropriate ESAR foot to store and return energy.
  • Consider a microprocessor-controlled ankle/foot that adapts to slopes and terrain, improving efficiency and stability.
  • Optimise socket fit to avoid pistoning and unnecessary muscular effort; reduce distal mass.

(B) Gait training and movement economy:

  • Train a smooth, symmetrical gait; avoid vaulting, hip hiking, circumduction and excessive trunk lean.
  • Use an appropriate, comfortable walking speed — energy cost per metre is minimised at the patient’s self-selected speed.
  • Teach controlled, rhythmic breathing and relaxed arm swing.

(C) Cardiovascular and muscular fitness:

  • Graded aerobic conditioning to raise the aerobic capacity ceiling (arm ergometry, cycling, swimming, aquatic therapy).
  • Strengthen hip abductors/extensors and knee extensors of both limbs to reduce compensatory effort and improve pelvic control.

(D) Activity and task modification (work simplification):

  • Plan the day: cluster activities, alternate heavy and light tasks, and pace with rest periods.
  • Use assistive devices and labour-saving equipment; sit to work; slide rather than lift objects.
  • Organise the home so frequently used items are at waist height; use a trolley, a stool and a shower seat.

(E) Environmental and mobility aids:

  • Use a wheelchair, scooter or crutches for long distances; reserve walking for essential trips.
  • Optimise footwear, floor surfaces and lighting; remove trip hazards.
  • Consider a walking aid that reduces load but does not compromise balance.

(F) General health: maintain optimal body weight, control diabetes and cardiovascular disease, avoid smoking, and manage pain — each directly lowers the energy cost of walking.

5Recent advances

  • Hafner et al. (2022) — Systematic review and meta-analysis in PM&R showed prosthetic feet with powered dorsiflexion lower the metabolic energy cost of walking versus dynamic-response feet in active transtibial users, informing energy-efficient prosthetic prescription.
  • Wong et al. (2014) — Systematic review in Prosthetics and Orthotics International found supervised walking, muscle strengthening, balance and functional gait training improve gait performance after lower-limb amputation — a Grade B evidence base for energy-conserving gait rehabilitation.
  • Mazzarini et al. (2024) — A semi-active energy-storing-and-return foot with a low-power actuator reduced the Physiological Cost Index by up to 16% in transtibial amputees, cutting the energy cost of walking.
  • Colas-Ribas et al. (2022) — Microprocessor-controlled ankles reduce metabolic cost on level ground without the expected penalty of added distal mass, supporting their use in energy-conservation programmes.

Question 7 · 10 marks

Q7. Describe the change in the mechanics seen in lumbar spine following L4, L5 disc prolapse.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit — Lumbar spine biomechanics & disc pathomechanics

★ Memory hook — "Flexion loads the back, the disc fails posterolaterally, and the facets inherit the load."

1Introduction

Lumbar disc prolapse (herniation) is commonest at L4–L5 and L5–S1, the segments carrying the greatest mechanical demand. Prolapse is not a random event: it is the endpoint of a mechanically driven process in which repetitive or excessive loading disrupts the load-sharing between the nucleus pulposus, the annulus fibrosus and the facet joints. Understanding the altered mechanics at and around the prolapsed segment explains the symptoms and guides conservative and surgical management.

2Physiology

A healthy intervertebral disc is a pressurised, hydrated structure. The nucleus pulposus is a gel that maintains hydrostatic pressure and transmits compressive load uniformly outward to the annulus fibrosus, whose criss-crossing collagen lamellae resist tensile and shear stress. The posterior longitudinal ligament reinforces the posterior disc. The facet joints share load, especially in extension and rotation. Segmental movement is a fine balance between the depressurised "soft" disc and the "hard" posterior elements. Under combined axial compression, flexion and shear, the annulus is loaded most posterolaterally, where its lamellae are thinnest and the ligament support weakest.

3Pathophysiology

Repeated flexion combined with compression and shear produces microdamage, delamination and radial fissures in the posterolateral annulus. Failure typically begins at the annulus–endplate junction and propagates, allowing nuclear material to bulge or extrude — most often paracentrally at L4–L5. Once herniation occurs, the mechanical environment reorganises: loss of nuclear pressurisation reduces disc height and internal pressure, shifting compressive load onto the posterior annulus and facet joints. Intradiscal pressure falls while annular stress, facet joint force and disc bulge rise. The herniated or bulging material can compress the adjacent nerve root. Muscle forces increase to maintain segmental moment equilibrium, adding further compression.

4Answer

Changes at the L4–L5 segment:

  • Reduced intradiscal pressure — loss of nuclear hydration and pressurisation; the disc no longer shares load hydrostatically.
  • Increased annular stress — load shifts to the annulus fibrosus; peak annular tensile and shear stress rise markedly.
  • Increased disc bulge — the depressurised disc bulges further, potentially impinging the nerve root.
  • Reduced segmental range of motion at the degenerated level, with the motion redistributed.
  • Reduced disc height and volume — altering the lever arms and load-sharing of the segment.

Changes at the facet joints:

  • Increased facet joint force — load transfers from the depressurised nucleus to the posterior elements (in one model, a 1.5–4.5-fold rise after nucleotomy).
  • Facet joint degeneration and pain (facetogenic component of low back pain).

Changes in the surrounding system:

  • Increased muscle activity — most trunk muscle groups show compensatory increased activation to maintain moment equilibrium and stability.
  • Increased compressive and shear forces on all lumbar motion segments during flexion and lifting.
  • Altered load-sharing to adjacent segments — adjacent (L3–L4, L5–S1) intradiscal pressure and facet forces rise, accelerating adjacent-segment degeneration.
  • Kinematic consequence — reduced flexion range and altered segmental motion curve at the affected level; compensatory increased motion at adjacent levels.

Clinical translation: flexion-loaded positions and asymmetric loading are the highest-risk postures; rehabilitation emphasises avoiding sustained loaded flexion, restoring lordosis control, building endurance of the deep spinal stabilisers, and using biomechanically informed loading.

5Recent advances

  • Kent et al. (2023) — The RESTORE randomised trial (Lancet) showed cognitive functional therapy produced large, sustained reductions in activity limitation and lower societal cost than usual care for chronic disabling low back pain — a landmark physiotherapy result.
  • Hill et al. (2011) — The STarT Back trial (Lancet) showed prognostic stratification with matched physiotherapy pathways improved disability outcomes and was cost-effective for low back pain with or without radiculopathy.
  • Plaza-Manzano et al. (2019) — Randomised trial found adding neurodynamic mobilisation to motor control training improved neuropathic symptoms and straight-leg-raise range in lumbar radiculopathy due to disc herniation.
  • Danazumi et al. (2023) — Randomised trial in Journal of Manual & Manipulative Therapy found Mulligan mobilisation with leg movement plus neurodynamic mobilisation gave better long-term pain, function and quality-of-life outcomes than manipulation in lumbar disc herniation with radiculopathy.

6References

Question 8 · 10 marks

Q8. Describe the various postural deformation seen in Ankylosis Spondylitis.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit — Spinal posture, sagittal balance & rheumatic disease

★ Memory hook — "The spine stiffens and the body folds forward — the hips and knees try to stand in for it."

1Introduction

Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a chronic inflammatory disease of the axial skeleton that causes progressive ossification of the spine, sacroiliac joints and entheses. The characteristic result is a rigid, progressively kyphotic spine with a distinctive set of postural deformations. These postural changes are not merely cosmetic: they displace the trunk’s centre of mass, load the posterior elements, impair balance and vision, and drive pain and disability. Recognising the postural pattern guides exercise therapy and surgical planning.

2Physiology

The normal spine has reciprocal sagittal curves: cervical lordosis, thoracic kyphosis, lumbar lordosis, with the centre of mass of the trunk sitting over the pelvis and feet. This alignment minimises muscle work and keeps the head level and gaze horizontal. The hips extend to place the pelvis in an efficient position, and the sacroiliac joints transmit load from spine to lower limbs. Flexibility of the spine and hips allows the body to keep its line of gravity within the base of support during movement.

3Pathophysiology

In AS, inflammation of the discs, ligaments and facet joints leads to ossification and fusion (ankylosis), progressively rigidifying the spine and flattening its mobile segments. Loss of lumbar lordosis and increased thoracic kyphosis shift the trunk centre of mass forward and downward. To keep the head level and maintain balance, the patient compensates: hip flexion, knee flexion, ankle dorsiflexion, posterior pelvic tilt (retroversion) and cervical hyperextension. Eventually these compensations are exhausted and sagittal imbalance, gait disturbance and fall risk result. The rigid, fused spine is also more vulnerable to fracture from minor trauma.

4Answer

Postural deformations in AS:

  • Loss of lumbar lordosis — the lumbar spine flattens or becomes kyphotic.
  • Increased thoracic kyphosis — dorsal hyperkyphosis, the hallmark "question-mark" or stooped posture.
  • Forward head posture / cervical hyperextension — the neck extends to keep the gaze horizontal (reduced cervical range, sometimes reversed cervical lordosis).
  • Posterior pelvic tilt (retroversion) — the pelvis rotates backward as the hips flex.
  • Hip flexion contracture — the hips are held flexed, further folding the trunk.
  • Compensatory knee flexion — the knees bend to lower the pelvis and maintain balance.
  • Ankle dorsiflexion and altered foot posture — ankle angles change as a final compensation.
  • Reduced chest expansion — costovertebral involvement limits rib excursion and breathing.
  • Reduced global spinal mobility — loss of flexion, extension, lateral flexion and rotation; the modified Schober test is reduced.
  • Sagittal imbalance and forward trunk inclination — the centre of mass sits forward of the base of support.

Functional consequences: difficulty looking straight ahead and with horizontal gaze, impaired balance and increased fall risk, reduced walking speed and stride length, altered pelvic and trunk motion in gait, difficulty with daily activities, and increased fracture risk from the rigid spine. Gait analysis shows reduced speed, shorter steps, reduced pelvic rotation and compensatory hip flexion.

Rehabilitation implication: exercise therapy — maintaining spinal mobility, extension, chest expansion, posture and hip flexibility — is central, and conservative therapy should particularly focus on preventing restriction of the hip joints.

5Recent advances

  • Kurtoglu et al. (2019) — Three-dimensional posture analysis quantified increased thoracic kyphosis (about 45° vs 37°) and reduced lumbar lordosis in ankylosing spondylitis, alongside knee flexion and pelvic retroversion, giving objective targets for posture re-education.
  • Sveaas et al. (2020) — Multicentre randomised trial in BJSM showed 3 months of high-intensity cardiorespiratory and strength exercise reduced disease activity and improved function and cardiovascular health in axial spondyloarthritis, debunking the fear that intense exercise worsens disease.
  • Ramiro et al. (2023) — The ASAS-EULAR 2022 recommendations make exercise and physiotherapy a cornerstone of axial spondyloarthritis management, endorsing structured mobility and postural exercise as core care.
  • Johnston et al. (2026) — Narrative review concluded that maintaining spinal mobility and function through exercise reduces pain and improves quality of life in axial spondyloarthritis.

6References

  2. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 7th ed. Elsevier.
  3. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. 8th ed. FA Davis.
  4. Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System. 5th ed. Wolters Kluwer.
  5. Bot SDM, et al. Biomechanical analysis of posture in patients with spinal kyphosis due to ankylosing spondylitis: a pilot study. Rheumatology. 1999.

Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. A 60 Years old woman is unable to dorsiflex her left ankle following prolonged crossed leg sitting. Describe the pathological gait.

Read this answer in plain English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit — Peripheral nerve injury & pathological gait (foot drop)

★ Memory hook — "Foot drop: the toe cannot clear the floor, so the knee lifts high and the foot slaps down."

1Introduction

This patient has developed a left foot drop — an inability to actively dorsiflex the ankle. The history of prolonged crossed-leg sitting points to compression of the common peroneal (fibular) nerve at the fibular head, the commonest site of lower-limb entrapment neuropathy. The peroneal nerve winds superficially around the fibular neck, where it is vulnerable to external pressure. The result is a characteristic pathological gait, which must be described systematically.

2Physiology

Normal ankle dorsiflexion is produced by tibialis anterior, aided by extensor hallucis longus and extensor digitorum longus (deep peroneal nerve), while ankle eversion is produced by peroneus longus and brevis (superficial peroneal nerve). During walking, dorsiflexion is needed twice: at initial contact to place the heel and control the foot, and during swing to clear the toes from the ground. The tibialis anterior contracts eccentrically at heel strike (to lower the foot gently) and concentrically in swing (to lift the foot). Loss of this muscle action removes both functions.

3Pathophysiology

Prolonged crossed-leg sitting compresses the common peroneal nerve against the fibular head, producing a conduction block (neurapraxia) or, if prolonged, axonal injury. This paralyses the dorsiflexors and evertors (and weakens toe extensors), while the plantarflexors (gastrocnemius–soleus, tibialis posterior) remain intact. The unopposed plantarflexor and gravity pull the foot into plantarflexion and inversion. Gait is disrupted in both stance and swing: at heel strike the foot cannot be controlled and slaps down or lands toe-first; during swing the foot hangs and the toes risk catching the ground, so the patient adopts compensations to gain clearance.

4Answer

The pathological gait is a "foot drop" / high-steppage (steppage) gait. Key features:

Swing phase:

  • Foot drop / plantarflexion of the affected foot — the foot hangs down because dorsiflexors are paralysed.
  • Excessive knee flexion (steppage) — the patient lifts the knee high to clear the toes.
  • Hip hiking (pelvic elevation) on the affected side as an alternative clearance strategy.
  • Circumduction — swinging the leg outward in an arc to clear the ground.
  • Increased inversion of the foot before contact, predisposing to lateral ankle sprain.

Stance phase:

  • Foot slap at initial contact — the foot drops rapidly because eccentric dorsiflexor control is lost; often a toe-first or flat-foot landing rather than heel strike.
  • Reduced heel-strike phase and reduced plantarflexion movement in early stance.
  • Instability in the frontal plane during midstance and push-off (increased inversion–eversion range).
  • Reduced second vertical force peak and reduced push-off, so step length is shortened.

Overall gait characteristics:

  • Reduced walking speed (often 40–50% slower) and cadence; shorter step and stride length.
  • Asymmetry between limbs; increased energy cost and early fatigue.
  • Compensatory over-activity at the knee and hip, with increased joint loading — potentially leading to long-term knee and hip overload.
  • Increased fall and trip risk, especially on uneven ground.

Management principle: protect the nerve (avoid further compression), preserve range, and provide an ankle-foot orthosis (AFO) to hold the foot in neutral or slight dorsiflexion, restoring safe clearance and a heel strike. Physiotherapy includes passive stretching, strengthening of remaining dorsiflexors, gait retraining and, where recovery is incomplete, functional electrical stimulation.

5Recent advances

  • Berenpas et al. (2018) — Implantable peroneal functional electrical stimulation improved ankle power, propulsion and gait symmetry compared with a conventional ankle-foot orthosis in drop foot, a landmark neuro-rehabilitation option.
  • Prenton et al. (2017) — Meta-analysis in Journal of Rehabilitation Medicine found functional electrical stimulation and ankle-foot orthoses produce equivalent positive effects on walking speed in foot drop of central neurological origin.
  • Nascimento et al. (2020) — Systematic review and meta-analysis in Physiotherapy showed both ankle-foot orthoses and continuous functional electrical stimulation significantly increase walking speed after stroke, supporting device-assisted gait training for foot drop.
  • Afacan et al. (2025) — Case report documented complete recovery from peroneal nerve palsy after prolonged cross-legged sitting with conservative management and rehabilitation, confirming neurapraxia as the usual mechanism and the value of supportive physiotherapy.

6References

  2. Perry J, Burnfield JM. Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function. 2nd ed. Slack.
  3. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. 7th ed. FA Davis.
  4. Dutton M. Dutton's Orthopaedic Examination, Evaluation and Intervention. 5th ed. McGraw Hill.
  5. Complete recovery from acute peroneal nerve palsy with neurapraxia after prolonged cross-legged sitting. Cureus. 2025.

Question 10 · 10 marks

Q10. Describe the effects of cold on skeletal muscle performance.

Read this answer in plain English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit — Electrophysical agents, muscle physiology & performance

★ Memory hook — "Cold slows the muscle: less force, less speed, less endurance — but less pain."

1Introduction

Cold (cryotherapy) is one of the most widely used physical agents in physiotherapy, applied for pain, swelling and muscle spasm. Its effect on skeletal muscle performance, however, is more complex than its analgesic reputation suggests. Cold reduces tissue temperature, and because muscle contraction is a temperature-sensitive process, cooling predictably alters strength, power, endurance and the speed of contraction. Clinicians must understand these effects to use cold appropriately — and to avoid applying it immediately before activities that require peak muscle performance.

2Physiology

Muscle contraction depends on the nervous impulse, calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, actin–myosin cross-bridge cycling and energy metabolism — all enzyme- and rate-dependent. Lowering muscle temperature slows these processes: nerve conduction velocity falls, the rate of calcium release and re-uptake decreases, cross-bridge cycling slows, and the rate of ATP production and glycogen resynthesis declines. Cooling also increases muscle–tendon stiffness and viscosity, so the tissue resists rapid stretch and generates force more slowly. Clinically, a muscle temperature of about 15°C (achieved with ice) produces measurable impairment of function.

3Pathophysiology

The reduced rate of excitation–contraction coupling directly lowers the muscle’s ability to produce force and power. Slowed nerve conduction and altered proprioceptive feedback reduce neuromuscular control, balance and coordination. Reduced blood flow (vasoconstriction) limits oxygen and substrate delivery and slows clearance of metabolites. After exercise-induced muscle damage, cooling may reduce perceived soreness but does not restore strength, and critically, it can slow glycogen resynthesis and impair the cellular signalling (mTOR pathway, satellite-cell activity) needed for hypertrophy and adaptation. Thus cold helps the symptoms but can hinder the performance and adaptive recovery of muscle.

4Answer

Acute effects of cold on skeletal muscle performance:

  • Reduced maximal force and strength — peak torque and maximal voluntary isometric contraction decrease after cooling.
  • Reduced power and explosive performance — rate of force development and jump height fall; dynamic, rate-dependent actions are more affected than static strength.
  • Slowed contraction and relaxation — longer contraction and half-relaxation times; slower cross-bridge cycling.
  • Reduced muscular endurance / fatigue resistance — cooling impairs the recovery of sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release and of fatigue resistance.
  • Reduced neuromuscular control — slower nerve conduction, altered proprioception, impaired balance and coordination.
  • Increased muscle–tendon stiffness — greater resistance to stretch, so flexibility and rapid movement are affected.

Effects on recovery and adaptation:

  • Reduced delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) — the most consistent benefit; cold reliably lowers perceived pain.
  • Reduced inflammatory markers (partly) — some modalities lower creatine kinase and interleukin-6, though evidence is mixed.
  • Little or no benefit for restoring strength — maximal voluntary contraction recovery is not improved by cooling.
  • Blunted long-term adaptation — repeated post-exercise cold-water immersion attenuates gains in muscle strength and hypertrophy.
  • Improved joint flexibility — the one fairly consistent functional benefit reported in athletes.

Clinical implications: use cold for acute pain, swelling, spasm and DOMS, and for short-term flexibility; avoid cold immediately before strength, power or skill performance, and avoid routine post-strength-training cooling if the goal is hypertrophy or strength adaptation. Re-warm before demanding activity.

5Recent advances

  • Pinero et al. (2024) — Systematic review and meta-analysis in European Journal of Sport Science found post-exercise cold-water immersion modestly attenuates resistance-training-induced muscle hypertrophy, a caution for cryotherapy after strength work.
  • Chen et al. (2024) — Network meta-analysis ranked cryotherapy best for relieving delayed-onset muscle soreness and preserving jump performance, while contrast water therapy was best for creatine kinase recovery.
  • Moore et al. (2022) — Systematic review and meta-analysis in Sports Medicine found cold-water immersion improved recovery of muscular power, soreness and creatine kinase 24 h after high-intensity exercise, but not strength after eccentric work.
  • Dubois & Esculier (2020) — The PEACE and LOVE framework in BJSM questioned routine ice/cryotherapy after soft-tissue injury, arguing it may disrupt optimal healing, and instead promoted active loading and exercise.

6References

  1. Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier.
  2. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. 8th ed. FA Davis.
  3. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. 7th ed. FA Davis.
  4. Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System. 5th ed. Wolters Kluwer.
  5. Throwing cold water on muscle growth: a systematic review and meta-analysis of post-exercise cold-water immersion and hypertrophy. European Journal of Sport Science. 2024.
  6. The effects of hydrotherapy and cryotherapy on recovery from acute post-exercise muscle damage: a network meta-analysis. BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders. 2024.
  7. Isolated and combined effects of cold, heat and hypoxia therapies on muscle recovery following exercise-induced muscle damage. Sports Medicine. 2025.
Question 1 · 10 marks

Q1. Describe the effects of strength training on the neuromuscular system.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit I – Neuromuscular physiology and adaptation to training

★ Memory hook — Train the nerve first, the muscle later — early strength is a learned skill.

1Introduction

Strength training (resistance training) is the systematic use of progressive resistance to improve the ability of the neuromuscular system to generate force. It is far more than a muscle phenomenon — it re-programs the entire pathway from the motor cortex to the sarcomere — and it is the single most frequently prescribed therapeutic tool in musculoskeletal physiotherapy: from post-operative quadriceps re-education and sarcopenia in the Indian elderly to deconditioning in sedentary office workers.

2Physiology

The functional unit is the motor unit — one anterior horn cell, its axon and every muscle fibre it innervates. The nervous system grades force by two mechanisms: recruitment, obeying Henneman's size principle (small, slow, fatigue-resistant units fire first; fast units are added as demand rises), and rate coding (raising discharge frequency). Fibres are typed I (slow oxidative, fatigue-resistant), IIa (fast oxidative-glycolytic) and IIx (fast glycolytic, fatiguable). Whole-muscle output also depends on the length–tension relationship (peak force near mid-range), the force–velocity relationship (concentric force falls as speed rises) and elastic energy stored in tendon.

  • Numbers to quote: a healthy young adult voluntarily activates about 95–98% of a muscle; untrained adults lose roughly 3–5% of muscle mass per decade after the third decade (sarcopenia), and strength falls two to five times faster than mass.
  • Central activation failure after injury or immobilisation lowers this voluntary drive, which is precisely why the earliest training gains are neural.

3Pathophysiology

Read the system without training — the disused or deconditioned state — and the effects of strength training emerge as corrections. Immobilisation and bed rest reduce motor-unit discharge rate, lower oxidative enzyme activity, drive type II fibres toward the fast-fatiguable end and cause disuse atrophy, so strength falls faster than bulk (force–mass dissociation). Pain adds arthrogenic (reflex) inhibition, and the deep stabilisers are inhibited first — a pattern that long outlives the original injury. Sarcopenia compounds this in the Indian elderly, where low protein intake and widespread vitamin D deficiency accelerate loss. Conversely, applied too fast, loading is itself pathological: tendon and bone remodel weeks behind muscle, so maximal loading in week one can tear what a graded programme would have strengthened — the basis of overtraining and tendinopathy.

4Answer

Strength training produces a coordinated cascade of adaptations along the whole motor pathway. Early gains (days to weeks) are dominated by neural factors; later gains (weeks to months) by morphological factors.

1. Neural adaptations (early)

  • Recruitment: more high-threshold (fast) motor units are recruited, and recruitment threshold falls, so force is produced with less effort.
  • Rate coding: discharge rate rises, increasing the rate of force development.
  • Discharge synchronisation: better temporal summation of motor-unit action potentials.
  • Central adaptation: reduced intracortical inhibition (short-interval intracortical inhibition and silent period), increased motor-evoked potential during contraction and a greater V-wave (voluntary drive).
  • Inter-muscular coordination: reduced antagonistic co-contraction and improved agonist synergy.

2. Morphological adaptations (later)

  • Muscle hypertrophy via myofibrillar protein synthesis (mTOR pathway) and satellite-cell activation; increased physiological cross-sectional area.
  • Fibre-type shift: type IIx converts to type IIa; the type I proportion may rise with high-volume work.
  • Increased pennation angle and, with eccentric or lengthened-range work, increased fascicle length.
  • Tendon and connective-tissue stiffening, increased capillarisation and mitochondrial density.
FeatureNeural adaptationMorphological adaptation
TimingDays to weeksWeeks to months
MechanismRecruitment, rate coding, cortical/spinal driveProtein synthesis, hypertrophy, fibre shift
Measured byEMG, V-wave, twitch interpolation, HD-sEMGUltrasound, MRI, biopsy
Reversible?Largely retainedLost with detraining

3. Functional consequences: increased maximal strength and power, improved rate of force development, better joint stability and balance, greater bone mineral density, enhanced tendon load tolerance and reduced injury risk.

Indian-practice context: in a resource-limited OPD, bodyweight and elastic-band progression — or low-load blood-flow-restriction training where heavy loads are not tolerated — delivers most of these neural gains cheaply. A practical prescription is two to three sessions per week, two to four sets of 8–12 repetitions at 60–80% 1RM for hypertrophy, respecting the tendon–muscle timing mismatch.

Conclusion: strength training rebuilds the neuromuscular system in a predictable sequence — nerve first, muscle later, tendon last — and understanding that sequence lets the physiotherapist load safely and measure progress objectively.

5Recent advances

  • Del Vecchio et al. (2019) — high-density surface EMG with motor-unit decomposition showed that just 4 weeks of strength training lowers motor-unit recruitment threshold and raises discharge rate, directly evidencing the early neural (not muscular) basis of strength gains.
  • Siddique et al. (2020) — a systematic review and meta-analysis of transcranial magnetic stimulation studies found resistance training reduces motor-cortical inhibition (short-interval intracortical inhibition and silent period) and increases V-wave amplitude, confirming adaptations above the spinal cord.
  • Loenneke et al. (2012) — a meta-analysis showed low-load (20–30% 1RM) blood-flow-restriction training produces hypertrophy comparable to high-load training, allowing strengthening when heavy loads are not tolerated.
  • Hughes et al. (2017) — a systematic review and meta-analysis in clinical musculoskeletal rehabilitation found low-load blood-flow-restriction training had a moderate effect on strength (Hedges’ g 0.52) and outperformed low-load training alone, establishing it as a practical rehabilitation tool.
  • Ratamess et al. (2009) — the American College of Sports Medicine position stand on progression models in resistance training sets the landmark framework of progressive overload and periodisation that guides exercise prescription in physiotherapy.

6References

  2. Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology. Elsevier.
  3. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques. 7th ed. F.A. Davis.
  4. Folland JP, Williams AG. The adaptations to strength training: morphological and neurological contributions to increased strength. Sports Med. 2007;37(2):145-168.
  5. Siddique U, Rahman S, Frazer AK, et al. Determining the sites of neural adaptations to resistance training: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2020;50(6):1107-1128.
  6. Del Vecchio A, Casolo A, Negro F, et al. The increase in muscle force after 4 weeks of strength training is mediated by adaptations in motor unit recruitment and rate coding. J Physiol. 2019;597(7):1873-1887.
  7. Loenneke JP, Wilson JM, Marin PJ, et al. Low intensity blood flow restriction training: a meta-analysis. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2012;112(5):1849-1859.
Question 2 · 10 marks

Q2. Describe the changes seen in the neuromuscular system following prolonged bed rest due to spinal fracture.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit IV – Effects of immobilisation, disuse and unloading

★ Memory hook — Disuse costs strength faster than it costs muscle — the nervous system switches off first.

1Introduction

Prolonged bed rest after a spinal fracture combines two insults: mechanical unloading of the trunk and limbs, and loss of the neural drive and weight-bearing stimulus that maintain the neuromuscular system. The result is a predictable, staged neuromuscular decline that is measurable within days and that determines how long re-ambulation and rehabilitation will take.

2Physiology

Normally, muscle protein synthesis and breakdown are balanced; motor units are recruited and discharged efficiently; the neuromuscular junction transmits reliably; and spinal reflexes, proprioception and vestibular input keep posture stable. Regular weight-bearing and movement maintain all of these. The antigravity muscles — the multifidus, gluteals and plantarflexors — carry the greatest postural load and therefore depend most on daily loading. Cross-sectional area, motor-unit discharge rate and junction integrity are all activity-dependent, so removing load removes their maintenance signal.

3Pathophysiology

Removing load and movement tips protein balance toward breakdown (disuse atrophy) and withdraws the neural drive that maintains motor-unit behaviour. The neuromuscular junction becomes unstable, proprioceptive input degrades, and cortical and spinal excitability fall. The longer the unloaded period, the more systems are affected, and recovery is slower than the decline. After a spinal fracture, bracing, pain and fear-avoidance further suppress trunk and limb activation, deepening the deconditioning and adding an asymmetric, guarded movement pattern.

4Answer

Prolonged bed rest after a spinal fracture imposes mechanical unloading of the trunk and limbs together with reflex and neural deconditioning. The decline follows a staged pattern across muscle, motor units, the neuromuscular junction and sensorimotor control.

Muscular changes

  • Disuse atrophy of antigravity and paraspinal muscles; multifidus and gluteals are particularly affected. Cross-sectional area falls, and strength is lost faster than mass (force–mass dissociation).
  • Type II fibre atrophy dominates, reducing power and rate of force development; fascicle length and pennation angle decrease.
  • Intramuscular fat and connective tissue increase; resting muscle stiffness rises.

Neural changes

  • Reduced motor-unit discharge rate and altered motor-unit potential size and complexity, reflecting both smaller fibres and impaired neural drive.
  • Reduced voluntary activation (central activation failure) and reduced spinal reflex excitability.
  • Neuromuscular-junction remodelling with impaired transmission, evidenced by raised C-terminal agrin fragment and increased jitter.
  • Altered integration of proprioceptive, visual and vestibular inputs, causing postural instability on re-ambulation.

Functional and secondary changes

  • Loss of balance, reduced gait speed and stride length, delayed transfers and increased fall risk.
  • Contracture (hip flexors, plantarflexors and trunk), bone loss, cardiovascular deconditioning and venous stasis — the last a particular risk in Indian post-operative patients with limited mobility.
  • Fear-avoidance and reduced self-efficacy slow functional recovery even after tissue healing.
DomainMain change after prolonged bed rest
MuscleAtrophy, type II fibre loss, reduced fascicle length
Motor unitsLower discharge rate, smaller/complex potentials
Neuromuscular junctionImpaired transmission, raised agrin fragment
SensorimotorProprioceptive and balance deficits
RehabilitationEarly loading, NMES, task-specific retraining

Recovery follows a rapid-decline, gradual-improvement course, but bilateral asymmetry and sub-baseline strength often persist for many months. In Indian practice, early mobilisation within the brace, graduated weight-bearing and task-specific retraining (sit-to-stand, bed mobility) are the priority once spinal stability is confirmed.

Conclusion: bed rest after spinal fracture dismantles the neuromuscular system from the top down and the outside in — nerve, junction and muscle together — so rehabilitation must reload all three early, not wait for the fracture to unite before starting.

5Recent advances

  • Sarto et al. (2025) — 21 days of bed rest reduced motor-unit discharge rate and altered motor-unit potential size and complexity at low and moderate contraction intensities, impairing neuromuscular transmission.
  • Monti et al. (2025) — 10 days of bed rest in older men produced morphological neuromuscular-junction remodelling (reduced terminal overlap) and raised circulating C-terminal agrin fragment, a marker of junction instability.
  • Hansen et al. (2025) — neuromuscular electrical stimulation during 5 days of bed rest preserved voluntary activation but did not protect peripheral muscle contractility, showing disuse acts both centrally and peripherally and supporting early electrical stimulation in rehabilitation.
  • Kortebein et al. (2007) — a controlled trial in older adults showed 10 days of bed rest caused substantial loss of lower-limb strength and lean mass, providing landmark evidence that even short unloading rapidly deconditions muscle and underpins early-mobilisation practice.
  • Schweickert et al. (2009) — this landmark Lancet randomised trial showed that early physical and occupational therapy during daily sedation interruption in critically ill patients more than doubled return to independent functional status at discharge, changing rehabilitation practice after prolonged bed rest.

6References

Question 3 · 10 marks

Q3. Elaborate the Kinetics & Kinematics of the wrist joint following carpal tunnel syndrome.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit III – Biomechanics of the wrist and hand

★ Memory hook — The carpal tunnel is a crowded room — bend the wrist and the door gets tighter.

1Introduction

Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) results from compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel, a fixed osteoligamentous space at the wrist. Because the tunnel cannot enlarge, both how the wrist moves (kinematics) and how much load and pressure build up inside it (kinetics) become abnormal — and these mechanical changes are the target of conservative physiotherapy.

2Physiology

The carpal tunnel is bounded dorsally and laterally by the carpal bones and palmarly by the transverse carpal ligament, and contains the median nerve and nine flexor tendons with their synovium. Wrist motion occurs at the radiocarpal and midcarpal joints, and the tunnel pressure is lowest in the neutral position. In health the nerve and tendons glide freely, the subsynovial connective tissue (SSCT) is compliant, and intraneural blood flow is preserved. The neutral wrist is the reference posture against which every deviation is read.

  • Wrist flexion–extension range is about 70–80 degrees each way; radial deviation about 20 and ulnar deviation about 30 degrees.
  • The median nerve glides longitudinally several millimetres during wrist and finger motion, and the flexor tendons glide several centimetres.

3Pathophysiology

In CTS the SSCT becomes fibrotic and stiff, tendon glide is impeded, shear strain rises, and carpal tunnel pressure is elevated — especially at the extremes of wrist flexion and extension, and with finger flexion and pinch grip. Raised pressure and shear impair median-nerve gliding and intraneural blood flow, producing the classic sensory and then motor symptoms. Because the change is mechanical, sustained end-range postures, repetitive high-force gripping and vibration all aggravate it, while neutral positioning relieves it.

4Answer

Carpal tunnel syndrome is a compression neuropathy of the median nerve within a confined osteoligamentous tunnel. Its biomechanics are best understood as an interplay of motion (kinematics) and load/pressure (kinetics) inside that tunnel.

Kinematics (motion)

  • Wrist motion: flexion–extension, radial–ulnar deviation and circumduction occur at the radiocarpal and midcarpal joints; the neutral position is the reference in which tunnel pressure is lowest.
  • Median nerve glide: in health the nerve glides longitudinally during wrist and finger motion. In CTS, longitudinal nerve mobility is reduced — used as a clinical biomarker.
  • Tendon excursion: the nine flexor tendons glide within the tunnel. Fibrotic SSCT hinders this glide, so relative motion between tendon and SSCT (shear strain) increases.
  • Nerve shape: the nerve flattens (increased flattening ratio) and its cross-sectional area changes with wrist posture and grip.

Kinetics (forces and pressure)

  • Carpal tunnel pressure (CTP): elevated in CTS and rising steeply at the extremes of wrist flexion and extension, and with finger flexion and pinch grip.
  • Shear and friction forces: relative sliding between tendon and SSCT generates shear stress; flexed wrist posture and faster movement speed increase the shear-strain index.
  • Nerve compression and ischaemia: raised pressure impairs intraneural blood flow, producing the sensory and motor symptoms.
  • Contact and gliding resistance: flexor-tendon gliding resistance rises with carpal tunnel pressure.
VariableNormalIn CTS
Nerve longitudinal glideFreeReduced
SSCT stiffnessLowHigh (fibrotic)
Intracarpal pressureLow near neutralElevated, worst at end-range
Nerve morphologyRoundFlattened, enlarged area

Clinical implication: positioning the wrist near neutral, limiting sustained end-range postures and repetitive high-speed, high-force gripping reduces CTP and shear, while tendon and nerve gliding exercises aim to restore normal kinematics. A neutral-position night orthosis is the mainstay conservative measure; the physiotherapist also screens the cervical spine and proximal nerve bed, since double crush is common in Indian patients with coexisting neck and wrist symptoms.

Conclusion: CTS is a mechanical problem of a fixed tunnel — motion lost and pressure gained — so treatment restores kinematics (glide) and reduces kinetics (pressure and shear) rather than merely treating the symptoms.

5Recent advances

  • Erickson et al. (2026) — the JOSPT clinical practice guideline revision for carpal tunnel syndrome recommends a neutral-position night orthosis, manual therapy directed at the cervical spine and upper limb, and a combined orthotic/stretching programme for non-surgical management.
  • Erickson et al. (2019) — the original APTA clinical practice guideline established the neutral-positioned night wrist orthosis and combined orthotic/stretching programme as first-line physical therapy for mild-to-moderate CTS.
  • Abdolrazaghi et al. (2021) — a randomised controlled trial found tendon- and nerve-gliding exercises improved symptoms and function in mild idiopathic CTS, supporting the kinematic rehabilitation rationale.
  • Page et al. (2012) — a Cochrane review found night splinting gives short-term symptom relief in CTS, the mainstay conservative option for a compressed median nerve.
  • Yao et al. (2019) — radioulnar wrist compression of about 10 N increased carpal-arch height and tunnel space, restoring median-nerve longitudinal mobility and reducing nerve flattening, informing conservative wrist-positioning strategies.

6References

  2. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 7th ed. Elsevier.
  3. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques. 7th ed. F.A. Davis.
  4. Festen-Schrier VJMM, Amadio PC. Carpal tunnel mechanics and its relevance to carpal tunnel syndrome. J Biomech. 2023;146:111399.

Question 4 · 10 marks

Q4. Describe various methods to improve efficiency of movement following soft tissue injury.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit V – Biomechanics of movement efficiency and rehabilitation

★ Memory hook — Get the tissue moving, get it strong, get the brain coordinating it again.

1Introduction

Efficiency of movement means producing the required task with optimal coordination and minimal wasted energy or joint load. After a soft tissue injury, pain, weakness and altered motor control make movement costly and poorly coordinated, so rehabilitation is organised around restoring efficient movement in five layers: mobility, force, control, proprioception and the whole task.

2Physiology

Efficient movement depends on adequate range, normal length–tension and force–velocity relationships, elastic energy storage in tendon, intact proprioception, reciprocal inhibition and well-organised muscle synergies. Together these allow a task to be performed with minimal energy cost and minimal joint load. The economy of normal gait (about 0.15 ml O2 per kg per metre at self-selected speed) is the benchmark of efficiency, and any deviation that raises energy cost or joint reaction force is the target of rehabilitation.

3Pathophysiology

Injury disrupts all of this: pain causes reflex inhibition, scar reduces extensibility, weakness lowers force capacity, and proprioceptive loss disturbs timing. The patient adopts compensatory strategies that raise energy cost and load other joints, so a vicious cycle develops — inefficiency causes overload, overload causes pain, and pain deepens the inhibition. Rehabilitation must therefore address each layer rather than a single impairment, because correcting strength alone while motor control remains poor simply re-loads the inefficient pattern.

4Answer

Efficiency of movement means producing the required task with optimal coordination and minimal wasted energy or joint load. After soft tissue injury, pain, weakness and altered motor control make movement costly and poorly coordinated, so rehabilitation aims to restore efficient movement.

1. Restore mobility and tissue extensibility

  • Progressive stretching and joint mobilisation to recover range of motion and reduce scar stiffness.
  • Soft-tissue mobilisation and scar management to restore glide between tissue layers.

2. Restore force-generating capacity

  • Progressive resistance training, emphasising eccentric loading, which improves strength, tendon stiffness and energy storage.
  • Blood-flow-restriction training to build strength when heavy loads are not yet tolerated.

3. Re-train motor control and coordination

  • Neuromuscular re-education and movement-pattern retraining to remove compensatory strategies.
  • Biofeedback, mirror therapy and external-focus cues to normalise timing and sequencing.
  • Muscle-synergy and dissociation training so the right muscles activate at the right time.

4. Restore proprioception and balance

  • Proprioceptive and balance training progressing from static to dynamic and from eyes-open to eyes-closed.
  • Perturbation and reactive training to rebuild automatic postural responses.

5. Optimise the whole task

  • Gait and functional re-education, then sport- or work-specific drills, to make the recovered movement automatic.
  • Load management and graded return to activity to avoid re-injury.
  • Pain education, orthoses and taping to allow pain-free practice.
GoalKey method
FlexibilityStretch, mobilisation
StrengthEccentric/resistance and BFR training
CoordinationMotor-control and synergy retraining
StabilityBalance and perturbation training
FunctionGait and task-specific retraining

Indian-practice context: efficiency gains are especially valuable where daily life involves squatting, floor-sitting, carrying loads and walking on uneven ground — retraining should therefore be functional and culturally specific, not confined to the treatment couch.

Conclusion: efficiency of movement after soft tissue injury is restored layer by layer — mobility, then force, then control, then proprioception, then the whole task — because each layer supports the next.

5Recent advances

  • van Dyk et al. (2019) — a systematic review and meta-analysis found programmes including the Nordic hamstring exercise cut hamstring injuries by up to 51% across multiple sports, the strongest evidence for eccentric exercise in injury prevention.
  • Petersen et al. (2011) — a cluster-randomised trial in 942 soccer players showed a 10-week progressive eccentric (Nordic) hamstring programme reduced acute hamstring injuries by about 70%, with a number-needed-to-treat of 13.
  • Wulf (2013) — a 15-year review showed that instructing an external focus of attention (on the movement effect rather than the body) improves movement efficiency, automaticity and retention across tasks and skill levels.
  • Gokeler et al. (2015) — external-focus instructions improved jump performance and produced safer knee-joint kinematics after ACL reconstruction compared with internal-focus instructions, showing motor-learning cueing changes movement quality.
  • Hughes et al. (2017) — a meta-analysis confirmed low-load blood-flow-restriction training can be used early in rehabilitation to build strength when high-load exercise is not yet tolerated.

6References

  1. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques. 7th ed. F.A. Davis.
  2. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. 7th ed. F.A. Davis.
  3. Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System. 5th ed. Wolters Kluwer.

Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. Describe the biomechanical changes seen in mobility of lower limbs in people with tendo-Achilles tightness.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit VI – Biomechanics of the ankle-foot complex and gait

★ Memory hook — A tight Achilles pulls the whole chain — the ankle pays, the knee, hip and back borrow.

1Introduction

Tendo-Achilles tightness means reduced ankle dorsiflexion, usually from shortening of the gastrocnemius–soleus complex. Because the foot is the base of support, this loss changes mechanics throughout the lower limb during walking and other weight-bearing tasks — the deficit is distal, but the consequences are proximal.

2Physiology

Normally the ankle needs roughly 10 degrees of dorsiflexion for walking and more for running, squatting and stair descent. The gastrocnemius and soleus control tibial progression over the planted foot and store and release elastic energy at push-off, while the plantar fascia supports the arch through the windlass mechanism. In single-limb support the ankle is the fulcrum of the inverted pendulum of the body, so its range and power set the timing of the whole limb.

3Pathophysiology

When the Achilles–gastrocnemius complex is short, dorsiflexion is limited, so the body borrows motion elsewhere: the foot pronates, the knee and hip change their angles and moments, the pelvis tilts forward and the lumbar spine extends. These compensations raise load and energy cost. A limited bent-knee dorsiflexion has been shown to predict mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy, so the tightness is both a cause and a consequence of overuse pathology.

4Answer

Tendo-Achilles (and gastrocnemius) tightness reduces ankle dorsiflexion range, and because the ankle is the base of the kinetic chain the limitation propagates upward, changing lower-limb mobility during gait and functional tasks.

At the ankle and foot

  • Reduced ankle dorsiflexion, most evident with the knee extended (the Silfverskiold test differentiates gastrocnemius from soleus).
  • Compensatory subtalar pronation and increased midfoot mobility to gain apparent dorsiflexion.
  • Earlier heel rise in stance and reduced terminal-stance push-off power.
  • Increased Achilles tendon and plantar-fascia tension (increased windlass effect).

At the knee

  • Reduced knee extension at midstance and altered knee–ankle joint moments; greater limb stiffness.
  • Increased knee flexion during loading and a tendency to increased knee adduction/valgus in some individuals.

At the hip and pelvis

  • Increased peak hip flexion and reduced peak hip extension; greater anterior pelvic tilt.
  • Altered hip moments (higher extensor, lower flexor moment).

At the trunk and gait as a whole

  • Increased lumbar extension and low-back loading; reduced step and stride length and slower gait.
  • Reduced shock absorption and increased energy cost — a proximal compensation strategy in which the distal deficit is redistributed to knee and hip.
LevelTypical change with Achilles tightness
AnkleReduced dorsiflexion, early heel rise
FootCompensatory pronation
KneeReduced midstance extension, higher moments
Hip/pelvisMore flexion, less extension, anterior tilt
TrunkIncreased lumbar extension

Clinical relevance and Indian context: dorsiflexion limitation predicts Achilles tendinopathy and is linked with overuse injury, so restoring ankle dorsiflexion (stretching, mobilisation, heel-raise work) improves both distal and proximal mechanics. This matters in Indian practice where barefoot walking, floor-sitting and squatting place high dorsiflexion demands on an already tight calf.

Conclusion: a tight tendo-Achilles is never a local problem — it reorganises stance-phase biomechanics up the whole lower limb, so treatment must restore distal range while re-educating proximal movement.

5Recent advances

  • Martin et al. (2018) — the JOSPT clinical practice guideline for midportion Achilles tendinopathy recommends mechanical loading (eccentric or heavy-load slow-speed exercise) to reduce pain and improve function, advising activity within pain tolerance rather than rest.
  • Martin et al. (2024) — the revised AOPT clinical practice guideline elevates progressive tendon-loading exercise, at loads as high as tolerated at least three times weekly, to first-line management of midportion Achilles tendinopathy.
  • Radford et al. (2006) — a systematic review and meta-analysis found static calf-muscle stretching produces a small but significant increase in ankle dorsiflexion, the common physiotherapy rationale for treating calf tightness.
  • Macklin et al. (2015) — a systematic review and meta-analysis showed static stretching, stretching combined with thermotherapy, and heel-raise exercises are effective for increasing ankle dorsiflexion range in people with ankle equinus.
  • Rabin et al. (2014) — a prospective cohort found limited bent-knee ankle dorsiflexion predicted mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy in infantry recruits (suggested cutoff about 22 degrees), supporting dorsiflexion screening in prevention.

6References

  2. Levangie PK, Norkin CC. Joint Structure and Function: A Comprehensive Analysis. 6th ed. F.A. Davis.
  3. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 7th ed. Elsevier.

Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. Describe how soft tissue injuries affect movements.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit II – Tissue mechanics and response to injury

★ Memory hook — Injury hurts, hurts inhibit, inhibition changes how you move — and that change outlasts the pain.

1Introduction

Soft tissue injuries change movement not only because tissue is damaged but because pain, inhibition and scar formation alter how the nervous system controls movement. Understanding this chain — damage, pain, inhibition, compensation — explains why movement dysfunction often outlasts the tissue injury itself.

2Physiology

Healthy movement relies on tissues that glide freely, transmit force and feed proprioceptive information to the nervous system, which then activates muscles in well-timed synergies. Length–tension and force–velocity relationships, elastic energy storage and intact mechanoreceptors (muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs, joint receptors) all contribute to efficient, coordinated movement.

3Pathophysiology

Injury introduces pain and inflammation that inhibit muscle activation, and healing produces scar tissue that is less extensible. Proprioceptive input is degraded and coordination changes, so the patient adopts compensatory movement that is less efficient and loads other structures. Crucially, inhibition may continue after the pain settles, so weakness and altered control persist even when the tissue has healed — the reason movement dysfunction outlives the injury.

4Answer

Soft tissue injuries (muscle, tendon, ligament, fascia, capsule, skin) alter movement through a chain of consequences: tissue damage, pain, inflammation, inhibition and finally maladaptive compensation.

1. Loss of range of motion

  • Oedema, pain and protective spasm limit movement in the acute stage.
  • Later, scar tissue and fibrosis reduce tissue extensibility and can cause adhesions and contracture.

2. Loss of force

  • Pain-driven reflex inhibition (arthrogenic or muscle inhibition) reduces voluntary activation.
  • Structural disruption and, later, atrophy reduce maximal force; eccentric strength and end-range force are affected most.
  • Altered length–tension relationship shifts the angle of peak torque.

3. Altered motor control and timing

  • Changed muscle activation onset and sequencing; loss of normal synergies.
  • Reduced proprioceptive acuity and joint position sense from damaged mechanoreceptors.
  • Increased antagonistic co-contraction as a protective strategy.

4. Compensatory movement and altered kinetics

  • The patient shifts load away from the injured tissue, altering joint angles and moments at neighbouring joints.
  • Increased energy cost and reduced movement efficiency; antalgic or altered gait patterns.
  • Secondary overload of other structures, predisposing to further injury.
EffectMovement consequence
Pain/inhibitionReduced activation, weakness
Scar/fibrosisReduced range and glide
Proprioceptive lossPoor joint position sense, instability
CompensationAltered kinematics and kinetics, higher energy cost

Why the pattern persists

  • Inhibition may continue after the pain settles, so weakness and altered control persist even when the tissue has healed.
  • Repeated compensation can itself cause overload of a second structure, producing a new problem.
  • Fear of re-injury reinforces protective, inefficient movement patterns.

Indian-practice context: these mechanisms matter in daily Indian life, where a sprained ankle from uneven ground, a meniscal tear from squatting or floor-sitting, or a rotator-cuff strain from carrying loads can all leave persistent inhibition and compensation unless movement is deliberately re-trained.

Conclusion: soft tissue injury changes movement through damage, pain, inhibition and compensation — and because the last two outlast the first two, treatment must control pain, restore extensibility, rebuild strength (especially eccentric) and re-train coordination and proprioception so that normal movement returns rather than a compensatory habit.

5Recent advances

  • Di Trani (2024) — neuromechanical studies show hamstring strain injury leaves a sensory disconnect, with reduced proprioceptive acuity and dysregulated stiffness that persist even after return to sport, explaining residual movement dysfunction.
  • Gong et al. (2026) — muscle-synergy analysis after ACL reconstruction identified a missing frontal-plane stabilisation module, showing how injury alters central coordination of movement.
  • Wulf (2013) — a review of attentional focus showed that external-focus instructions improve movement effectiveness and efficiency, giving clinicians a motor-learning tool to retrain movement after injury.
  • Gokeler et al. (2015) — after ACL reconstruction, external-focus cueing produced safer landing kinematics and better jump performance than internal-focus cueing, linking motor-learning strategy to movement quality.
  • van Dyk et al. (2019) — a meta-analysis showed eccentric (Nordic) hamstring exercise roughly halves hamstring injury rates, evidence that targeted loading counteracts the movement and strength deficits that follow muscle injury.

6References

  1. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. 7th ed. F.A. Davis.
  2. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques. 7th ed. F.A. Davis.
  3. Dutton M. Dutton's Orthopaedic Examination, Evaluation and Intervention. McGraw Hill.
  4. Fyfe JJ, Opar DA, Williams MD, Shield AJ. The role of neuromuscular inhibition in hamstring strain injury recurrence. J Electromyogr Kinesiol. 2013;23(3):523-530.
