Describe the changes in male and female body structure and composition.

Full answer →

Compare male and female size, body composition, skeleton and hormones, and give the clinical relevance.

  • What earns marks: start with the two-component model (fat mass + fat-free mass = body mass) before giving numbers · finish with "per kilogram of lean mass the strength gap narrows" — one sentence that shows you think, not just memorise · link the female Q angle to knee problems — it converts this from anatomy to physiotherapy.
  • Size: on average men are taller (roughly 12 to 13 centimetres globally) and heavier, with broader shoulders and narrower hips.
  • Women have a lower shoulder-to-hip ratio, a relatively wider pelvis, shorter limbs relative to trunk, and more subcutaneous fat in the gluteofemoral (pear) pattern versus the male abdominal (apple) pattern.
  • The female centre of gravity sits lower, and the carrying angle of the forearm is about 2 degrees greater in women.
  • Body composition (two-component model): women carry substantially more body fat.
  • Healthy young women average roughly 20 to 30 percent fat against 12 to 20 percent in men.
  • Essential fat is about 12 to 15 percent in women versus about 3 to 5 percent in men — the female body banks fat for reproductive function.
  • Conversely, fat-free mass — muscle, bone, water — is absolutely and relatively greater in men.
  • Men have about 40 percent more muscle mass in the upper body and 25 to 33 percent more in the lower body.
  • Men have larger muscle fibre cross-sectional areas (especially type II), greater bone mineral density and less total body water percentage-wise.
  • So men generate higher absolute strength and power; but when strength is expressed per kilogram of lean mass the gap narrows considerably — the examiner's favourite nuance.
  • Skeletal and pelvic: the female pelvis is adapted for childbearing — wider and shallower, rounder inlet, broader subpubic angle (80 to 85 degrees versus 50 to 60 degrees in men), and greater inclination of the femur with a larger Q angle at the knee.
  • That larger Q angle is the mechanical link to the higher female incidence of patellofemoral pain and anterior cruciate ligament injury.
  • Men have larger, denser, more robust long bones with more prominent muscle attachments; women have lighter bones and, after menopause, accelerated bone loss with higher osteoporosis and fracture risk.
  • Hormonal basis: testosterone drives male muscle mass, haemoglobin concentration and visceral fat deposition.
  • Oestrogen directs female fat to the gluteofemoral depot, supports bone density, and its menopausal withdrawal reverses both the fat distribution and the bone protection.
  • This is why the sex differences in strength are largely, though not completely, hormonal.
  • Functionally, male anatomy favours absolute power; female anatomy favours endurance and flexibility (greater joint laxity).
  • Clinically: female Q angle and ligament laxity inform knee rehabilitation; gluteofemoral fat and the lower centre of gravity alter balance training; female lower lean mass means lower absolute strength benchmarks and slower basal metabolic rates; and postmenopausal bone loss demands early weight-bearing and resistance exercise.
  • Sex-specific normative values — never unisex ones — should be used when interpreting skinfold, body mass index and strength data.

Per kilogram of lean mass the strength gap narrows; larger Q angle links to the female knee.

Sources
  • Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — anthropometry and sex differences.
  • Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — body composition, metabolism and hormonal regulation.
  • ACSM's Resource Manual — body composition assessment and normative values.
  • American Health Foundation roundtable, American Journal of Clinical Nutrition — healthy body fat percentages (primary).
1010 marks

Describe the effects of thermal agents on soft tissue repair.

Full answer →

Match each thermal agent (cold, superficial heat, ultrasound) to the healing phase, and show how it helps repair.

  • What earns marks: structure the whole answer around the three healing phases and you cannot drift · learn the contraindication trio for each agent — viva examiners love asking about heat over acute inflammation and cold over ischaemic skin · use the closer "thermal agents manage the environment; movement directs the repair."
  • Healing phases first: soft tissue repair runs through three overlapping phases.
  • Inflammatory phase: roughly days 0 to 6 — haemostasis, vasodilation, exudation, phagocytosis.
  • Proliferative phase: about weeks 1 to 3 — fibroblast proliferation, collagen synthesis, angiogenesis, granulation.
  • Remodelling phase: months up to a year — collagen reorganises along lines of stress and strength gradually returns to perhaps 80 percent of original.
  • Every thermal agent earns its place by speeding, slowing or reshaping one of these phases.
  • Superficial heat: heating to 40 to 45 degrees Celsius produces vasodilation and increased blood flow, raising oxygen and nutrient delivery and accelerating local metabolic rate — helpful in the late inflammatory and proliferative phases.
  • Heat increases collagen extensibility, so heated tissue stretches further with less risk — the basis of heating before stretch in contracture and scar work.
  • Heat decreases pain (gate control plus later endorphin effects), reduces muscle spasm and decreases joint stiffness; useful in subacute and chronic low back pain, before mobilisation.
  • Applied in the acute inflammatory phase, heat would worsen oedema and pain — the classic caution.
  • Cryotherapy: cold is the acute-phase agent.
  • Cold causes vasoconstriction, limiting bleeding and oedema formation in the first 24 to 48 hours.
  • Cold reduces metabolic rate and secondary hypoxic injury.
  • Cold slows nerve conduction velocity, raising the pain threshold and providing analgesia.
  • Cold reduces muscle spasm by cooling muscle spindles.
  • Used correctly — with protection of the skin and careful timing — cold shortens the painful acute window, and early controlled motion on a numb, less swollen joint begins healing in a better mechanical environment.
  • Cold should not be used over ischaemic tissue or poor circulation, and excessive duration risks nerve injury (watch the ulnar nerve at the elbow and the peroneal nerve at the fibular head).
  • Deep heating — therapeutic ultrasound: typically 1 megahertz for 3 to 5 centimetres depth, it heats collagen-rich tissue selectively — tendon, ligament, joint capsule — from within.
  • Ultrasound increases extensibility for stretching of dense connective tissue and raises blood flow; at non-thermal intensities it promotes cellular activity — proposed stimulation of fibroblast proliferation and protein synthesis — aiding the proliferative and early remodelling phases.
  • Avoid ultrasound over acute inflammation, malignancy, the pregnant uterus, growth plates and cemented implants.
  • Phase-wise timetable: cold in the inflammatory phase, heat and gentle ultrasound in the proliferative phase, and heat plus deep heating before stretching and strengthening in remodelling.
  • Combined with early graded movement — the real driver of organised collagen — thermal agents manage the environment while mechanotransduction directs the repair.
  • Conclusion: thermal agents do not heal tissue themselves; cold buys time in the acute phase by controlling oedema and pain, and heat plus deep energy later increase circulation and extensibility so that movement can do its work — they are assistants to, not substitutes for, therapeutic exercise.

Match the agent to the phase; movement directs the repair — cold first, heat later.

Sources
  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — thermal agents and tissue healing.
  • O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation — physical agents in rehabilitation.
  • Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — local blood flow and temperature regulation.
  • Levangie & Norkin, Joint Structure and Function — connective tissue injury and repair.
110 marks

Explain the components of the skeletal system.

Full answer →

Name the parts of the skeleton, give the bone counts, then finish with a clinical point on bone remodelling.

  • Marks first: start with a definition, then the axial and appendicular bone counts, then classification — that is where the easy marks sit.
  • Marks first: name the five functions — support, protection, movement, haemopoiesis, mineral storage.
  • Marks first: the last 2 marks are clinical — write Wolff's law plus one Indian-context line (vitamin D deficiency, osteoporotic kyphosis).
  • Definition: the skeletal system is the body's living framework — 206 bones in the adult, plus the cartilage, ligaments and joints that bind them.
  • Key idea: bone is living, active tissue that keeps remodelling in response to the loads it feels.
  • Function — support: rigid levers that hold posture.
  • Function — protection: the skull protects the brain, the rib cage protects the heart and lungs.
  • Function — movement: bones act as levers for muscles to pull.
  • Function — haemopoiesis: red marrow makes blood cells.
  • Function — mineral storage: about 99% of body calcium and most phosphorus are stored in bone; yellow marrow stores fat.
  • Axial skeleton: the upright axis of the body — 80 bones in all.
  • Axial — skull: 22 bones, plus 6 ear ossicles and the hyoid.
  • Axial — vertebral column: 26 bones — 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 1 sacrum, 1 coccyx.
  • Axial — thoracic cage: 24 ribs and the sternum.
  • Mechanism: the axial column carries all the body weight downwards and protects the spinal cord, so axial loading injuries (like a fall from a scaffold) hurt it most at the thoracolumbar junction.
  • Appendicular skeleton: the limbs and their girdles — 126 bones in all.
  • Appendicular — pectoral girdles: clavicle and scapula, 4 bones, anchoring the upper limbs of 60 bones.
  • Appendicular — pelvic girdles: 2 hip bones, anchoring the lower limbs of 60 bones.
  • Mechanism: the pectoral girdle gives up stability for mobility (shallow glenoid); the pelvic girdle gives up mobility for stability (deep socket, strong ligaments) to bear weight.
  • Classification by shape: long (femur), short (carpals), flat (ilium), irregular (vertebra), sesamoid (patella).
  • Patella note: the largest sesamoid, sitting in the quadriceps tendon to improve leverage and shield the knee.
  • Classification by structure: compact bone (dense outer shell, resists bending) and cancellous bone (spongy inner mesh with trabeculae along stress lines, resists compression).
  • Development: bones form by intramembranous or endochondral ossification.
  • Associated structures: articular hyaline cartilage covers joint surfaces — low friction, no blood supply, so it heals poorly.
  • Associated structures: fibrocartilage forms menisci and discs and resists compression.
  • Associated structures: ligaments passively limit joint range.
  • Joints: classified as fibrous, cartilaginous or synovial.
  • Synovial joint: capsule, synovial membrane, cartilage and reinforcing ligaments — the unit we treat every day.
  • Clinical: Wolff's law — bone remodels along lines of mechanical stress, thickening where loaded and resorbing where unloaded.
  • Clinical: prolonged immobilisation causes disuse osteoporosis; graduated weight bearing rebuilds bone.
  • Indian context: widespread vitamin D deficiency and postmenopausal osteoporosis make axial bone loss show up as thoracic kyphosis and fragility fractures.
  • Prevention: early weight-bearing exercise and DEXA screening are our tools.

206 bones = axial 80 + appendicular 126

Sources
  • Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — skeletal tissue structure.
  • Lehmkuhl & Smith, Brunnstrom's Clinical Kinesiology — axial and appendicular divisions.
  • Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — bone remodelling and calcium homeostasis.
210 marks

Enumerate the tools for measurement of body fat analysis.

Full answer →

List the tools from cheap field methods to laboratory methods, and end with the Indian cutoffs.

  • Marks first: the question says "enumerate" — the marks are for the complete list, so name seven or more tools with one mechanism line each.
  • Marks first: finish with the Asian-Indian cutoffs — that is your last mark.
  • Why measure: body mass splits into fat mass and fat-free mass (water, protein, bone mineral).
  • Why measure: total body weight alone hides the difference between a muscular athlete and a sarcopenic obese patient — both can share a BMI of 28.
  • Why measure: fat measurement quantifies obesity, tracks rehabilitation progress and stratifies cardiometabolic risk.
  • Structure: arrange your answer as a ladder — from cheap field tools to criterion laboratory methods.
  • Measuring tape: waist circumference and waist–hip ratio estimate central (visceral) fat.
  • Indian cutoffs for waist: 90 cm in men and 80 cm in women — lower than the western 102/88 — because Indians develop diabetes at lower BMI.
  • BMI: weight in kg divided by height in metres squared — an obesity screen.
  • Indian BMI action point: 23 kg/m², not 25.
  • Skinfold caliper: pinches subcutaneous fat at standard sites to estimate total body fat using regression equations.
  • Standard skinfold sites: Durnin–Womersley four sites (biceps, triceps, subscapular, suprailiac) or Jackson–Pollock three or seven sites.
  • BIA (bioelectrical impedance analysis): a painless, portable 50 kHz current is passed through the body.
  • BIA mechanism: fat-free mass is water- and electrolyte-rich and conducts better, while fat resists, so impedance predicts total body water and hence fat-free mass.
  • BIA caution: it assumes constant tissue hydration, so dehydration or post-exercise readings distort it.
  • Hydrostatic (underwater) weighing: the patient is submerged and fully exhales; body density is found from underwater weight by Archimedes' principle.
  • Hydrostatic: the two-compartment Siri equation then converts density to fat percentage — accurate but laborious and unpleasant.
  • Air-displacement plethysmography (Bod Pod): replaces water with air displacement in a sealed chamber — same principle, far better tolerated.
  • DEXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry): today's practical gold standard — splits the body into fat, lean soft tissue and bone mineral at a low radiation dose, with regional (trunk vs limb) output.
  • Isotope dilution (deuterated water): measures total body water.
  • Others to name for the enumeration mark: near-infrared interactance, ultrasound of subcutaneous fat, and, for research, CT and MRI volumetry.
  • If you remember it: potassium-40 whole-body counting.
  • Choosing: match the tool to the purpose — tape and BMI for every clinic screening, calipers for percentage fat on a budget, DEXA when you need regional fat and bone together.
  • Comparison line: field tools are cheap and repeatable but population-specific; criterion methods are accurate but costly and immobile.

Ladder: tape/BMI → skinfold caliper (4 Durnin–Womersley sites) → BIA → tank/Bod Pod → DEXA (criterion)

Sources
  • ACSM's Resource Manual for Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription — body composition assessment.
  • O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation — anthropometry in clinical practice.
  • Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — body fluid compartments underlying BIA.
310 marks

Describe the applications of Newton's second law in the human body.

Full answer →

State the law in both linear and angular form, then give named body examples in each domain.

  • Marks first: write BOTH the linear equation and the angular (torque) equation — giving only force = mass × acceleration caps you at 4 of 10.
  • Marks first: give one named example per domain — gait, throwing, fall injury, and one treatment application.
  • The law: the net force on a body equals its mass times its acceleration (net force = mass × acceleration).
  • Direction: acceleration is in the direction of the net force.
  • Angular form: net torque = moment of inertia × angular acceleration.
  • Mechanism: the law is the bridge between muscle (which creates force) and motion (which is acceleration); almost every therapeutic exercise is an application of it.
  • Walking: the ground reaction force is roughly 1.1 to 1.5 times body weight at loading response.
  • Running: this rises to 2 to 3 times body weight — every step is your mass being decelerated and re-accelerated.
  • Vertical jump: the athlete must generate force well above body weight to leave the ground.
  • Sit-to-stand: quadriceps force must exceed body weight enough to produce upward acceleration of the trunk — which is why elderly patients rock forward first, building acceleration over a longer path.
  • Indian context: head-load carriers and porters walk with shorter, smoother steps — minimising the acceleration component lowers peak force on the spine.
  • Angular: muscles create torque about joints, and a segment's angular acceleration depends on its moment of inertia (how mass is distributed about the axis).
  • Example: a figure skater pulling the arms in reduces moment of inertia and spins faster with unchanged angular momentum.
  • Example: a cricket bowler or badminton-smash player sequences proximal-to-distal so each segment accelerates off the previous one — the kinetic chain.
  • Example: a long lever arm (outstretched arm holding a dumbbell) multiplies the torque demand on the shoulder compared with the elbow-bent position.
  • Injury: injury happens when net force produces an acceleration the tissue cannot survive.
  • Fall on the outstretched hand: the body's momentum is dissipated through the wrist in milliseconds — large deceleration, large force, hence Colles' fracture.
  • Whiplash: the head accelerates forward on a fixed trunk, loading cervical soft tissue beyond its tolerance.
  • Non-contact ACL rupture: a strong quadriceps contraction decelerates an extending tibia rapidly — the same force that protects also tears.
  • Helmets: helmets and crash helmets work by extending the deceleration time, which by the impulse relationship lowers the peak force.
  • Treatment: progressive resistance training works because strength adapts to the force demand.
  • Treatment: in osteoarthritis we teach slow, controlled movement — small accelerations mean small peak joint forces.
  • Treatment: plyometrics deliberately train rate of force development.
  • Treatment: a walker with a heavy patient needs a controlled, gradual rise from a chair rather than a quick push, because the force needed falls when acceleration falls.

F = ma · torque = I × angular acceleration

Sources
  • Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — kinetics chapters.
  • Lehmkuhl & Smith, Brunnstrom's Clinical Kinesiology — torque and levers.
  • Saunders, Inman & Eberhart, JBJS 1953 — determinants of gait and force in locomotion.
410 marks

Write basic concepts of exercise metabolism during core muscle strengthening.

Full answer →

Explain which energy system fuels core holds and how a sustained hold changes muscle metabolism — not a list of exercises.

  • Marks first: the question asks for metabolism, not a list of core exercises — anchor every paragraph to ATP.
  • Marks first: end with one line on avoiding Valsalva — that shows theory turned into safe practice.
  • Core anatomy: the core is a cylinder with two systems.
  • Local stabilisers: transversus abdominis, multifidus, diaphragm and pelvic floor — working at low intensity, continuously, anticipating limb movement.
  • Global movers: rectus abdominis, external and internal obliques, erector spinae — producing force and trunk motion.
  • Mechanism: the deep system gives segmental stiffness (spinal stability at low energetic cost); the superficial system produces torque.
  • Energy systems: three systems supply ATP.
  • Phosphagen system: immediate, about 10 seconds of all-out work.
  • Anaerobic glycolysis: up to roughly 2 minutes, lactate-forming.
  • Aerobic metabolism: unlimited in duration at low intensity, yielding about 36 ATP per glucose molecule in the mitochondria.
  • Core work fits aerobic: core strengthening is classically low-load, high-duration — sustained submaximal isometric holds of 10 to 30 seconds, repeated many times.
  • So it runs predominantly on the aerobic system, with anaerobic glycolysis contributing as hold time and fatigue build up.
  • Inside a hold — recruitment: follows the size principle — small, fatigue-resistant type I motor units fire first; type II units join only as force demand rises.
  • Inside a hold — blood flow: a sustained isometric hold above about 15 to 20% of maximal voluntary contraction compresses intramuscular vessels, occluding local blood flow.
  • Inside a hold — oxygen: oxygen delivery falls while the muscle keeps consuming ATP, so stored phosphocreatine depletes, glycolysis accelerates, and hydrogen ions and inorganic phosphate accumulate.
  • Burning feeling: that accumulation — not lactate itself — is what the student feels as burning, trembling and the breath-holding urge.
  • Recovery: releasing the hold restores reperfusion and clears metabolites.
  • Adaptations — neural first: better anticipatory activation timing of transversus abdominis and multifidus.
  • Adaptations — then peripheral: increased mitochondrial density and capillarisation of the deep stabilisers, higher oxidative enzyme activity, and greater fatigue resistance.
  • Why: stabiliser training emphasises endurance — more repetitions, longer holds, brief rests — rather than heavy loading, which would merely recruit the global movers.
  • Prescription: begin with 5 to 10 second holds with rest, progress to 20 to 30 seconds, because brief rests allow reperfusion and metabolite clearance.
  • Breathing: teach diaphragmatic breathing during holds — a core exercise is also a breathing exercise.
  • Valsalva: breath-holding (a Valsalva manoeuvre) spikes blood pressure, which matters in the many hypertensive Indian patients in our OPDs.
  • Diabetes: in type 2 diabetes, regular aerobic-dominant core and endurance work improves glucose uptake.
  • Clinical sign: if a patient trembles or burns early, that is metabolic fatigue telling you the load — not the willpower — is wrong.

Low-load long holds = aerobic (~36 ATP/glucose) · isometric hold over 15–20% MVC occludes blood flow → metabolite burn · progress 5 s to 30 s holds

Sources
  • Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — energy systems and muscle metabolism.
  • ACSM's Resource Manual for Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription — metabolic responses to resistance training.
  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — core stabilisation progression.
510 marks

Explain mechanics and pathomechanics of the knee joint.

Full answer →

Describe normal knee mechanics first, then the abnormal (pathomechanics) — keep the two halves balanced.

  • Marks first: "mechanics and pathomechanics" means normal first, abnormal second — keep the symmetry.
  • Marks first: the easy anchors are screw-home (with popliteus unlocking), meniscal hoop stress, the Q angle with 3×–7× body weight patellofemoral reaction, and one named malalignment with its compartment consequence.
  • Osteokinematics: the knee moves mainly in the sagittal plane — flexion about 0 to 135 or 150 degrees, extension to 0, with hyperextension up to about 5 to 10 degrees in some.
  • Rotation: rotation is only possible when the knee is unlocked — about 45 degrees total when flexed — and it is coupled.
  • Screw-home mechanism: as the knee approaches terminal extension the tibia rotates laterally about 10 to 15 degrees, locking the knee into a close-packed, energy-efficient standing position.
  • Reference note: the femur rotates medially on the tibia if you describe it from the femur's side — state your reference.
  • Unlocking: popliteus unlocks the knee by laterally rotating the femur.
  • Arthrokinematics: the femoral condyles both roll and glide posteriorly on the tibia during flexion, and the menisci travel with the femur — moving posteriorly in flexion, anteriorly in extension.
  • Menisci structure: fibrocartilage, mostly circumferentially arranged type I collagen, carrying roughly half the joint load.
  • Menisci mechanism: their wedge shape converts vertical compression into hoop stress along their circumference, spreading load onto the tibial rim.
  • Consequence: after total meniscectomy, contact stress in that compartment rises several-fold — which is why degenerative changes follow, and why we now preserve, repair or transplant menisci.
  • Patella: the patella acts as a pulley, increasing the quadriceps extensor moment arm by roughly 30% in early flexion.
  • Q angle: anterior superior iliac spine to patella centre to tibial tuberosity, about 13 to 18 degrees.
  • Q angle effect: it directs the quadriceps pull laterally on the patella, resisted by the vastus medialis obliquus and the medial retinaculum.
  • Patellofemoral reaction force: rises with knee flexion — near 3 times body weight climbing stairs, up to about 7 times body weight in a deep squat.
  • Why it matters: that single number explains anterior knee pain in deep-squatting activities.
  • Pathomechanics — coronal malalignment: genu varum (bow legs, not uncommon in India from nutritional rickets) shifts load medially and accelerates medial compartment osteoarthritis; genu valgum shifts it laterally.
  • Pathomechanics — ligament failure: ACL insufficiency removes the check to anterior tibial translation and rotational laxity — the pivot-shift give-way on pivoting.
  • Pathomechanics — PCL: posterior cruciate injury reverses the translation, worse on downhill steps.
  • Pathomechanics — extensor mechanism: excessive Q angle, weak vastus medialis obliquus or tight lateral retinaculum cause lateral patellar tracking, retropatellar compression and eventual chondromalacia.
  • Pathomechanics — meniscal derangement: a locked bucket-handle tear blocks terminal extension — a knee that will not fully straighten is a mechanical sign, not pain behaviour.
  • Assessment: varus and valgus stress tests for the collateral ligaments; Lachman (most sensitive) and the anterior drawer for the ACL; posterior sag and drawer for the PCL; McMurray for meniscal tears; patellar apprehension for instability.
  • Treatment: strengthen quadriceps (especially vastus medialis) and hamstrings, correct dynamic valgus in landing and squatting, restore full extension after a locked knee.
  • Cultural note: respect the deep squat and cross-legged sitting central to Indian daily life — after meniscal repair or arthroplasty, graded return to floor sitting is a realistic, culturally relevant goal.

Screw-home: tibia laterally rotates in terminal extension; popliteus unlocks · PF reaction ~3× BW stairs, ~7× deep squat · Q angle 13–18°

Sources
  • Levangie & Norkin, Joint Structure and Function — knee arthrokinematics.
  • Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — joint forces and meniscal load sharing.
  • Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment — knee special tests.
610 marks

Explain postural abnormalities seen in the thoracic region.

Full answer →

Give the normal thoracic curve first, then each abnormality with its one discriminating feature, and finish with assessment.

  • Marks first: the structure of this answer is the marks — normal parameters first, then each abnormality with its one discriminating feature, and always end with assessment.
  • Marks first: don't write four kyphosis paragraphs and forget flat back and scoliosis — that loses 2 easy marks.
  • Normal: the thoracic spine is a primary (kyphotic) curve, present from birth, measuring roughly 20 to 45 degrees of forward convexity.
  • Purpose: the curve is a shock absorber — it increases column flexibility and raises load-bearing capacity.
  • Purpose: the attached rib cage converts the thorax into a stiff protective cylinder for heart and lungs.
  • Normal posture test: assessed against a plumb line through the ear, shoulder and greater trochanter.
  • Normal posture: the small compensatory interplay of cervical lordosis, thoracic kyphosis and lumbar lordosis keeps the head over the pelvis at minimal energy cost.
  • Postural (flexible) kyphosis: increased round-back from sustained slouched sitting, weak thoracic extensors and tight anterior structures.
  • Flexible kyphosis test: the deformity corrects on voluntary extension or on lying prone over a bolster.
  • Flexible kyphosis symptoms: fatigue-type ache across the mid-scapular region.
  • Flexible kyphosis treatment: postural re-education, thoracic extension strengthening and ergonomic correction.
  • Indian clinic: in young students, heavy backpacks carried on one shoulder make this a daily OPD presentation.
  • Scheuermann's disease: a structural adolescent kyphosis — at least three adjacent vertebrae each wedged 5 degrees or more, with irregular vertebral end-plates and Schmorl's nodes.
  • Scheuermann's typical patient: classically in the thoracic or thoracolumbar spine of teenage boys.
  • Scheuermann's key test: it is rigid — it does not correct on extension or prone hyperextension over a bolster.
  • Scheuermann's features: pain is variable; cardiopulmonary compromise appears only in severe curves.
  • Diagnostic hinge: differentiating rigid from flexible is the key of the whole answer.
  • Thoracic flat back: loss of the normal kyphosis — a straight, stiff thoracic spine that transmits axial load more like a column, reducing shock absorption.
  • Flat back associations: often a flat scapular posture and posterior ligamentous strain.
  • Thoracic scoliosis: a lateral curvature with vertebral rotation — most often adolescent idiopathic.
  • Scoliosis signs: asymmetric shoulder height, a prominent scapula, and a rib hump on forward bending.
  • Third structural kyphosis: osteoporotic compression fractures in the elderly.
  • Osteoporotic spine: multiple wedge fractures in the postmenopausal Indian woman present as the dowager's hump, with loss of height and a compensatory cervical extension posture to keep the eyes level.
  • Assessment: inspect from the side and behind with the patient standing — plumb line alignment, shoulder and scapular symmetry, depth of the cervical and lumbar curves.
  • Assessment: the prone extension test distinguishes flexible from rigid kyphosis.
  • Assessment: the Adam's forward bend test with a scoliometer quantifies the rib hump.
  • Assessment: radiographic Cobb angle grades scoliosis (10 degrees defines it; bracing is usually considered above 25 to 40 degrees in a growing child).
  • Always: screen the whole spine — a primary lumbar curve produces a compensatory thoracic one.
  • Treatment — flexible kyphosis: postural re-education, thoracic extensor and scapular retractor strengthening, anterior chest stretching, ergonomic advice.
  • Treatment — structural kyphosis: extension exercises over a roll or bolster; for progressive Scheuermann's in the growing child, a brace plus a structured exercise programme.
  • Treatment — scoliosis: observation for small curves, bracing for moderate progressive curves in the immature, physiotherapeutic scoliosis-specific exercises as an adjunct, and surgery for severe ones.
  • Treatment — osteoporotic spine: medical bone protection, safe weight-bearing and balance training to prevent the next fracture.

Normal kyphosis 20–45° · flexible corrects on extension; Scheuermann's is rigid: 3 vertebrae × 5° wedging + Schmorl's nodes · Cobb 10° defines scoliosis

Sources
  • Lehmkuhl & Smith, Brunnstrom's Clinical Kinesiology — spinal curves and posture.
  • McKenzie & May, The Lumbar Spine — postural syndrome and sagittal alignment.
  • Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment — scoliosis and kyphosis examination.
710 marks

Write the biomechanical analysis of gait in ankle instability.

Full answer →

Analyse gait phase by phase — normal trace first, then stance, swing and the measurable kinetics.

  • Marks first: "biomechanical analysis" demands a phase-by-phase structure — normal first, then stance, then swing, then the measurable kinetics.
  • Marks first: spend the first paragraph on the normal trace — deviations only earn marks when the reader can see what they deviate from.
  • Normal — initial contact: the ankle is neutral.
  • Normal — loading response: it plantarflexes, then dorsiflexes progressively to about 10 degrees by terminal stance as the tibia advances over the foot.
  • Normal — push-off: it finally plantarflexes sharply to about 20 degrees at push-off.
  • Normal — subtalar: the subtalar joint pronates at loading response (mobile adapter, shock absorption), then supinates into a rigid lever through push-off.
  • Normal — muscles: the ankle plantarflexors deliver the burst for push-off, and the triceps surae works eccentrically through mid-stance to control tibial advancement.
  • Two halves of instability: chronic instability follows the typical inversion sprain.
  • Mechanical instability: ligament laxity (anterior talofibular ligament, calcaneofibular ligament) on stress testing.
  • Functional ankle instability: recurrent giving way without measurable laxity — a sensorimotor failure.
  • Mechanism: damaged mechanoreceptors in the torn ligaments and capsule feed inaccurate proprioception to the central nervous system, so reflex correction of sudden inversion arrives late.
  • Stance deviations: excessive or prolonged pronation or sudden inversion episodes at loading response.
  • Stance deviations: early heel rise from a shortened, guarded push-off.
  • Stance deviations: reduced single-limb support time on the affected limb.
  • Stance deviations: decreased stride and step length, slower comfortable speed, and a wider base of support.
  • Stance mechanism: the ground reaction force vector passes lateral to the ankle precisely when the peroneals are least ready.
  • Swing deviations: the unstable foot is carried in slight plantarflexion and inversion to protect the lateral structures, so toe clearance suffers.
  • Swing compensations: increased hip and knee flexion (an exaggerated steppage-like strategy), hip hiking of the swing-side pelvis, and sometimes circumduction.
  • Swing result: an energy-costly swing with poor foot placement accuracy at the next initial contact — and the cycle of self-distrust continues.
  • Kinetics: reduced peak plantarflexion moment and power burst at push-off (a weak push).
  • Kinetics: altered vertical ground reaction force shape with a flattened second peak, and increased ankle inversion moments in some patients.
  • EMG: delayed peroneal reaction time, reduced peroneus longus strength, and co-contraction of the pretibial group with the triceps surae to splint the joint.
  • Clinic test: the Star Excursion Balance Test anterior reach — an anterior reach deficit greater than about 4 cm between limbs predicts future sprain.
  • Clinic test: single-leg hop tests also objectify it.
  • Rehabilitation: because the mechanism is sensorimotor, rehabilitation is more than strengthening — proprioceptive and balance training (single-leg stance progressions, wobble board, eyes closed).
  • Rehabilitation: peroneal strength and reaction training, perturbation and hopping/landing control, agility before return to sport, and taping or bracing during the vulnerable early weeks.
  • Indian setting: barefoot balance work on uneven surfaces is practical where much daily life occurs unshod — a culturally native form of proprioceptive training.

Mechanical = laxity (ATFL); functional = give-way without laxity · SEBT anterior reach deficit over 4 cm predicts sprain

Sources
  • Levangie & Norkin, Joint Structure and Function — ankle complex mechanics.
  • Saunders, Inman & Eberhart, JBJS 1953 — determinants of gait framework.
  • Donatelli & Wooden, Orthopaedic Physical Therapy — ankle rehabilitation.
810 marks

Explain the theories and models of pain.

Full answer →

Show the progression of pain theories, name each with date/journal, and give one clinical application each.

  • Marks first: name, date, journal — Melzack and Wall, Science, 1965; Melzack, Pain, 1999.
  • Marks first: give one clinical application per theory — theories with no application read like history.
  • Why theories exist: pain is the commonest reason a patient reaches a physiotherapist, yet it correlates poorly with tissue damage.
  • Example: phantom limb pain hurts in a limb that no longer exists; imaging-identical disc bulges incapacitate one patient and not another.
  • Structure: show the progression — each model fixes the failure of the one before it, not four unrelated paragraphs.
  • Specificity theory (Descartes' pathway concept, refined by von Frey): pain is a dedicated modality with its own receptors, dedicated A-delta and C afferents, and a specific line to a pain centre in the brain.
  • Specificity — strong point: it predicted nociceptors, which were later found.
  • Specificity — weak point: it cannot explain why gentle touch relieves pain or why pain persists after healing.
  • Pattern (intensity) theory (Goldscheider): there are no dedicated pain fibres; pain results from intense stimulation producing a specific spatio-temporal pattern of firing.
  • Pattern — strong point: it recognised central summation.
  • Pattern — weak point: intense stimuli do not always cause pain.
  • Study tip: keep each theory to a strong-point, weak-point pair — that is the analytical style that scores.
  • Gate control theory (Melzack and Wall, published in Science in 1965): modulation sits in the dorsal horn.
  • Gate mechanism: large-diameter A-beta (touch) fibres and small-diameter A-delta and C (nociceptive) fibres both end on transmission cells in the substantia gelatinosa.
  • Gate mechanism: large-fibre activity closes the gate (inhibits transmission); small-fibre activity opens it.
  • Gate control: descending fibres from the brain can set the gate too — the first theory to put the brain inside the pain loop.
  • Gate explains: why rubbing an injury helps, why TENS at high frequency relieves pain, and why distraction and mood matter.
  • Gate limitation: it stops at the spinal cord, so it still cannot fully explain chronic pain or phantom phenomena.
  • Neuromatrix theory (Melzack, Pain, 1999): pain is the output of a widely distributed neural network — the body-self neuromatrix.
  • Neuromatrix inputs: it integrates somatosensory, limbic, thalamic and cortical inputs with genetic and experiential determinants.
  • Neuromatrix idea: pain is a multidimensional percept produced by the brain's "neurosignature" of the body, not a direct readout of tissue signals.
  • Neuromatrix explains: phantom limb pain (the neurosignature persists after the input is gone), chronic pain without ongoing damage, and why stress, sleep and beliefs modulate pain.
  • Neuromatrix role: the conceptual foundation of modern pain neuroscience education.
  • Biopsychosocial model: the current working model treats pain as the product of interacting biological (tissue state, sensitisation), psychological (fear, catastrophising, expectations) and social (family, work, culture) factors.
  • Translation: TENS, massage, thermal agents and movement all act by closing the gate with large-fibre input.
  • Translation: graded exposure and pain education target fear-avoidance; exercise remodels the neurosignature.
  • Indian clinic: pain beliefs shaped by family opinion and the cultural meaning of rest versus activity are genuinely part of the biology you are treating — address them or your exercise programme fails.

Specificity → pattern → gate control (Melzack & Wall, Science 1965) → neuromatrix (Melzack, Pain 1999) → biopsychosocial · TENS and rubbing = closing the gate

Sources
  • Melzack R, Wall PD. Pain mechanisms: a new theory. Science 1965;150:971–979.
  • Melzack R. From the gate to the neuromatrix. Pain 1999;Suppl 6:S121–S126.
  • Butler DS, Jones MA. Mobilisation of the Nervous System — pain physiology and clinical translation.
  • O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation — pain management principles.
910 marks

Describe soft tissue repair and healing in meniscal injury.

Full answer →

Link meniscal structure and blood supply to the three healing phases and explain why the meniscus heals poorly.

  • Marks first: this is two answers braided into one — soft tissue healing phases AND meniscal specifics.
  • Marks first: the braiding sentence is "the blood supply decides whether the general healing script even begins."
  • Structure: the menisci are C-shaped fibrocartilaginous wedges built of densely packed type I collagen, predominantly circumferential with a few radial tie fibres.
  • Structure mechanism: that architecture converts compressive load into hoop tension.
  • Cells: their cells are fibrochondrocytes — hybrids that behave part-fibroblast, part-chondrocyte — sitting sparse and avascular in the deep matrix.
  • Blood supply: the peripheral third receives blood from the genicular arterial network; the inner two-thirds are nourished only by diffusion from synovial fluid.
  • Surgical zones: red-red (outer, vascular), red-white (middle, transitional), and white-white (inner, avascular).
  • Key idea: every prediction about healing follows from this one anatomical fact — build the answer on it.
  • Inflammatory (bleeding) phase, roughly days 0 to 7: only a red-zone tear forms a fibrin clot scaffold, releasing platelet-derived growth factor and attracting inflammatory cells.
  • Critical point: a white-zone tear does not even bleed — the healing cascade never starts.
  • Proliferative (fibroblastic) phase, roughly 2 to 6 weeks: fibrochondrocytes and invading vascular buds migrate into the clot and lay down disorganised type I and III collagen.
  • Proliferative: a fibrovascular scar bridges the tear, weakest at about 1 to 2 weeks.
  • Remodelling phase, months: scar collagen reorients to withstand shear and compression, cellularity falls, and the tissue approaches — but never equals — native organisation and strength.
  • Poor healing reason 1: the avascular inner two-thirds cannot mount the inflammatory first phase without a clot.
  • Poor healing reason 2: fibrochondrocyte density is low and their proliferative capacity is modest.
  • Poor healing reason 3: constant loading and motion in synovial fluid dilutes and washes out the fibrin scaffold and growth factors.
  • Poor healing reason 4: the complex load environment — hoop tension plus shear — repeatedly tests the immature scar.
  • Summary: this is why a peripheral vertical tear can heal while a complex degenerative white-zone tear cannot.
  • Factors — zone: red-red heals, white-white does not.
  • Factors — tear pattern: peripheral vertical-longitudinal heals best; complex, horizontal and degenerative tears poorly.
  • Factors — rim width: tears within about 3 mm of the synovial attachment heal best.
  • Factors — patient: age and vascularity.
  • Factors — knee stability: an unstable ACL-deficient knee repeatedly displaces the meniscus and impairs healing.
  • Factors — rehabilitation quality: protected weight bearing and controlled motion stimulate; premature deep flexion under load disrupts.
  • Treatment: repairable red-zone tears in the young (peripheral vertical tears) are sutured (inside-out, all-inside techniques) because they can heal.
  • Treatment: irreparable white-zone degenerative tears in the older patient undergo partial meniscectomy, sacrificing the least tissue possible.
  • Rehabilitation: a phased progression of range and weight bearing over about 4 to 6 weeks, avoiding deep loaded flexion in the early scar phase.
  • Rehabilitation: then a graded return to the squats and cross-legged sitting of daily Indian life, and back to sport with landing-control training.

Zones: red-red (vascular, heals) / red-white / white-white (avascular, no clot, no healing) · inflammation 0–7 d → proliferation 2–6 wk (weakest scar) → remodelling months

Sources
  • Levangie & Norkin, Joint Structure and Function — meniscal structure and load sharing.
  • Donatelli & Wooden, Orthopaedic Physical Therapy — meniscal injury management.
  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — soft tissue healing and rehabilitation timelines.
  • Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment — meniscal testing and surgical decision context.
1010 marks

Describe mechanics and pathomechanics of the hip joint.

Full answer →

Give the hip's structure and lever mechanics with the key numbers, then the pathomechanics and gait changes.

  • Marks first: the lever arm diagram is the highest-yielding single drawing of this paper.
  • Marks first: numbers that must appear — 3× body weight joint reaction in single-leg stance, the roughly 2:1 moment arm ratio, and cane in the opposite hand.
  • Marks first: then one line each on OA, Trendelenburg, impingement and childhood hip — breadth plus one mechanism drawn deep.
  • Structure: the hip is a synovial ball-and-socket joint — the femoral head (about two-thirds of a sphere) seated in the deep acetabulum.
  • Structure: the socket is deepened by the fibrocartilaginous labrum and secured by the iliofemoral, pubofemoral and ischiofemoral ligaments — the strongest ligament in the body among them.
  • Ranges: flexion about 0 to 120 degrees (more with knee flexion), extension 0 to 10 or 15 degrees, abduction 0 to 45, adduction 0 to 30, and medial and lateral rotation about 0 to 45 each.
  • Mechanism: the socket trades the shoulder's mobility for near-dislocation-proof stability, because this joint must transmit the largest loads in the body.
  • Load mechanics: in single-leg stance, body weight acts through a vertical line roughly two-thirds of the way between the hip and the midline, at a moment arm about twice that of the hip abductors (gluteus medius and minimus).
  • Equilibrium: abductor force must therefore be roughly two times body weight.
  • Joint reaction: the femoral head compresses under a joint reaction force of about two to three times body weight in single-leg stance.
  • Higher loads: rising toward about four times body weight in fast walking or stairs (Levangie & Norkin, 6th ed.).
  • Practical: add 10 kg of shopping and the arithmetic punishes the head.
  • Master key: this lever model is the key to the pathomechanics below.
  • Pathomechanics — osteoarthritis: cartilage loss and superolateral femoral head migration shorten the abductor moment arm, raise the required abductor force, and increase joint stress.
  • OA pattern: pain, effusion and capsular contracture produce the classic pattern of flexion, abduction and lateral rotation deformity, with apparent (not true) shortening.
  • Pathomechanics — abductor failure: weakness of gluteus medius or superior gluteal nerve palsy produces a positive Trendelenburg sign — the pelvis drops on the unsupported side.
  • Pathomechanics — femoroacetabular impingement: a cam deformity (aspherical head) or pincer over-coverage jams the head against the labrum in deep flexion and adduction.
  • FAI sign: the sitting-induced anterior groin pain of the younger patient.
  • Pathomechanics — childhood hip: developmental dysplasia (shallow socket, unstable head) and Perthes disease (avascular necrosis of the capital epiphysis) deform the growing head and cause secondary osteoarthritis decades later.
  • Childhood screening: Barlow and Ortolani manoeuvres at birth matter in Indian screening programmes.
  • Gait — Trendelenburg: in gluteus medius weakness, an uncompensated Trendelenburg gait shows lateral trunk lurch toward the weak side during its stance phase.
  • Gait compensation: most patients lean over the stance hip to shorten the body-weight moment arm and reduce the required abductor force.
  • Gait — flexion contracture: produces an anterior pelvic tilt and compensatory lumbar hyperlordosis in stance, and a shorter step on the affected side.
  • Gait — hip OA: antalgic shortening of stance phase, and a coxalgic limp with the trunk lurching toward the painful side to reduce joint reaction force.
  • Treatment: strengthen gluteus medius (side-lying abduction, supported single-leg stance), stretch the hip flexors and adductors that contracture shortens.
  • Treatment: teach trunk-lean economy when weakness is fixed.
  • Cane biomechanics: a cane held in the hand opposite the affected hip lengthens the counter-lever of the body-weight moment arm and reduces the joint reaction force by up to half or so.
  • Post-arthroplasty: the same lever logic underlies gait re-education and abductor protection.
  • Cultural goal: in floor-sitting Indian habits, a graded return to cross-legged posture after arthroplasty is a culturally real functional goal.

Single-leg stance: abductors ~2× BW, joint reaction ~3× BW, body-weight arm ≈ 2× abductor arm · cane in OPPOSITE hand

Sources
  • Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — hip joint forces and lever arms.
  • Lehmkuhl & Smith, Brunnstrom's Clinical Kinesiology — hip mechanics and Trendelenburg analysis.
  • Levangie & Norkin, Joint Structure and Function — hip joint structure and pathomechanics.
  • Hislop, Avers & Brown, Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing — gluteus medius testing.
110 marks

Explain the structure and functions of the neuro-muscular system.

Full answer →

Describe how the nervous system and muscle are wired together, then link every structure to a function and to physiotherapy practice.

  • What earns marks: put structure first, then map each structure onto a function. Do not write pages on fibre chemistry and forget the loop back to movement · draw the labelled motor-unit diagram before you write. Make sure the phrases "size principle", "alpha–gamma co-activation" and "final common pathway" each appear once · end with clinical application — muscle testing, the Ashworth scale and resistance training.
  • Big idea: the neuro-muscular system is the nervous system joined to skeletal muscle. Sherrington called it the "final common pathway" — the one route through which every intention to move becomes force on bone.
  • Structural unit = the motor unit: one anterior horn cell, its axon, and every muscle fibre that axon supplies.
  • Motor unit size varies: fine-control muscles such as the extraocular muscles have a few fibres per unit; postural giants such as gastrocnemius may have over a thousand. The CNS trades precision for power by choosing unit size.
  • Muscle fibre types: type I (slow, oxidative, fatigue-resistant, postural), type IIa (fast oxidative-glycolytic) and type IIx (fast glycolytic, fatiguable).
  • Sensory receptors: the muscle spindle senses length and the rate of length change (intrafusal fibres; Ia and II afferents).
  • The Golgi tendon organ senses tension (Ib afferent).
  • Joint, skin and vestibular receptors feed the same loop.
  • The wiring is a closed loop: command travels down, information about length and tension travels back.
  • Function — force production and grading: force is raised by recruitment obeying Henneman's size principle (small units first) and by rate coding of discharge.
  • Function — posture and tone: alpha–gamma co-activation keeps the spindle sensitive while the muscle shortens, so the antigravity muscles hold a steady background tone.
  • Function — protection: the myotatic stretch reflex, the withdrawal (flexor) reflex and the crossed extensor reflex guard the limb within milliseconds.
  • Function — proprioception: the same afferents give the cortex its map of joint position — the raw material for movement re-education.
  • Clinical use: manual muscle testing interrogates the motor output; the Ashworth scale interrogates tone.
  • Progressive resistance training works because recruitment and rate coding respond to load within weeks, while fibre transformation takes months.
  • Lower motor neuron lesions waste the muscle and abolish reflexes; upper motor neuron lesions do the opposite — knowing the wiring tells them apart at the bedside.
  • One-line summary: the neuro-muscular system converts electrical intention into graded mechanical force and reports back; every assessment and treatment we give is read or written through that loop.

One command wire — many force generators.

Sources
  • Guyton and Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — motor unit and reflex physiology.
  • Lehmkuhl and Smith, Brunnstrom's Clinical Kinesiology — muscle structure and fibre types.
  • Hislop, Montgomery, Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing — clinical application of motor output.
210 marks

How would you analyze, using the various anthropometry methods, to differentiate normal and abnormal curvature of the spine?

Full answer →

Show, step by step, how you measure spinal curvature with anthropometric tools and where you draw the line between normal and abnormal.

  • What earns marks: the question says "how would you analyse", so phrase everything as what YOU do next, in order: observe, plumb, flexicurve, scoliometer, refer. Method marks live in the sequence · quote the scoliometer threshold of about 5–7 degrees and the Cobb criterion of 10 degrees — this shows you know where field anthropology ends and radiology begins · state the reference values — examiners award the definition marks for numbers, not for adjectives.
  • Anchor the answer in "normal" first. In the coronal plane the spine is straight; a plumb line dropped from the external auditory meatus should pass through the shoulder, the greater trochanter, just behind the knee and the lateral malleolus.
  • Sagittal reference values: cervical lordosis about 20–40 degrees, thoracic kyphosis about 20–45 degrees and lumbar lordosis about 40–60 degrees.
  • Method 1 — observation with a plumb line and a marked grid: check shoulder level, scapular and iliac crest levels, skin folds at the waist and head tilt. Free, repeatable, and the backbone of any school-screening camp in India.
  • Method 2 — the flexible ruler (flexicurve): mould it along the spinous processes from C7 to the sacrum, trace it on paper, and measure the kyphosis angle or the lateral deviation index on the tracing.
  • Method 3 — the inclinometer and scoliometer: with the patient in Adam's forward-bend position, read the angle of trunk rotation at the apex. An angle of about 5–7 degrees or more is the accepted referral threshold.
  • Method 4 — goniometric inclinometry in standing for sagittal curves: two inclinometers over T12–L1 and the sacrum give a lumbar lordosis angle.
  • Method 5 — stature anthropometry: standing height, sitting height and arm span, which expose growth-related changes and track progression in adolescent deformity. A rib hump can be quantified with callipers or a level and ruler in centimetres.
  • Coronal plane interpretation: any measurable lateral curvature is suspicious. Scoliosis as a diagnosis is reserved radiologically for a Cobb angle of 10 degrees or more.
  • So the anthropometric job is to find the asymmetry that predicts it: trunk rotation above about 5–7 degrees, a positive plumb deviation, or unequal shoulder or iliac crest levels by more than about 1 cm.
  • Sagittal plane interpretation: kyphosis beyond about 45–50 degrees, a lumbar lordosis outside roughly 40–60 degrees, or a C7 plumb line falling well ahead of the sacrum signals abnormal curvature — for example postural kyphosis versus Scheuermann or a flat-back.
  • In a growing child, progressive loss of sitting-height gain flags a worsening curve.
  • Clinical algorithm: observe with plumb line and levels; if asymmetry is found, flexicurve and scoliometer quantify it.
  • If the scoliometer reads above the threshold or the curve progresses on serial measurement, refer for radiographic Cobb measurement, which remains the gold standard.
  • Conclusion: anthropometry gives you a cheap, radiation-free way to screen, document and follow up.

Observe, plumb, flexicurve, scoliometer, refer — method marks live in the sequence.

Sources
  • Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment — posture and spinal alignment assessment.
  • Nordin and Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — spinal curvatures and loads.
  • Levangie and Norkin, Joint Structure and Function — vertebral column mechanics.
310 marks

Explain the concepts of energetics in chronic osteoarthritis of knee.

Full answer →

Define work, energy, efficiency and oxygen cost first, then apply them to why a chronic knee OA patient spends more energy to walk.

  • What earns marks: the phrase "concepts of energetics" signals that definitions of work, efficiency and oxygen cost must come before the disease talk. Write the four definitions, then apply them to OA in the same order · name the deconditioning spiral — it earns the analysis mark · state it as one chain — OA raises the cost of walking, and our job is to lower the cost, raise the capacity, or both.
  • Movement costs fuel. Mechanical work is the product of force moving through displacement.
  • Mechanical work divides into internal work (moving limb segments against each other) and external work (moving the body against gravity and ground).
  • Metabolic energy is the fuel bill, paid in oxygen — roughly five kilocalories per litre of oxygen consumed.
  • Efficiency links the two: mechanical work divided by metabolic cost. For level walking the body manages only about 25–30 percent.
  • The oxygen cost of walking is expressed per kilogram per metre walked.
  • What OA does — pain and effusion drive co-contraction: simultaneous quadriceps and hamstring activation that splints the joint.
  • Protection has a price: a stiff, co-contracted knee does not swing freely, so internal work rises.
  • Cartilage loss and varus alignment shift the ground reaction force medially, enlarging the knee adduction moment — so the same step demands more muscle force at the knee.
  • The patient responds with a slower, shorter-stride, more flexed-knee gait — comfortable per second, but costlier per metre.
  • The energetic optimum for walking is near the self-selected speed that OA now forces them to abandon.
  • Quadriceps weakness — partly arthrogenic inhibition — means each newton of support costs a larger fraction of the available muscle, so higher relative intensity for the same stroll to the bus stop.
  • The deconditioning spiral: walking feels expensive, so the patient walks less; walking less lowers cardiovascular fitness; lower fitness makes the same walk a higher percentage of maximum capacity — breathlessness, fatigue, then still less activity.
  • Measuring energetics: indirect calorimetry from expired gases gives oxygen cost per metre.
  • When a metabolic cart is unavailable — the usual Indian OPD reality — the physiological cost index approximates it: heart rate while walking minus resting heart rate, divided by walking speed.
  • Always document speed too, because cost per metre without speed is half a story.
  • Treatment read energetically: aerobic and strengthening training raise the efficiency of the engine; weight loss shrinks the load — every kilogram of body weight transmits roughly three to four kilograms of force through the knee during stairs and squats.
  • A cane in the opposite hand unloads the medial compartment and trims the adduction moment; pacing and energy conservation spread the budget across the day.

OA raises the cost of walking — lower the cost, raise the capacity, or both.

Sources
  • Nordin and Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — work, energy and efficiency of gait.
  • ACSM's Resource Manual for Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription — oxygen cost and training implications.
  • O'Sullivan and Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation — functional training and energy conservation in chronic disease.
410 marks

Discuss the changes in gait in older adults.

Full answer →

Set the baseline mature gait, then list the spatiotemporal and joint-level changes in older adults and separate normal ageing from pathology.

  • What earns marks: quote double support 18 to 26 percent and speed 1.3 to 1.0 metres per second — the numbers that separate a pass from a distinction · say "shorter stride, not slower steps" — most candidates write the reverse · give the baseline mature gait first, then measure every change against it.
  • Baseline mature gait is free, reciprocal and economical: self-selected speed near 1.3 metres per second in healthy younger adults.
  • Stride length is about one and a half times leg length; stance phase is 60 percent and swing 40 percent of the cycle; smooth arm swing is opposite the legs.
  • Saunders' classic determinants of gait — pelvic rotation, pelvic tilt, knee flexion in stance, foot and ankle mechanisms, and lateral pelvic displacement — flatten the path of the centre of gravity and minimise the metabolic cost of transport.
  • Spatiotemporal change — older adults walk slower, nearer 1.0 metre per second by the seventies.
  • The slowing is driven mainly by shorter stride length rather than slower steps; cadence changes little or even rises slightly.
  • Stance phase lengthens, and double support time grows from about 18 percent of the cycle in youth toward 26 percent and beyond.
  • Both feet on the ground longer means the body spends less time balancing on one leg — the biomechanical signature of trading speed for safety.
  • Base of support widens slightly, and step-to-step variability increases — a better falls predictor than slow speed alone.
  • Joint-level change: the consistent finding is a reduced ankle plantarflexor burst at push-off (the A2 power peak), with compensation at the hip — a hip strategy gait.
  • Ankle range falls, knee flexion in stance may be slightly reduced, and arm swing diminishes.
  • The head-and-trunk path oscillates a little more, so the determinants that once smoothed the ride work less efficiently and oxygen cost per metre rises.
  • Fear of falling adds co-contraction of the shank muscles — the older person carries a stiffer, more guarded leg.
  • Sarcopenia of the plantarflexors removes the engine.
  • Normal ageing versus pathology: slowing alone is an adaptation, not a disease.
  • What should alarm the clinician: a speed below about 0.8 metres per second (the rough threshold for independent community ambulation), marked variability, a Parkinsonian or hemiplegic pattern, or a new widening of the base.
  • Assessment combines observation, the timed up-and-go, and 10-metre walk timing.
  • Treatment is strength and balance training, supervised challenge to the balance systems, and management of vision, vestibular function and foot-wear.
  • Message for the exam: the older gait is a negotiated compromise between mobility and stability, and our job is to keep it from tipping into falls.

More time on two feet = trading speed for safety.

Sources
  • Saunders, Inman and Eberhart, JBJS 1953 — the major determinants of gait.
  • Nordin and Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — gait kinetics and kinematics.
  • O'Sullivan and Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation — gait assessment and balance training in older adults.
510 marks

Explain the adaptation of different systems during an exercise program.

Full answer →

Go system by system — cardiovascular, respiratory, neuromuscular, metabolic, tissue — giving a time-scale or number for each, and separate acute response from chronic adaptation.

  • What earns marks: organise strictly system by system — cardiovascular, respiratory, neuromuscular, metabolic, tissue — with one number or time-scale in each. General essays about "exercise is good" score nothing · say overload, specificity and reversibility in your first paragraph · distinguish acute responses (one bout) from chronic adaptations (a program).
  • Frame it: every single session produces acute responses — heart rate climbs, ventilation rises, muscle burns substrate — which subside within hours.
  • A program is repeated, progressive doses; chronic adaptation is the body rebuilding itself between sessions in the direction of the imposed demand.
  • The overload principle decides the direction, specificity decides the system, and reversibility decides the fate of anyone who stops.
  • Cardiovascular: resting heart rate falls because stroke volume rises — a larger, more compliant ventricle filling better through an expanded plasma volume.
  • Submaximal heart rate for a given workload drops, and cardiac output at max rises.
  • Capillary density and mitochondrial density in trained muscle increase, and endothelial function improves with a modest fall in resting blood pressure.
  • Clinical link: the post-MI or post-arthroplasty patient who could barely walk the ward corridor ends up comfortably walking to the market within months.
  • Respiratory: the lungs change little structurally in healthy adults, but ventilation becomes more efficient — lower breathing frequency at a given workload, better coordination, and improved lactate buffering through adaptations in muscle.
  • Neuromuscular: this is the early superstar. In the first two to four weeks, strength rises out of proportion to any visible muscle growth because the nervous system learns — better recruitment, higher discharge rates, less antagonist co-activation, refined motor unit synchrony.
  • Clinical link: the frail elderly patient on the ward doubles her sit-to-stand score in week two, long before hypertrophy could account for it.
  • Metabolic: insulin sensitivity improves within days of a single session's effect on GLUT4 translocation and persists with training; oxidative enzymes multiply; fat oxidation becomes a larger share of the fuel mix.
  • Bone follows Wolff's law — it thickens where the load is imposed, which is why weight-bearing and resistance exercise, not just tablets, are part of osteoporosis management.
  • Tendon and ligament gain tensile strength slowly, weeks behind muscle — a timing mismatch the prescribing therapist must respect.
  • Sleep quality, mood and pain thresholds also shift — worth one line, because our musculoskeletal patients notice these first.
  • Conclusion as a prescription: adaptation is predictable and time-sequenced — neural in the first month, cardiovascular and metabolic across the first two months, structural tissue over months to a year.
  • A program that ignores this sequence — maximal loads to a tendon in week one — invites injury; a program that respects it turns a deconditioned MSK patient into a functioning one.

Neural first, cardiovascular and metabolic next, structural last.

Sources
  • ACSM's Resource Manual for Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription — systemic adaptations to training.
  • Guyton and Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — cardiovascular and metabolic responses.
  • Kisner and Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — progression and tissue-healing timelines.
610 marks

Explain the mechanics and pathomechanics of non-specific neck pain.

Full answer →

Define "non-specific" first, then show the load-versus-capacity mechanics of the forward head and the chain of creep and motor-control change that produces the pain.

  • What earns marks: "non-specific" is the trap word. Define the term — no fracture, no tumour, no radiculopathy. Do NOT list disc prolapses and radiculopathy; those are specific · show the load-versus-capacity mechanics — the forward-head moment arm story · name the pathomechanical chain: creep, sustained postures, motor control change.
  • Normal mechanics: the cervical spine is a lordotic mobile column carrying a head of about four and a half to five kilograms.
  • The lordosis is not decoration: it places the compressive load closer to the axes of the posterior muscles and the uncovertebral joints, distributing stress.
  • Functionally it is two regions — the craniovertebral complex for nodding and rotation, and the mid and lower cervical segments for combined movements.
  • Coupling rule: side-flexion in the mid and lower cervical spine is classically coupled with rotation to the same side. This rule is broken only at the craniovertebral joints, where rotation is coupled with slight opposite side-flexion.
  • Motion segments each contribute roughly 13–23 degrees of flexion-extension on in-vivo studies, with the mid-cervical levels (C4–C5/C5–C6) among the most mobile — which is why degeneration shows there first.
  • Loading: in neutral, the head's centre of mass sits almost over the cervical column and the extensor moment arm is small.
  • Every centimetre the head drifts forward lengthens the horizontal moment arm of that five-kilogram head, so the extensor force must multiply to balance it — the biomechanics of the computer-and-mobile posture, which now includes young adults with text-neck patterns.
  • The flexion moment also loads the posterior elements, capsules and intervertebral discs eccentrically.
  • Pathomechanics: sustained static flexion imposes a constant load on viscoelastic tissue, and creep follows — ligaments and the posterior annulus lengthen under a load they were built to carry only briefly.
  • Recovery lags minutes to hours behind the insult; repeated daily, microstrain accumulates in poorly vascularised tissue.
  • The deep neck flexors (longus capitis and colli) become inhibited while the superficial sternocleidomastoid and upper trapezius take over, so the segment loses its fine local control.
  • Proprioception from fatigued cervical muscles degrades, and the patient now holds posture by passive structures rather than active control.
  • Nociception from ligament, disc and muscle triggers protective spasm and referred pain over the scapula.
  • Nothing here is structurally "specific" — no fracture, no tumour, no radiculopathy — yet the mechanics fully explain the pain, which is precisely why the question says non-specific.
  • Treatment reverses the chain: posture re-education shrinks the moment arm; micro-breaks every 20–30 minutes outlast creep recovery; deep neck flexor training restores the local control the superficial muscles stole.
  • McKenzie's assessment of directional preference — often retraction and extension in postural syndromes — tests which movement re-centres the segment.
  • Conclusion: non-specific neck pain is a load-management problem — the tissues are normal, the dose they receive is not.

Non-specific neck pain is a load-management problem — the tissues are normal, the dose they receive is not.

Sources
  • McKenzie and May, The Cervical and Thoracic Spine: Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy — directional preference and postural syndromes.
  • Levangie and Norkin, Joint Structure and Function — cervical coupled motion and loading.
  • Butler and Jones, Mobilisation of the Nervous System — mechanosensitivity in persistent pain.
