How would you distinguish the mechanics and pathomechanics of the anterior cruciate ligament of the knee?

Full answer →

Contrast how the ACL works when intact with how the knee misbehaves after injury, and close with the clinical tests.

  • What earns marks: "distinguish" is the operative verb. Structure your answer as a two-column comparison — how the ligament behaves intact versus after injury · close with the Lachman test and the pivot-shift mechanism · keep mechanism (how it tore) separate from pathomechanics (how the knee misbehaves afterwards) — that distinction is exactly what the question tests.
  • Structure: the ACL runs from the posteromedial aspect of the lateral femoral condyle down to the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia.
  • That oblique course makes it the primary restraint to anterior tibial translation — it provides about 85 percent of that restraint — and a secondary restraint to rotation and hyperextension.
  • Mechanoreceptors within the ACL feed the CNS (Hilton's law), so ACL injury damages not just stability but reflex control.
  • Two functional bundles: the anteromedial (AM) bundle, taut in flexion, and the posterolateral (PL) bundle, taut in extension. This reciprocal tensioning keeps some fibres loaded throughout the arc.
  • Terminal extension holds the screw-home mechanism: as the knee locks, the tibia externally rotates on the femur, and the ACL winds up and tightens.
  • Pathomechanics — the classic non-contact mechanism: deceleration with the foot planted; the femur internally rotates and adducts over a fixed tibia with the knee near 20 degrees of flexion — valgus collapse.
  • The lateral tibial plateau subluxes anteriorly under the lateral femoral condyle and reduces with a clunk as the knee extends — the pivot shift episode, often remembered by the patient as "it went out and came back".
  • Hyperextension injuries and direct blows, as on a two-wheeler, tear it by other routes.
  • A partial tear leaves the checkrein intact; a complete tear removes anterior restraint, so the quadriceps — pulling up the slope of the tibial plateau — now drags the tibia forward on every attempted extension under load.
  • Consequences: episodes of giving way on pivoting, Indian-style squatting and cross-legged sitting, stairs and uneven roads.
  • Secondary meniscal and chondral damage from repeated subluxation; arthrogenic inhibition weakening the quadriceps; accelerated osteoarthritis; and lost proprioceptive acuity delaying protective reflexes further.
  • The ligament does not heal to functional competence because synovial fluid bathes the torn ends — a one-line justification for why conservative care must build muscle instead of waiting for the ligament.
  • Bedside test: the Lachman test — knee near 30 degrees, anterior drawer of the tibia — is the most sensitive clinical test and should be named first.
  • The pivot-shift test is the most specific though hardest to elicit in a guarded patient; the instrumented arthrometer quantifies the translation.

Mechanism is how it tore; pathomechanics is how the knee misbehaves afterwards.

Sources
  • Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment — Lachman, pivot shift and arthrometer testing.
  • Nordin and Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — ACL restraint and knee kinematics.
  • Donatelli and Wooden, Orthopaedic Physical Therapy — rehabilitation after ACL injury.
810 marks

Explain the mechanism of control of posture.

Full answer →

Structure the answer as input, integration and output — the three sensory streams, the central hierarchy and the postural strategies.

  • What earns marks: structure the answer as input, integration, output — the three words examiners subconsciously tick · add the feed-forward versus feedback distinction — most candidates know only the reactive side, and that one sentence often separates the grades · give the latency hierarchy numbers — spinal 30–50 ms, long loop 100–150 ms, voluntary beyond 200 ms.
  • Definition: postural control is the continuous regulation of the body's centre of mass over its base of support.
  • In standing it is an inverted pendulum that would topple were it not corrected several times a second.
  • The continual small corrections appear as postural sway — sway itself is the measurable proof that control exists; perfectly rigid posture would mean falling, not standing.
  • Distinguish static control (quiet standing) from dynamic control (maintaining equilibrium while moving). Dynamic is the one our MSK and neurological patients struggle with most.
  • Sensory input 1 — visual: supplies a stable external reference, though an inaccurate one when the environment itself moves.
  • Sensory input 2 — vestibular: gives head position and acceleration.
  • Sensory input 3 — somatosensory: pressure on the soles, joint and muscle afferents. It is the dominant stream on firm ground.
  • The CNS weights the three according to context: on a compliant bus floor the somatosensory stream lies, so weighting shifts toward vision and the labyrinth; in the dark, vision is withdrawn and the remainder must cope.
  • This sensory re-weighting is why Romberg's test works: remove vision, and a somatosensory or vestibular deficit is unmasked.
  • Central integration is a hierarchy, not a switchboard: spinal circuits generate the fastest, crudest corrections.
  • The brainstem (vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts) manages the antigravity set against perturbation; the cerebellum calibrates and updates them; the basal ganglia select the strategy; the cortex overrides everything for voluntary, anticipatory control.
  • Latency tells the hierarchy apart: spinal reflexes act within roughly 30–50 milliseconds, long-loop corrections within about 100–150, and voluntary corrections beyond 200. Knowing these orders of magnitude helps interpret delayed balance reactions after stroke.
  • Motor output — anticipatory (feed-forward) postural adjustments prepare the body before movement: lift your arm and the trunk and leg muscles fire before the deltoid does.
  • Reactive (feedback) strategies correct unexpected displacement and scale with the size of the threat: the ankle strategy for small sway on a firm surface, the hip strategy for larger or faster displacement, and a step or a grasping arm when the base itself is exceeded.
  • Older adults, neuropathic feet and post-operative patients drift from ankle toward hip and stepping strategies — the physiological story behind the falls that fill our OPDs.
  • Clinical application: assessment maps to the mechanism — quiet stance with eyes open and closed on firm and compliant surfaces (the clinical sensory-organisation test), limits-of-stability and reaction to external perturbation.
  • Training follows the same map — challenge each sensory stream, then train each strategy under progressively harder conditions.
  • Conclusion: postural control is a closed sensorimotor loop, and every fall we prevent is a loop we repaired.

Sensors, processor, actuators — input, integration, output.

Sources
  • Nordin and Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — standing posture and equilibrium.
  • Guyton and Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — vestibular and motor control hierarchy.
  • O'Sullivan and Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation — balance assessment and training.
910 marks

Discuss the specific pain states and syndromes in musculoskeletal conditions.

Full answer →

Classify pain by mechanism, name each specific state with one discriminating clinical feature, and attach a treatment direction to each syndrome.

  • What earns marks: the word "specific" invites you to be precise — name each state with one discriminating clinical feature (morning stiffness over an hour, dermatomal versus non-dermatomal, claudication distance), and attach a treatment direction to each syndrome · classify pain by mechanism (nociceptive, neuropathic, nociplastic), not by body part · cite gate control theory (Melzack and Wall, 1965) and the neuromatrix (Melzack, 1999) briefly.
  • Nociceptive pain arises from actual or threatened tissue damage — the sprained ankle, the arthritic knee. It is usually proportional, mechanical and well localised.
  • Neuropathic pain arises from a lesion or disease of the nervous system itself — radicular pain, peripheral neuropathy.
  • Nociplastic pain arises from altered nociception without clear tissue or nerve damage: the nervous system has turned its own gain up.
  • Gate control theory (Melzack and Wall, 1965) and Melzack's later neuromatrix (1999) explain how modulation — spinal gating, descending inhibition, brain-body maps — lets the same input hurt differently in different people.
  • Acute pain is protective, time-limited and proportional; it resolves with healing.
  • Chronic pain — beyond three months — outlives healing and, in the International Association for the Study of Pain's framing, has become a disorder in its own right.
  • Inflammatory pain: rest and night pain, morning stiffness over about an hour and swelling — think rheumatoid, not osteoarthritis.
  • Ischaemic pain — claudication — is brought on by walking and relieved by standing still in under ten minutes; it must not be confused with night cramps.
  • Referred pain is felt remote from its source but is non-dermatomal and deep — a hip referring to the knee.
  • Radicular pain follows a dermatome and often has lancinating qualities — a C6 or L5 root.
  • Myofascial pain syndrome: a taut band with a focal trigger point that reproduces the patient's pain on pressure and refers in a characteristic pattern, with a local twitch response on snapping palpation.
  • Fibromyalgia: widespread pain for over three months with fatigue and non-restorative sleep, diagnosed on widespread distribution and symptom severity, commonly accompanied by central sensitisation — allodynia, hyperalgesia and spread beyond any tissue story.
  • Complex regional pain syndrome: disproportionate regional pain with sensory, vasomotor (colour and temperature change), sudomotor (sweating, oedema) and motor or trophic findings, classically after a minor limb injury or immobilisation — a familiar complication of an over-cautiously splinted Colles fracture.
  • Whiplash-associated disorder sits in the same spectrum of persistent MSK pain with sensitisation features.
  • Screen every persistent MSK patient for the pattern: pain disproportionate to findings, spread beyond one region, allodynia, poor response to tissue-directed treatment, and distress (the yellow flags of fear-avoidance and catastrophising). Pain drawings and simple questionnaires document it.
  • Treatment must match the mechanism: nociceptive pain responds to tissue-directed manual therapy and graded loading; neuropathic to pharmacological co-management and desensitisation; nociplastic and syndromic pain to pain neuroscience education, graded activity and exercise in dosages that do not flare the system.
  • Conclusion: we classify pain by mechanism because the mechanism, not the region, dictates the treatment.

Load the tissue OR calm the system.

Sources
  • Melzack R, Wall PD. Pain mechanisms: a new theory. Science 1965.
  • Melzack R. From the gate to the neuromatrix. Pain 1999.
  • Butler and Jones, Mobilisation of the Nervous System — neuropathic and sensitisation states.
  • O'Sullivan and Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation — chronic pain management.

Explain the biophysical effects of heat in adhesive capsulitis.

Full answer →

Describe heat's four biophysical effects, choose a modality deep enough for the capsule, and show the sequence heat-then-stretch with honest dosage and precautions.

  • What earns marks: the marking heart is sequence and honesty — heat first, stretch at the heated barrier, and admit that the stretch, not the heat, produces the range. Claiming heat alone cures a frozen shoulder loses the application marks · name the four effect families — vascular, metabolic, neural, connective tissue · choose the depth — the capsule is deep, so ultrasound or shortwave, not just a hot pack.
  • Raising tissue temperature produces four effect families, each with a physiotherapy use.
  • Vascular effects: vasodilatation and increased blood flow, which improves nutrition and clears metabolites.
  • Metabolic effects: tissue metabolic rate rises roughly 10–13 percent for every degree Celsius — healing and enzymatic repair accelerate.
  • Neural effects: warmth alters nerve conduction and, through the gate mechanism of Melzack and Wall, produces analgesia — large-fibre thermal input closing the gate on small-fibre pain.
  • Muscle spindle and gamma activity quietens, so muscle spasm eases.
  • Connective tissue effects: heated collagen becomes more extensible — and, the effect that matters in this question, elongation produced while the tissue is heated is retained after cooling, where the same stretch applied to cold tissue largely recoils.
  • Superficial agents — hot packs, paraffin wax, infrared — heat skin and subcutaneous tissue to about 1–2 centimetres, warming the shoulder mostly by conduction from the surface.
  • Because the glenohumeral capsule lies deeper, deep heating is traditionally preferred: shortwave diathermy at 27.12 MHz, and therapeutic ultrasound (which heats at the 3–5 centimetre depth of the capsule and can be focused on the coracohumeral ligament and anterior capsule).
  • In the thawing or frozen stage, where the capsule is the contractured tissue, the depth of the agent is the first clinical decision.
  • Adhesive capsulitis is, mechanically, a capsular contracture with pain-guarded loss of external rotation and abduction.
  • Heat is the preparation, not the cure: heat the capsule for 15–20 minutes, then apply grade II–IV mobilisations and sustained stretching to the barrier in the restricted directions — external rotation, abduction, internal rotation behind the back.
  • Heated collagen lengthens under less force, so the same stretch gains more and holds it; analgesia and reduced spasm raise the patient's tolerance, letting you work closer to the true barrier.
  • Controlled comparisons of combined heat-and-stretch programmes report better range gain than stretch alone — Lehmann's classic principle that tissue heated before stretch retains its elongation.
  • Dosage: hot packs 15–20 minutes, adequate towel layers, checking skin in insensate or diabetic patients — a real concern in Indian OPDs where diabetic frozen shoulders abound.
  • Deep agents: ultrasound at about 1 MHz for the deeper capsule, avoiding direct bone contact; shortwave not used over cardiac pacemakers, metal implants, malignancy, pregnancy or acute inflammation with shortwave.
  • Conclusion: heat does not melt a frozen shoulder; it lowers the pain cost and raises the tissue's willingness to be stretched — the stretch and the exercise still do the mechanical work. Prescribed that way, heat is a valuable assistant, not the hero.

Heat before stretch — the stretch, not the heat, produces the range.

Sources
  • Kisner and Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — thermal agents and stretching of connective tissue.
  • O'Sullivan and Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation — physical agents in rehabilitation.
  • Donatelli and Wooden, Orthopaedic Physical Therapy — management of the stiff shoulder.

Q1. Explain the various classification of joints.

Full answer →

Examiners want the two main systems — structural and functional — plus the six synovial subtypes, each with an example and the stability–mobility principle.

  • A joint (articulation) is where two or more bones meet.
  • Joints are grouped by structure (what tissue joins them) and by function (how much they move).
  • Fibrous: sutures, gomphoses, syndesmoses — little or no movement.
  • Cartilaginous: primary (synchondrosis, e.g. growth plate) and secondary (symphysis, e.g. intervertebral disc).
  • Synovial: has a joint cavity with synovial fluid — the most mobile joints.
  • Functionally: synarthrosis (immovable), amphiarthrosis (slightly movable), diarthrosis (freely movable).
  • The two maps agree: fibrous→synarthrosis, cartilaginous→amphiarthrosis, synovial→diarthrosis.
  • Six synovial shapes: plane, hinge, pivot, condyloid, saddle, ball-and-socket.
  • Synovial joints are named by axes of movement: uniaxial, biaxial, multiaxial.
  • Biomechanically, joints are also classed as simple, compound or complex.
  • More mobility means less stability — mobile joints rely on ligaments and muscles.
  • Joint type predicts which diseases and injuries occur (OA, disc degeneration, syndesmotic sprain, AS fusion).

Structure names the tissue, Function names the freedom, and the two maps always agree.

Sources
  • Levangie & Norkin, Joint Structure and Function, 6th ed.
  • Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics, 5th ed.
  • Neumann, Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System, 3rd ed.
  • StatPearls: Anatomy, Joints (2024).
  • Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed.

Q2. Describe how body size influence musculoskeletal disorder.

Full answer →

Examiners want the two mechanisms — mechanical load and metabolic inflammation — with joint-level effects and clinical implications.

  • Body size (BMI, mass, fat distribution) is a major modifiable musculoskeletal risk factor.
  • It acts by two routes: mechanical (more load) and metabolic (fat-driven inflammation).
  • More body mass means bigger ground reaction and muscle forces across joints.
  • Obese gait: wider stride, longer double support, higher knee adduction moment.
  • Knee models show raised cartilage, ligament and muscle stress, worst on the medial plateau.
  • This accelerates medial knee osteoarthritis and varus deformity.
  • At the spine, higher L5–S1 compression and shear raise low back pain and disc degeneration.
  • Fat tissue releases leptin, IL-6, CRP — chronic low-grade inflammation.
  • This explains disease at non-weight-bearing joints (hand, shoulder).
  • Also linked to meniscal tears, plantar heel pain, foot posture change and tendinopathy.
  • Higher muscle co-contraction means earlier fatigue and more falls.
  • Weight reduction lowers joint load, so it is a first-line treatment.

Weight loads the joint; fat inflames it too — so body size hits bone twice.

  • Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics, 5th ed.
  • Adouni et al., Scientific Reports 2024 (obesity knee biomechanics).

Q3. Describe the Kinetic & Kinematic change following Patellectomy.

Full answer →

Examiners want the patella's role as a pulley, then the separate kinematic (movement) and kinetic (force) changes, and the functional result.

  • The patella is a pulley/sesamoid at the knee, not a spare part.
  • It lengthens the quadriceps moment arm and centralises its pull.
  • Patellectomy removes this lever advantage.
  • Kinematic: reduced active extension and a terminal extensor lag.
  • Altered sagittal motion from changed tendon length–tension.
  • Loss of normal patellar tracking in the trochlea.
  • Gait compensations: slower, shorter steps, more hip/ankle work.
  • Kinetic: quadriceps must generate more force for the same moment.
  • Lower peak knee extension torque (about 15–30% loss).
  • Increased tibiofemoral stress without patellofemoral load-sharing.
  • Functional loss in stairs, chair-rising and slopes.
  • If later arthroplasty is needed, outcomes are worse and flexion arc smaller.

Lose the patella, lose the pulley — the quadriceps must work harder for less.

  • Neumann, Kinesiology, 3rd ed.

Q4. Role of equilibrium following Total Hip Replacement.

Full answer →

Examiners want equilibrium explained in two senses — mechanical joint stability and postural balance — and why both matter after THR.

  • "Equilibrium" after THR means balance of forces at the joint and postural balance of the patient.
  • The normal hip is stable via congruence, labrum, capsule, ligaments and abductors.
  • In single-leg stance the abductors balance body weight; joint reaction force is several times body weight.
  • Mechanical equilibrium depends on jump distance and the impingement-free arc.
  • Bigger effective head size increases both — less dislocation risk.
  • Correct cup inclination (~45°) and anteversion (~15°) give a high safety factor.
  • Restoring offset, leg length and abductor tension re-seats the head.
  • Dual-mobility bearings widen the safe arc and reduce dislocation.
  • Postural balance uses ankle and hip strategies.
  • Abductor/extensor strength restores pelvic control (prevents Trendelenburg).
  • Precautions (avoid flexion+adduction+internal rotation) protect the joint while it heals.
  • Good equilibrium means fewer dislocations, better gait and fewer falls.

A hip replacement is only as stable as the balance of forces around it.

  • Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics, 5th ed.
  • Lancet 2026 (Duality dual-mobility RCT).
  • BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders 2022 (hip stability parameters).

Q5. Describe the changes seen in gait following Osteoarthritis knee.

Full answer →

Examiners want gait changes grouped as spatiotemporal, kinematic and kinetic, with the knee adduction moment as the key concept.

  • Knee OA is a mechanically driven disease; gait shows its mechanics.
  • Normal cycle: ~60% stance, ~40% swing.
  • Key measure: the external knee adduction moment (KAM) — surrogate for medial load.
  • In medial OA the limb drifts into varus, shifting load medially.
  • Spatiotemporal: slower speed, shorter steps, more double support, wider stance.
  • Kinematic: less loading-phase flexion, flexion contracture, reduced knee range.
  • Varus thrust during loading.
  • Compensatory trunk forward flexion; altered foot progression angle.
  • Kinetic: raised KAM (both peaks) — the hallmark.
  • Reduced knee flexion and extensor moments; more hip/ankle work.
  • Kinetic conversion (flexion→adduction dominance) appears as early as grade 2.
  • Gait retraining (toe-out/toe-in, wider step) is used to lower the KAM.

The knee shifts load inward, so the patient shifts time, speed and stance to cope.

Q6. Write in detail about various methods of energy conservation following below knee amputation.

Full answer →

Examiners want the reason (lost ankle push-off) plus a structured list of methods: prosthetic, gait, fitness, activity and environment.

  • After below-knee amputation the energy cost of walking rises (often 20–40%).
  • Cause: the prosthetic ankle cannot replace the biological push-off and energy return.
  • The hip and knee of both limbs must work harder.
  • Compensations (vaulting, hip hiking, trunk lean) also cost energy.
  • Prosthetic: light, well-aligned limb with an energy-storing-and-return (ESAR) foot.
  • Consider a microprocessor ankle for slopes/terrain; reduce distal mass.
  • Gait: train smooth, symmetrical walking; avoid wasteful deviations.
  • Walk at a comfortable self-selected speed; relax arms and breathing.
  • Fitness: aerobic conditioning and hip/knee strengthening.
  • Activity: pace the day, cluster tasks, sit to work, use labour-saving aids.
  • Environment: wheelchair/scooter for long trips, home organisation, safe flooring.
  • General: control weight, diabetes and pain — all lower walking cost.

Walk less, walk better, walk lighter — conserve the energy the missing ankle used to give.

Q7. Describe the change in the mechanics seen in lumbar spine following L4, L5 disc prolapse.

Full answer →

Examiners want the normal disc mechanics, the mechanism of prolapse, and the changes at the disc, facets and adjacent segments.

  • Prolapse is commonest at L4–L5 and L5–S1 — the most loaded segments.
  • A healthy disc is pressurised and hydrated; the nucleus shares load hydrostatically.
  • The annulus is weakest posterolaterally.
  • Mechanism: repeated flexion + compression + shear.
  • Failure starts at the annulus–endplate junction; nuclear material extrudes paracentrally.
  • Disc changes: intradiscal pressure falls; annular stress rises.
  • Disc bulge increases — may compress the nerve root.
  • Segmental range of motion decreases; disc height falls.
  • Facet changes: facet joint force rises as load shifts posteriorly.
  • Trunk muscle activity increases to keep equilibrium.
  • Compressive and shear forces rise on all lumbar segments.
  • Adjacent segments take more load — risk of adjacent-segment degeneration.

Flexion loads the back, the disc fails posterolaterally, and the facets inherit the load.

Q8. Describe the various postural deformation seen in Ankylosis Spondylitis.

Examiners want the spinal and pelvic deformations, the compensatory limb changes, and the functional consequences.

  • AS is inflammation of the axial skeleton causing ossification and fusion.
  • The spine becomes rigid and progressively kyphotic.
  • Lost lumbar lordosis — flattens or reverses.
  • Increased thoracic kyphosis — the classic stooped "question-mark" posture.
  • Forward head / cervical hyperextension to keep gaze level.
  • Posterior pelvic tilt (retroversion).
  • Hip flexion contracture folds the trunk forward.
  • Compensatory knee flexion to keep balance.
  • Ankle/foot changes as final compensation.
  • Reduced chest expansion — limits breathing.
  • Reduced global spinal mobility; forward sagittal imbalance.
  • Result: balance loss, falls, rigid-spine fracture risk, altered gait.

The spine stiffens and the body folds forward — the hips and knees try to stand in for it.

Q9. A 60 Years old woman is unable to dorsiflex her left ankle following prolonged crossed leg sitting. Describe the pathological gait.

Examiners want the diagnosis (peroneal nerve palsy / foot drop) and a structured description of swing, stance and overall gait features.

  • This paralyses the ankle dorsiflexors and evertors — "foot drop".
  • The foot hangs in plantarflexion and inversion (gravity + intact plantarflexors).
  • Swing phase: foot drops; knee lifts high (steppage).
  • Hip hiking and circumduction to clear the toes.
  • Foot tends to invert before contact.
  • Stance phase: foot slap at contact; toe-first landing.
  • Reduced heel strike and push-off; frontal-plane instability.
  • Overall: slower speed, shorter steps, asymmetry, higher energy cost.
  • Knee and hip overwork — long-term overload risk.
  • Increased trips and falls, especially on uneven ground.
  • Treat with AFO for clearance, stretching, strengthening and gait retraining.

Foot drop: the toe cannot clear the floor, so the knee lifts high and the foot slaps down.

Q10. Describe the effects of cold on skeletal muscle performance.

Full answer →

Examiners want the acute performance effects (force, power, endurance, control) plus the recovery and adaptation effects, with clinical implications.

  • Cold lowers muscle temperature; contraction is temperature-sensitive.
  • It slows nerve conduction and calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
  • Result: less maximal force and strength.
  • Less power and slower rate of force development.
  • Slower contraction and relaxation.
  • Reduced endurance / fatigue resistance.
  • Impaired proprioception, balance and coordination.
  • Increased muscle–tendon stiffness — affects flexibility.
  • Reliably reduces DOMS (soreness) — the main benefit.
  • May reduce some inflammatory markers (mixed evidence).
  • Does not restore strength after exercise.
  • Repeated post-training cooling can blunt strength and hypertrophy gains.

Cold slows the muscle: less force, less speed, less endurance — but less pain.

Q1. Describe the effects of strength training on the neuromuscular system.

Full answer →

Name the neural and muscular changes that strength training produces, and separate early neural gains from later muscle growth.

  • Strength training makes the nervous system work better first, then the muscle gets bigger.
  • The brain sends stronger signals to the muscle (more voluntary drive).
  • More motor units switch on, and they switch on at a lower threshold.
  • Each motor unit fires faster (higher discharge rate).
  • Firing of motor units becomes better synchronised.
  • Inhibition in the motor cortex decreases, so output increases.
  • Muscles co-contract less, so movement is more efficient.
  • Later, muscle fibres thicken (hypertrophy) and cross-sectional area grows.
  • Fast fibres shift from type IIx to type IIa.
  • Pennation angle and fascicle length increase.
  • Tendons get stiffer and store more elastic energy.
  • Result: more strength and power, better balance and joint stability.
  • Bone also gets stronger, reducing injury risk.

Train the nerve first, the muscle later — early strength is a learned skill.

Q2. Describe the changes seen in the neuromuscular system following prolonged bed rest due to spinal fracture.

Full answer →

List the muscle, motor-unit, neuromuscular-junction and sensorimotor changes after prolonged bed rest, and note the rehabilitation implication.

  • Bed rest after a spinal fracture unloads the body and switches off muscle activity.
  • Muscles shrink (atrophy), especially antigravity and back muscles.
  • Strength falls even faster than muscle size.
  • Type II (fast) fibres are lost most, so power drops.
  • Motor units fire more slowly and their potentials change.
  • Voluntary activation falls — the brain cannot fully switch the muscle on.
  • The neuromuscular junction becomes unstable (jitter, agrin fragment rises).
  • Proprioception and balance are impaired.
  • Joints can stiffen into contracture.
  • Bone density falls and the heart and circulation decondition.
  • Gait becomes slow and unsteady, with high fall risk.
  • Recovery needs early loading, electrical stimulation and task practice.

Disuse costs strength faster than it costs muscle — the nervous system switches off first.

Sources
  • Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology.
  • Sarto et al., J Physiol 2025 (21 days bed rest and motor units).
  • Kortebein et al., JAMA 2007 (10 days bed rest in older adults).
310 marks

Q3. Elaborate the Kinetics & Kinematics of the wrist joint following carpal tunnel syndrome.

Full answer →

Give the kinematic (motion) and kinetic (pressure/force) changes in the wrist in carpal tunnel syndrome.

  • The carpal tunnel is a narrow space holding the median nerve and tendons.
  • Kinematics = how things move; kinetics = forces and pressure.
  • Normally the nerve and tendons glide smoothly.
  • In CTS the nerve glides less (reduced longitudinal mobility).
  • The tendon sheath becomes stiff, so tendons glide poorly.
  • Friction between tendon and sheath (shear strain) increases.
  • Pressure inside the tunnel is raised, worst at wrist flexion and extension.
  • The nerve becomes flattened and enlarged on ultrasound.
  • High pressure reduces blood flow to the nerve.
  • Symptoms are worst with gripping and end-range postures.
  • Keeping the wrist neutral and doing gliding exercises helps.
  • Radioulnar compression can open the tunnel and restore glide.

The carpal tunnel is a crowded room — bend the wrist and the door gets tighter.

Sources
  • Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System.
  • Festen-Schrier & Amadio, J Biomech 2023 (carpal tunnel mechanics).
  • Keir & Wells, Clin Biomech 1999 (tendon geometry in the tunnel).
410 marks

Q4. Describe various methods to improve efficiency of movement following soft tissue injury.

Full answer →

List practical methods that restore efficient movement after soft tissue injury, across mobility, strength, control, balance and function.

  • Soft tissue injury makes movement inefficient and tiring.
  • First restore range of motion: stretching and mobilisation.
  • Reduce scar stiffness with soft-tissue and scar mobilisation.
  • Rebuild strength, especially with eccentric (lengthening) exercise.
  • Use blood-flow-restriction training if heavy loads are not tolerated.
  • Re-train motor control so the right muscles work at the right time.
  • Use biofeedback and mirror therapy to correct movement.
  • Retrain muscle synergies and reduce compensatory patterns.
  • Restore proprioception and balance (static to dynamic).
  • Re-educate gait and then sport- or work-specific tasks.
  • Manage load and progress activity gradually to avoid re-injury.
  • Use pain education and taping to allow pain-free practice.

Get the tissue moving, get it strong, get the brain coordinating it again.

Sources
  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise.
  • van Dyk et al., Br J Sports Med 2019 (Nordic hamstring exercise).
  • O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation.
510 marks

Q5. Describe the biomechanical changes seen in mobility of lower limbs in people with tendo-Achilles tightness.

Full answer →

Describe how reduced ankle dorsiflexion from a tight Achilles changes mechanics at the ankle, knee, hip and pelvis during walking.

  • A tight Achilles means the ankle cannot bend up (reduced dorsiflexion).
  • The foot compensates by rolling in (pronation).
  • The heel lifts early during walking.
  • Push-off power at the ankle is reduced.
  • The knee does not straighten fully at midstance.
  • Knee and ankle forces (moments) increase.
  • The hip flexes more and extends less.
  • The pelvis tilts forward (anterior tilt).
  • The lower back arches more (increased lordosis).
  • Step and stride length get shorter and walking slows.
  • Shock absorption is poorer and energy cost rises.
  • Stretching the calf can improve both ankle and upper mechanics.

A tight Achilles pulls the whole chain — the ankle pays, the knee, hip and back borrow.

Sources
  • Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System.
  • Levangie & Norkin, Joint Structure and Function.
  • Gastrocnemius tightness affects hip and pelvic movement in gait, Biomed Eng Appl Basis Commun 2020.
610 marks

Q6. Describe how soft tissue injuries affect movements.

Full answer →

Explain the chain from tissue injury to altered movement: pain and inhibition, loss of range and force, changed control and compensation.

  • Soft tissue injury changes movement in several linked ways.
  • Pain and swelling limit movement straight away.
  • Pain inhibits muscles, so they cannot switch on fully (weakness).
  • Scar tissue makes the injured tissue stiffer and less stretchy.
  • This reduces range of motion and can cause contracture.
  • Proprioception (position sense) is impaired.
  • Muscle activation timing and order change.
  • The person co-contracts muscles protectively.
  • They compensate by shifting load to other joints.
  • This changes joint angles and forces elsewhere.
  • Movement becomes less efficient and costs more energy.
  • Treatment: control pain, restore range, rebuild strength, retrain control.

Injury hurts, hurts inhibit, inhibition changes how you move — and that change outlasts the pain.

Sources
  • O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation.
  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise.
  • Fyfe et al., J Electromyogr Kinesiol 2013 (neuromuscular inhibition).
710 marks

Q7. Describe the mechanics of the shoulder following Deltoid injury.

Full answer →

Explain the deltoid's role, the force couples, and what happens mechanically when the deltoid is injured.

  • The deltoid is the shoulder's main lifting (abduction) muscle.
  • It works with the rotator cuff in force couples.
  • Deltoid plus supraspinatus push the ball into the socket during abduction.
  • The cuff also stops the ball sliding upwards.
  • Scapular rhythm keeps the socket moving with the arm.
  • If the deltoid is torn or paralysed, abduction becomes weak.
  • The force couple is lost, so the ball drifts upward.
  • Joint reaction forces change, stressing the socket.
  • The shoulder blade compensates with a shrug.
  • If the nerve is damaged, there is also numbness.
  • Treatment re-trains deltoid and cuff together.
  • The mover and the stabiliser must work as a team.

Deltoid moves the arm, cuff steers the head — injure the mover and the head drifts up.

Sources
  • Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System.
  • Levangie & Norkin, Joint Structure and Function.
  • Lee et al., Am J Sports Med 2018 (deltoid and cuff during abduction).
810 marks

Q8. Describe various changes in lower cross syndrome.

Full answer →

State the tight and weak muscles in lower cross syndrome and the postural and lumbopelvic changes they cause.

  • Lower cross syndrome is a pattern of tight and weak muscles around the hips and lower back.
  • Tight: hip flexors (front of hip).
  • Tight: lower-back (lumbar extensor) muscles.
  • Weak: tummy (abdominal) muscles.
  • Weak: buttock (gluteal) muscles.
  • This tilts the pelvis forward (anterior pelvic tilt).
  • The lower back arches more (hyperlordosis).
  • The chest and upper back may round to compensate.
  • Lumbopelvic rhythm changes, loading the discs and facets.
  • Gluteal activation is delayed; hamstrings may substitute.
  • Core stability and endurance are reduced.
  • Treatment: stretch tight muscles, strengthen weak ones, then integrate.

Crossed at the hips: front hip flexors tight with weak tummy, back extensors tight with weak bottom.

Sources
  • Page, Frank & Lardner, Assessment and Treatment of Muscle Imbalance: The Janda Approach.
  • Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment.
  • NASM-based corrective exercises in lower cross syndrome, PLoS One 2026.
910 marks

Q9. A 30 year old man comes with a history of pelvic fracture following which he is unable to stabilize his right knee. Describe the pathological gait.

Full answer →

Give a systematic analysis of the gait: mechanisms, spatiotemporal, kinematic, kinetic findings and management.

  • A pelvic fracture can weaken the hip abductors and the quadriceps.
  • Weak hip abductors cause the opposite hip to drop (Trendelenburg).
  • The trunk may lurch over the standing leg (Duchenne limp).
  • Weak quadriceps make the knee give way or over-flex.
  • Walking speed, step length and cadence all reduce.
  • Support time on the affected leg is shorter.
  • The hip abducts and extends less on that side.
  • Hip abduction and extension forces (moments) are lower.
  • Pelvic drop increases loading on the inner (medial) knee.
  • Shock absorption is poor and energy cost is high.
  • Treatment: strengthen abductors and quadriceps, retrain gait and balance.
  • A cane in the opposite hand reduces the load on the hip.

Weak abductors drop the opposite hip; weak quads make the knee give way — two faults, one limp.

Sources
  • Levangie & Norkin, Joint Structure and Function.
  • Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment.
  • Kubota et al., Gait Posture 2013 (gait after pelvic ring fracture).
1010 marks

Q10. Write in detail about the various methods of assessing subjects.

Full answer →

Outline the main categories of assessment methods and the measurement properties a good method must have.

  • Assessment identifies the problem, guides treatment and measures progress.
  • Start with the history and pain scales.
  • Observe posture, gait, swelling and alignment.
  • Palpate for tenderness, warmth and tone.
  • Measure range of motion with a goniometer or inclinometer.
  • Test muscle strength with manual testing or a dynamometer.
  • Test nerves: sensation, power, reflexes, and EMG if needed.
  • Test proprioception and joint position sense.
  • Analyse gait and balance (observation, sensors, Timed Up and Go).
  • Use outcome questionnaires (DASH, LEFS, ODI).
  • Use special tests and imaging when indicated.
  • A good method must be reliable, valid and responsive.

Assess the person, not just the joint — impairment, activity and participation.

Sources
  • Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment.
  • Norkin & White, Measurement of Joint Motion.
  • Lam et al., J NeuroEng Rehabil 2023 (markerless motion capture).

Glossary of difficult terms (76)

Dotted-underlined words also show the definition on hover or tap.

  • allodynia — Pain from a stimulus that is not normally painful.
  • arthrogenic muscle inhibition — Reflex weakness of a muscle caused by a problem inside its joint (abbreviated AMI).
  • arthrokinematics — The small gliding, rolling and spinning movements between joint surfaces.
  • atrophy — Wasting or shrinking of muscle or tissue.
  • biomechanics — The study of the mechanical laws relating to the movement of living organisms.
  • biopsychosocial — An approach that considers biological, psychological and social factors together.
  • capsular pattern — The characteristic order in which a joint loses range when the whole capsule is involved.
  • capsule — The fibrous sleeve that surrounds and stabilises a joint.
  • catastrophising — Interpreting pain in an exaggerated, worst-case way.
  • central sensitisation — Increased excitability of the central nervous system that makes normal inputs feel painful.
  • collagen — The main structural protein in tendon, ligament, skin and bone.
  • concentric — Muscle work while it shortens under load (the lifting phase).
  • contracture — A permanent tightening or shortening of tissue that restricts movement.
  • contraindication — A condition that makes a treatment unsafe or inadvisable.
  • creep — Slow progressive lengthening of tissue under a constant sustained load over time.
  • cryotherapy — Treatment using cold.
  • dermatome — The area of skin supplied by a single spinal nerve root.
  • dorsal horn — The rear part of the spinal cord's grey matter where sensory nerves first relay pain signals.
  • dorsiflexion — Bending the ankle or wrist so the angle at the front decreases (e.g. lifting the toes up).
  • eccentric — Muscle work while it lengthens under load (the lowering phase).
  • effleurage — A smooth gliding massage stroke.
  • effusion — Fluid collecting inside a joint.
  • electrotherapy — Treatment using electrical currents or electromagnetic energy.
  • end-feel — The quality of resistance felt at the very end of a joint's movement, used to judge what limits it.
  • eversion — Turning the sole of the foot outward.
  • fear-avoidance — Avoiding activity because of fear of pain, which over time worsens disability.
  • gait — The manner of walking.
  • gate control theory — The idea that non-painful input (rubbing, TENS) can 'close a gate' in the spinal cord and reduce pain.
  • golgi tendon organ — A sensor in tendon that detects tension and helps regulate muscle force.
  • goniometry — Measuring joint angles with a goniometer.
  • hyperalgesia — An increased sensitivity to pain.
  • hypermobility — Excessive movement at a joint, usually from lax or torn ligaments.
  • hypertrophy — An increase in muscle or tissue size.
  • hypomobility — Reduced movement at a joint, usually from tight or stiff tissue.
  • ICF — The International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health.
  • inflammation — The body's protective response to injury - heat, redness, swelling and pain.
  • inversion — Turning the sole of the foot inward.
  • isometric — A muscle contraction with no change in length (no joint movement).
  • joint play — The small accessory movement available at a joint beyond voluntary control.
  • kinesiophobia — Fear of movement or of re-injury.
  • laser therapy — Red/near-infrared light therapy that stimulates cell repair (photobiomodulation).
  • ligament — Strong fibrous tissue that connects bone to bone and stabilises a joint.
  • manipulation — A quick, small thrust applied to a joint by a clinician.
  • manual muscle testing — Grading a muscle's strength by resisting a voluntary contraction (abbreviated MMT).
  • mechanoreceptors — Sensory receptors that detect mechanical stimuli such as touch, pressure and joint position.
  • mechanotransduction — How cells turn mechanical load into chemical signals that change the tissue.
  • moment arm — The perpendicular distance from a force to the joint axis; a longer moment arm produces more torque.
  • muscle spindle — A stretch sensor inside muscle that helps control posture and movement.
  • myofascial — Relating to muscle and its surrounding fascia.
  • myotome — The group of muscles supplied by a single spinal nerve root.
  • neurodynamic — Relating to the mechanical and physiological function of nerves; neural mobilisation treats nerve sensitivity.
  • nociceptive — Relating to the detection of painful stimuli.
  • nociceptor — A sensory nerve ending that detects painful or tissue-damaging stimuli.
  • oedema — Swelling caused by fluid trapped in the tissues.
  • osteokinematics — The visible movements of bones at a joint, such as flexion and extension.
  • outcome measure — A standardised tool used to measure a patient's status or change over time.
  • palpation — Examining the body by touch to feel for tenderness, swelling or tissue change.
  • plantarflexion — Pointing the foot downward, as when standing on tiptoe.
  • posture — The position of the body and its parts relative to gravity.
  • precaution — A situation requiring extra care during treatment.
  • proprioception — The sense of body and joint position and movement.
  • proprioceptive — Relating to the body's sense of position and movement.
  • radiculopathy — A nerve-root problem causing pain, numbness or weakness along a limb.
  • range of motion — How far a joint can move (abbreviated ROM).
  • red flag — A sign or symptom suggesting serious pathology that needs medical referral.
  • ROM — Short for range of motion - how far a joint can move.
  • sensitivity — A test's ability to correctly identify people who have the condition.
  • special test — A clinical test used to confirm or rule out a specific structure or condition.
  • specificity — A test's ability to correctly identify people who do not have the condition.
  • synovial — Relating to the fluid-filled lining of a joint.
  • tendinopathy — A tendon disorder causing pain and reduced function.
  • tendon — Strong fibrous tissue that attaches muscle to bone.
  • TENS — Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation - a mild current passed through the skin to relieve pain.
  • torque — A turning force around an axis - the product of force and its moment arm.
  • traction — A gentle pulling force applied to a joint or the spine to relieve pressure.
  • trigger point — A tender, tight knot in a muscle that can refer pain elsewhere.
